Notable spaceflight events during the year 2026.

== Overview ==

=== Astronomy and astrophysics ===
On 11 January, [[NASA]] launched the [[Pandora (spacecraft)|Pandora]] small space telescope to study [[exoplanet]] atmospheres.<ref>{{Cite web |title=NASA Pandora Mission--with operations based at U of A--featured in TIME Magazine {{!}} Steward Observatory |url=https://astro.arizona.edu/news/nasa-pandora-mission-operations-based-u-featured-time-magazine |access-date=2026-01-03 |website=astro.arizona.edu}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Apai |first=Daniel |date=2025-11-08 |title=Hello, Pandora! Goodbye, Pandora! |url=https://distantearths.com/seeing-pandora-for-the-first-time-and-last-time/ |access-date=2026-01-03 |website=Distant Earths |language=en-US}}</ref> The [[List of spaceflight launches in January–March 2026#SpXTwilight|same Falcon 9 flight]] also carried two [[CubeSat]]-type space telescopes by NASA: [[SPARCS]] and [[BlackCAT]], alongside other payloads.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2026-01-08 |title=A cereal-box-sized space telescope heads for the stars {{!}} ASU News |url=https://news.asu.edu/20260108-science-and-technology-asu-built-cubesat-sparcs-spacex-launch-weekend |access-date=2026-01-10 |website=news.asu.edu |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=NASA's Pandora Satellite, CubeSats to Explore Exoplanets, Beyond |url=https://www.ipac.caltech.edu/news/406 |access-date=2026-01-10 |website=IPAC}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Wall |first1=Mike |title=Watch SpaceX launch NASA's Pandora exoplanet-studying satellite on Jan. 11 |url=https://www.space.com/space-exploration/launches-spacecraft/watch-spacex-launch-nasas-pandora-exoplanet-studying-satellite-on-jan-11 |access-date=11 January 2026 |work=Space |date=10 January 2026 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Foust |first=Jeff |date=2026-01-11 |title=NASA astrophysics, commercial satellites launch on SpaceX rideshare mission |url=https://spacenews.com/nasa-astrophysics-commercial-satellites-launch-on-spacex-rideshare-mission/ |access-date=2026-01-11 |work=SpaceNews |language=en-US}}</ref> Pandora completed its commissioning phase and started scientific observations in August 2026.<ref>{{Cite web |title=NASA's Pandora Mission Begins Study of Exoplanets, Host Stars |url=https://www.ipac.caltech.edu/news/pandora-mission-begins-study |access-date=2026-08-26 |website=IPAC}}</ref>

In February, [[European Space Agency|ESA]]'s experimental [[heliophysics]] mission [[PROBA-3]] suffered an anomaly which led to the loss of contact with one of the two spacecraft.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Parsonson |first=Andrew |date=2026-03-06 |title=ESA Has Lost Contact With One of Its PROBA-3 Spacecraft |url=https://europeanspaceflight.com/esa-has-lost-contact-with-one-of-its-proba-3-spacecraft/ |access-date=2026-03-07 |website=European Spaceflight |language=en-US}}</ref> Contact was re-established with PROBA-3 in March<ref>{{Cite web |last=Wall |first=Mike |date=2026-03-19 |title='A great relief!' Europe's Proba-3 solar-eclipse satellite phones home after a month of silence |url=https://www.space.com/space-exploration/missions/a-great-relief-europes-proba-3-solar-eclipse-satellite-phones-home-after-a-month-of-silence |access-date=2026-03-20 |website=Space |language=en}}</ref> and the spacecraft resumed observations in July.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Total Solar Eclipse 2026 - Proba-3 - Cosmos |url=https://www.cosmos.esa.int/web/proba-3/total-solar-eclipse-2026 |access-date=2026-08-03 |website=Proba-3 |language=en-GB}}</ref>

On 19 May, [[European Space Agency|ESA]] and [[Chinese Academy of Sciences|CAS]] launched their joint [[heliophysics]] mission [[SMILE (spacecraft)|SMILE]] to study the dynamic interaction between solar wind and Earth's magnetosphere.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Jones |first=Andrew |date=2026-05-19 |title=ESA-China SMILE mission lifts off to deliver first global images of Earth's magnetosphere |url=https://spacenews.com/esa-china-smile-mission-lifts-off-to-deliver-first-global-images-of-earths-magnetosphere/ |access-date=2026-05-19 |work=SpaceNews |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Smile lifts off on quest to reveal Earth's invisible shield against the solar wind |url=https://www.esa.int/Science_Exploration/Space_Science/Smile/Smile_lifts_off_on_quest_to_reveal_Earth_s_invisible_shield_against_the_solar_wind |access-date=2026-05-19 |website=www.esa.int |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Wall |first=Mike |date=2026-05-18 |title=Vega C rocket launches European-Chinese space weather satellite to orbit |url=https://www.space.com/space-exploration/launches-spacecraft/european-chinese-space-weather-mission-smile-launch |access-date=2026-05-19 |website=Space |language=en}}</ref> The spacecraft reached its final science orbit on 20 June<ref>{{Cite web |title=Smile reaches science orbit |url=https://www.esa.int/ESA_Multimedia/Images/2026/06/Smile_reaches_science_orbit |access-date=2026-06-25 |website=www.esa.int |language=en}}</ref> and started science observations on 23 September.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Science begins for Smile |url=https://www.esa.int/Science_Exploration/Space_Science/Smile/Science_begins_for_Smile |access-date=2026-09-30 |website=www.esa.int |language=en}}</ref>

On 3 July, Katalyst Space Technologies launched the [[Swift boost mission]] under a contract from NASA to save the [[Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory]] by boosting it to a higher orbit.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2026-07-03 |title=Nasa launches robot to save Swift telescope falling to Earth |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/c0ry4xx7rk8o |access-date=2026-07-03 |website=www.bbc.com |language=en-GB}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2026-07-03 |title=Mission To Boost NASA's Swift Launches From Marshall Islands - NASA Science |url=https://science.nasa.gov/blogs/swift/2026/07/03/mission-to-boost-nasas-swift-launches-from-marshall-islands/ |access-date=2026-07-03 |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2026-06-29 |title=NASA launches rescue mission to save the Swift space telescope |url=https://www.space.com/space-exploration/launches-spacecraft/nasa-successfully-launches-rescue-mission-to-save-swift-space-telescope-from-burning-up-in-earths-atmosphere |access-date=2026-07-03 |website=Space |language=en}}</ref> They used the LINK spacecraft launched on a [[Northrop Grumman]] [[Pegasus XL]] aircraft-borne rocket. This was the final launch of Pegasus XL and means there are no remaining active orbital [[Air-launch-to-orbit|air launch]] systems anywhere in the world.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2026-04-17 |title=Testing Begins for Katalyst-NASA Swift Boost Mission - NASA Science |url=https://science.nasa.gov/blogs/swift/2026/04/17/testing-begins-for-katalyst-nasa-swift-boost-mission/ |access-date=2026-04-20 |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last1=Foust |first1=Jeff |title=Katalyst selects Pegasus to launch Swift reboost mission |url=https://spacenews.com/katalyst-selects-pegasus-to-launch-swift-reboost-mission/ |access-date=2025-11-21 |website=spacenews.com |date=19 November 2025 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2026-04-17 |title=NASA and Katalyst Begin Testing for Swift Satellite Boost Mission - Greenbelt Today |url=https://nationaltoday.com/us/md/greenbelt/news/2026/04/17/nasa-and-katalyst-begin-testing-for-swift-satellite-boost-mission/ |access-date=2026-04-20 |website=National Today |language=en-US}}</ref> Once in orbit, LINK suffered a series of technical issues, and on 19&nbsp;August, NASA cancelled the rescue efforts.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Dinner |first=Josh |date=2026-08-19 |title=Private mission to save NASA's Swift space telescope fails |url=https://www.space.com/space-exploration/missions/private-mission-to-save-nasas-swift-space-telescope-fails |access-date=2026-08-19 |website=Space.com |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=No-Go for Katalyst's Reboost of NASA's Swift Observatory |url=https://spacepolicyonline.com/news/no-go-for-katalysts-reboost-of-nasas-swift-observatory/ |access-date=2026-08-19 |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Foust |first=Jeff |date=2026-08-19 |title=Katalyst Space and NASA abandon plans for Swift reboost |url=https://spacenews.com/katalyst-space-and-nasa-abandon-plans-for-swift-reboost/ |access-date=2026-08-19 |website=SpaceNews |language=en-US}}</ref>

On 30 August, NASA launched the [[Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope]], an infrared space telescope for [[cosmology]] and search for [[Exoplanet|exoplanets]], to Sun-Earth [[Lagrange point|Lagrange Point]] 2.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope has launched |url=https://www.planetary.org/articles/the-nancy-grace-roman-space-telescope-launch |access-date=2026-08-30 |website=The Planetary Society |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Cartier |first=Kimberly M. S. |date=2026-08-30 |title=Roman Telescope Begins Quest to Reveal Evolving Universe |url=https://eos.org/research-and-developments/roman-telescope-begins-quest-to-reveal-evolving-universe |access-date=2026-08-30 |website=Eos |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Warren |first=Haygen |date=2026-08-29 |title=NASA, SpaceX successfully launch the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope from Florida |url=https://www.nasaspaceflight.com/2026/08/roman-telescope-launch/ |access-date=2026-08-30 |website=NASASpaceFlight.com |language=en-US}}</ref>

In 2026, [[NASA]] plans to launch the [[Sun Radio Interferometer Space Experiment|SunRISE]] mission consisting of six [[CubeSat|CubeSats]] for studying [[Solar phenomena|solar activity]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=SunRISE |url=https://www.jpl.nasa.gov/missions/sun-radio-interferometer-space-experiment/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251216164242/https://www.jpl.nasa.gov/missions/sun-radio-interferometer-space-experiment/ |archive-date=2025-12-16 |access-date=2026-01-03 |website=NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Priebe |first=Melissa F. |date=2025-10-29 |title=Launch Vehicle Selected for SunRISE Mission |url=https://clasp.engin.umich.edu/2025/10/29/launch-vehicle-selected-for-sunrise-mission/ |access-date=2026-01-03 |website=Climate and Space Sciences and Engineering |language=en-US}}</ref>

[[Taiwan]] plans to launch its first space telescope, the [[The Gamma-ray Transients Monitor|Gamma-ray Transients Monitor (GTM)]], as a secondary payload on the [[Formosat-8]]B satellite, in December.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Chang |first1=Hao-Min |last2=Chang |first2=Hsiang-Kuang |last3=Team |first3=G. T. M. |date=2025-06-27 |title=Gamma-ray Transients Monitor (GTM) onboard Formosat-8B |url=https://baas.aas.org/pub/2025n4i240p22/release/1 |journal=Bulletin of the AAS |language=en |volume=57 |issue=4 |issn=2330-9458}}</ref>

=== Solar system exploration ===
On 15 May, [[NASA]]'s [[Psyche (spacecraft)|Psyche spacecraft]] performed a [[gravity assist]] maneuver at [[Mars]], flying 4,500 km from the planet's surface on its way to the asteroid [[16 Psyche|Psyche]].<ref>{{Cite web |author1=Sharmila Kuthunur |date=2026-05-16 |title=NASA's Psyche spacecraft is flying to a metal asteroid. So, why did it just visit Mars? |url=https://www.space.com/space-exploration/asteroid-comet-missions/nasas-psyche-spacecraft-is-flying-to-a-metal-asteroid-so-why-did-it-just-visit-mars |access-date=2026-05-18 |website=Space |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Moon |first=Mariella |date=2026-05-16 |title=NASA's Psyche spacecraft just got an assist from Mars on the way to its asteroid namesake |url=https://www.engadget.com/2174433/nasa-psyche-spacecraft-got-an-assist-from-mars-on-way-to-asteroid/ |access-date=2026-05-18 |website=Engadget |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2026-05-15 |title=Psyche: Nasa spacecraft captures rare pic of Mars on way to asteroid |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/newsround/articles/cq5pjw80e9jo |access-date=2026-05-18 |website=BBC Newsround |language=en-GB}}</ref>

National Space Administration|CNSA]]'s [[Tianwen-2]] arrived at the [[near-Earth asteroid]] [[469219 Kamoʻoalewa|Kamoʻoalewa]], a [[quasi-satellite]] of Earth, for sample collection<ref>{{Cite web |title=China's Tianwen-2 mission has (probably) arrived at a quasi-moon of… |url=https://www.planetary.org/articles/chinas-tianwen-2-mission-has-probably-arrived-at-a-quasi-moon-of-earth near-Earth asteroid [[98943 Torifune|Torifune]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Flyby of asteroid Torifune on July 5, 2026 {{!}} ISAS |url=https://www.isas.jaxa.jp/en/topics/004151.html |access-date=2025-12-31 The joint [[European Space Agency|ESA]]-[[JAXA]] mission [[BepiColombo]] is expected to enter orbit around [[Mercury (planet)|Mercury]] in late 2026.<ref>{{Cite web |last= |title=BepiColombo mission will start to unpick Mercury's secrets in 2026 |url=https://www.newscientist.com/article/2508106-bepicolombo-mission-will-start-to-unpick-mercurys-secrets-in-2026/ |access-date=2025-12-31 |website=New Scientist |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=BepiColombo {{!}} CNES |url=https://cnes.fr/en/projects/bepicolombo |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250720025749/https://cnes.fr/en/projects/bepicolombo |archive-date=2025-07-20 |access-date=2025-12-31 |website=cnes.fr |language=en}}</ref> The arrival operations began on 3&nbsp;September 2026 with the separation of the propulsion module from the remaining spacecraft.<ref>{{Cite web |last=missions." |first=Josh Dinner "Arriving to Mercury is not as simple as other |date=2026-09-03 |title='A new mission starting today': 8 years after launch, BepiColombo begins Mercury arrival |url=https://www.space.com/space-exploration/missions/a-new-mission-starting-today-8-years-after-launch-bepicolombo-begins-mercury-arrival |access-date=2026-09-03 |website=Space |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Latest updates: BepiColombo's arrival at Mercury |url=https://www.esa.int/Science_Exploration/Space_Science/BepiColombo/Latest_updates_BepiColombo_s_arrival_at_Mercury |access-date=2026-09-03 |website=www.esa.int |language=en}}</ref>

On 20 October, [[JAXA]] launched the [[Martian Moons eXploration|Martian Moons eXploration (MMX)]] mission to the moons of [[Mars]] with the aim of bringing back the first samples from [[Phobos (moon)|Phobos]]. The mission also carries the European Phobos rover [[Idefix (rover)|Idefix]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Clark |first=Stephen |date=2026-10-20 |title=Japan launches mission to bring home a piece of the Martian moon Phobos |url=https://arstechnica.com/space/2026/10/japan-launches-mission-to-bring-home-a-piece-of-the-martian-moon-phobos/ |access-date=2026-10-20 |website=Ars Technica |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Dickinson |first=David |date=2026-10-20 |title=Japan Launches the Martian Moons Exploration Mission |url=https://skyandtelescope.org/astronomy-news/japan-launches-the-martian-moons-exploration-mission/ |access-date=2026-10-20 |website=Sky & Telescope |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=McCurry |first=Justin |date=2026-10-19 |title=‘Once-in-a-lifetime chance’: Japan launches historic mission to collect rocks from Mars’s moon Phobos |url=https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/oct/20/japan-mars-moon-mission-phobos-collect-rocks |access-date=2026-10-20 |work=The Guardian |language=en-GB |issn=0261-3077}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Marín |first=Daniel |date=2026-10-19 |title=Lanzamiento de la sonda MMX con el rover europeo IDEFIX para traer muestras de Fobos |url=https://danielmarin.naukas.com/2026/10/20/lanzamiento-de-la-sonda-mmx-con-el-rover-europeo-idefix-para-traer-muestras-de-fobos/ |access-date=2026-10-20 |website=Eureka |language=es}}</ref>

[[European Space Agency|ESA]]'s [[Hera (space mission)|Hera]] spacecraft is expected to arrive at the double asteroid [[65803 Didymos|Didymos]] in November.<ref>{{Cite web |title=ESA's Hera targets early arrival at Didymos asteroids |url=https://www.esa.int/Space_Safety/Hera/ESA_s_Hera_targets_early_arrival_at_Didymos_asteroids |access-date=2025-12-31 |website=www.esa.int |language=en}}</ref>

On 15 November, [[Voyager 1]] will be one [[light-day]] from Earth.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2025-11-25 |title=Voyager 1 is almost one light-day from Earth |url=https://www.popsci.com/science/voyager-one-light-day-earth/ |access-date=2026-08-12 |website=PopSci }}</ref>

In November, [[NASA]]'s twin [[ESCAPADE]] spacecraft are expected to perform a [[gravity assist]] maneuver at Earth that will send them towards Mars.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Studio |first=NASA Scientific Visualization |date=2025-11-13 |title=NASA Scientific Visualization Studio {{!}} ESCAPADE Trajectory Animations |url=https://svs.gsfc.nasa.gov/14915/ |access-date=2025-12-31 |website=NASA Scientific Visualization Studio |language=english}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Aeromorning |date=2025-11-14 |title=Rocket Lab-Built Twin Spacecraft Begin Mars Journey for NASA and UC Berkeley's ESCAPADE Mission |url=https://aeromorning.com/en/rocket-lab-built-twin-spacecraft-begin-mars-journey-for-nasa-and-uc-berkeleys-escapade-mission/ |access-date=2025-12-31 |website=AeroMorning |language=en-US}}</ref>

On 24 December, [[European Space Agency|ESA]]'s [[Solar Orbiter]] is expected to perform its 5th [[Venus]] flyby, which will tilt its heliocentric orbit from 17° to 24°.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Solar Orbiter gets world-first views of the Sun's poles |url=https://www.esa.int/Science_Exploration/Space_Science/Solar_Orbiter/Solar_Orbiter_gets_world-first_views_of_the_Sun_s_poles |access-date=2025-12-31 |website=www.esa.int |language=en}}</ref>

=== Lunar exploration ===

No earlier than November,<ref>{{Cite web |date=2026-09-15 |title=NASA expects one lunar launch this year, Moon Base manager says |url=https://aerospaceamerica.aiaa.org/nasa-expects-one-lunar-launch-this-year-moon-base-manager-says/ |access-date=2026-09-26 |website=Aerospace America |language=en-US}}</ref> [[NASA]] and [[Astrobotic Technology|Astrobotic]] plan to launch [[Griffin Mission One]] aiming to land near the Moon's south pole.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Astrobotic delays Griffin-1 Moon mission to NET July 2026 – Spaceflight Now |url=https://spaceflightnow.com/2025/10/28/astrobotic-delays-griffin-1-moon-mission-to-net-july-2026/ |access-date=2026-01-03 |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=CLPS Flight: Astrobotic's Griffin Mission One - NASA |url=https://www.nasa.gov/event/clps-flight-astrobotics-griffin-mission-one/ |access-date=2026-01-03 |language=en-US}}</ref>

=== Human spaceflight ===

==== International Space Station ====
On 8 January, [[Michael Fincke|Mike Fincke]],<ref>{{Cite web |date=2026-02-25 |title=NASA's SpaceX Crew-11 Astronaut Update - NASA |url=https://www.nasa.gov/blogs/commercialcrew/2026/02/25/nasas-spacex-crew-11-astronaut-update/ |access-date=2026-02-25 |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Foust |first=Jeff |date=2026-02-26 |title=NASA astronaut says his medical issue led to early return from the ISS |url=https://spacenews.com/nasa-astronaut-says-his-medical-issue-led-to-early-return-from-the-iss/ |access-date=2026-02-26 |website=SpaceNews |language=en-US}}</ref> one of [[SpaceX Crew-11|Crew-11]] astronauts on the [[ISS]], suffered a serious medical issue, which included a loss of ability to speak for approximately 20 minutes.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2026-03-27 |title=NASA astronaut Mike Fincke lost ability to speak while aboard ISS |url=https://www.independent.co.uk/bulletin/news/nasa-medical-emergency-mike-fincke-iss-b2947264.html |access-date=2026-04-16 |website=The Independent |language=en}}</ref> In response, [[NASA]] called off a spacewalk that was under preparation at that time and later decided to return the entire Crew-11 mission back to Earth earlier than planned in a "controlled medical evacuation". This marks the first time in U.S. history, as well as in the ISS program, that a space mission has been cut short due to a medical issue,<ref>{{Cite web |title=Crew-11 to cut mission short and return to Earth due to medical issue – Spaceflight Now |url=https://spaceflightnow.com/2026/01/09/crew-11-to-cut-mission-short-and-return-to-earth-due-to-medical-issue/ |access-date=2026-01-09 |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Clark |first=Stephen |date=2026-01-09 |title=NASA orders "controlled medical evacuation" from the International Space Station |url=https://arstechnica.com/space/2026/01/in-a-first-nasa-orders-astronauts-home-after-unspecified-medical-issue/ |access-date=2026-01-09 |website=Ars Technica |language=en}}</ref> although such cases happened before during Soviet space station missions.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Soyuz 21 |url=http://www.astronautix.com/s/soyuz21.html |access-date=2026-01-09 |website=www.astronautix.com}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=EO-2 mission |url=https://weebau.com/flights/eo2.htm |access-date=2026-01-09 |website=weebau.com}}</ref><ref>[https://www.planet4589.org/space/misc/vas.pdf "Illness in orbit"] by Bart Hendrickx (March 2011). ''[[Spaceflight (magazine)|Spaceflight]]''. '''53''' (3). British Interplanetary Society: 104–109. ([https://web.archive.org/web/20260109190627/https://planet4589.org/space/misc/kw.pdf archived])</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Marín |first=Daniel |date=2026-01-09 |title=Enfermedad en el espacio: los regresos de emergencia de naves espaciales por motivos de salud |url=https://danielmarin.naukas.com/2026/01/10/enfermedad-en-el-espacio-los-regresos-de-emergencia-de-naves-espaciales-por-motivos-de-salud/ |access-date=2026-01-10 |website=Eureka |language=es}}</ref> The Crew Dragon [[Crew Dragon Endeavour|Endeavour]] with all 4 crew members of Crew-11 safely [[Splashdown|splashed down]] off California coast on 15&nbsp;January.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Foust |first=Jeff |date=15 January 2026 |title=Crew-11 makes early return from ISS |url=https://spacenews.com/crew-11-makes-early-return-from-iss/}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Luciani 0 |first=Massimo |date=2026-01-15 |title=Mission Crew-11: in a medical evacuation, the SpaceX Crew Dragon Endurance spacecraft has come back to Earth |url=https://english.tachyonbeam.com/2026/01/15/mission-crew-11-in-a-medical-evacuation-the-spacex-crew-dragon-endurance-spacecraft-has-come-back-to-earth/ |access-date=2026-01-15 |language=en-US}}</ref>

On 13 February, NASA launched the first crewed spaceflight of the year, the [[SpaceX Crew-12|Crew-12]] mission carrying four NASA, ESA, and Roscosmos astronauts to ISS,<ref>{{Cite news |last=Lewis |first=Russell |date=2026-02-13 |title=On their way! 4 people on NASA Crew-12 mission launch to International Space Station |url=https://www.npr.org/2026/02/13/nx-s1-5712808/nasa-spacex-crew-12-launch-iss |access-date=2026-02-13 |work=NPR |language=en}}</ref> returning the station to its normal crew complement of seven in a rare indirect handover caused by the early return of [[SpaceX Crew-11|Crew-11]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Casillas|first=Beverly|date=2026-02-14|title=Crew-12 Arrives on Station|url=https://www.spacescout.info/2026/02/crew-12-arrives-on-station/|access-date=2026-02-15|website=Space Scout|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Casillas |first=Beverly |date=2026-02-09 |title=Crew-12 to Return ISS to Normal Complement |url=https://www.spacescout.info/2026/02/crew-12-to-return-iss-to-normal-complement/ |access-date=2026-02-15 |website=Space Scout |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Replacement crew docks at space station, boosts crew back to seven – Spaceflight Now |url=https://spaceflightnow.com/2026/02/15/replacement-crew-docks-at-space-station-boosts-crew-back-to-seven/ |access-date=2026-02-15 |language=en}}</ref> The second crewed flight of the year to ISS was [[Soyuz MS-29]] launched on 14 July<ref>{{Cite web |title=New Russian-American Crew Arrives at ISS |url=https://spacepolicyonline.com/news/new-russian-american-crew-arrives-at-iss/ |access-date=2026-08-05 |language=en-US}}</ref> and the third was [[SpaceX Crew-13|Crew-13]] launched on 1 October.<ref>{{Cite news |last=B |last2=r |last3=e |last4=n |last5=d |last6=a |last7=n |last8=B |last9=y |date=2026-10-01 |title=New space station crew launches from Florida on SpaceX's Crew Dragon capsule |url=https://www.npr.org/2026/10/01/nx-s1-5987698/nasa-crew-13-spacex-international-space-station-iss |access-date=2026-10-01 |work=NPR |language=en}}</ref>

On 22 March, [[Roscosmos]] launched [[Progress MS-33]] to ISS, the first space station uncrewed cargo flight of the year and the first launch from the [[Baikonur Cosmodrome Site 31]] after substantial repairs necessitated by the damage caused by the November 2025 launch of [[Soyuz MS-28]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Clark |first=Stephen |date=2026-03-27 |title=Rocket Report: Russia reopens gateway to ISS; Cape Canaveral hosts missile test |url=https://arstechnica.com/space/2026/03/rocket-report-russian-megaconstellation-takes-off-isar-preps-for-second-launch/ |access-date=2026-04-11 |website=Ars Technica |language=en}}</ref> Further resupply missions to ISS were: [[Cygnus NG-24]] on 11 April,<ref>{{Cite web |last= |first= |date=2026-04-11 |title=SpaceX launches huge 'Cygnus XL' cargo ship carrying over 5 tons of supplies to ISS astronauts (video) |url=https://www.space.com/space-exploration/international-space-station/northrop-grumman-second-cygnus-xl-cargo-launch-spacex-iss |access-date=2026-04-11 |website=Space |language=en}}</ref> [[Progress MS-34]] on 25 April,<ref>{{Cite web |last=Wall |first=Mike |date=2026-04-25 |title=Russia launches 3 tons of cargo to the International Space Station from Kazakhstan (video) |url=https://www.space.com/space-exploration/launches-spacecraft/progress-95-cargo-ship-launch-soyuz-international-space-station |access-date=2026-04-26 |website=Space |language=en}}</ref> [[SpaceX CRS-34]] on 15 May,<ref>{{Cite web |last= |first= |date=2026-05-12 |title=SpaceX launches 6,500 pounds of cargo to the International Space Station after delay (video) |url=https://www.space.com/space-exploration/launches-spacecraft/spacex-dragon-cargo-launch-iss-crs-34 |access-date=2026-05-15 |website=Space |language=en}}</ref> and [[Progress MS-35]] on 16 September.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Wall |first=Mike |date=2026-09-16 |title=Russia launching 3 tons of cargo to the space station today: Watch it live |url=https://www.space.com/space-exploration/international-space-station/russia-progress-96-cargo-launch-international-space-station |access-date=2026-09-16 |website=Space |language=en}}</ref>

[[NASA]] and [[Sierra Space]] plan to launch [[SSC Demo-1|Dream Chaser Demo-1]], the first free flyer orbital demonstration flight of the uncrewed cargo [[spaceplane]] [[Dream Chaser]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Dream Chaser Slips to End of 2026 for Free-Flyer Demo Only |url=https://spacepolicyonline.com/news/dream-chaser-slips-to-end-of-2026-for-free-flyer-demo-only/ |access-date=2026-01-03 |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Erwin |first=Sandra |date=2026-09-02 |title=Sierra Space books national security customers for first Dream Chaser mission |url=https://spacenews.com/sierra-space-books-national-security-customers-for-first-dream-chaser-mission/ |access-date=2026-09-02 |website=SpaceNews |language=en-US}}</ref>

==== Artemis program ====

ambitions]] for "about five to seven years" in order to focus on lunar missions.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Gorman |first=Douglas |date=2026-02-09 |title=SpaceX Delays Mars Plans in Favor of the Moon On 27 February, [[NASA]] announced a number of changes to the [[Artemis program]] with the stated purpose of increasing its cadence of missions,<ref>{{Cite web |title=NASA Adds Mission to Artemis Lunar Program, Updates Architecture - NASA |url=https://www.nasa.gov/news-release/nasa-adds-mission-to-artemis-lunar-program-updates-architecture/ |access-date=2026-03-07 |language=en-US}}</ref> including changing the [[Artemis III]] mission to a [[Low Earth orbit|LEO]] demonstration flight, moving the first Artemis Moon landing to [[Artemis IV]],<ref>{{Cite web |last=Bergin |first=Chris |date=2026-03-06 |title=NASA's Artemis 'Course Correction' Boosts Moonward Momentum: Key Details Still Maturing |url=https://www.nasaspaceflight.com/2026/03/artemis-course-correction-moonward-details/ |access-date=2026-03-07 |website=NASASpaceFlight.com |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Berger |first=Eric |date=2026-02-27 |title=NASA shakes up its Artemis program to speed up lunar return |url=https://arstechnica.com/space/2026/02/nasa-shakes-up-its-artemis-program-to-speed-up-lunar-return/ |access-date=2026-03-07 |website=Ars Technica |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |author1=Josh Dinner |date=2026-03-04 |title=NASA is overhauling its Artemis program. What does that mean for humanity's return to the moon? |url=https://www.space.com/space-exploration/artemis/nasa-is-overhauling-its-artemis-program-what-does-that-mean-for-humanitys-return-to-the-moon |access-date=2026-03-07 |website=Space |language=en}}</ref> and replacing the [[Exploration Upper Stage]] with another stage,<ref>{{Cite web |last=Berger |first=Eric |date=2026-03-06 |title=Ding-dong! The Exploration Upper Stage is dead |url=https://arstechnica.com/space/2026/03/ding-dong-the-exploration-upper-stage-is-dead/ |access-date=2026-03-07 |website=Ars Technica |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |author1=Josh Dinner |date=2026-03-06 |title=NASA wants to accelerate its Artemis missions to the moon. It will need to drop some big hardware to do it. |url=https://www.space.com/space-exploration/artemis/nasa-wants-to-accelerate-its-artemis-missions-to-the-moon-it-will-need-to-drop-some-big-hardware-to-do-it |access-date=2026-03-07 |website=Space |language=en}}</ref> later identified as [[Centaur V]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=NASA contract confirms selection of ULA's Centaur 5 as new upper stage for the SLS rocket – Spaceflight Now |url=https://spaceflightnow.com/2026/03/07/nasa-contract-confirms-selection-of-ulas-centaur-5-as-new-upper-stage-for-the-sls-rocket/ |access-date=2026-03-07 |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Foust |first=Jeff |date=2026-03-06 |title=NASA selects Centaur for new SLS upper stage |url=https://spacenews.com/nasa-selects-centaur-for-new-sls-upper-stage/ |access-date=2026-03-07 |website=SpaceNews |language=en-US}}</ref>

On 1 April 2026, [[NASA]] launched the [[Artemis II]] mission on the [[Space Launch System]], sending astronauts around the Moon on a ten-day lunar flyby.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Artemis II |url=https://www.nasa.gov/mission/artemis-ii/ |access-date=2026-04-02 |website=[[NASA]]}}</ref> On 6 April, Artemis II became the farthest human spaceflight in history when it surpassed the previous distance record of [[Apollo 13]].<ref>{{cite web |last1=Warner |first1=Cheryl |last2=Kraft |first2=Rachel |title=NASA's Artemis II Crew Eclipses Record for Farthest Human Spaceflight |url=https://www.nasa.gov/news-release/nasas-artemis-ii-crew-eclipses-record-for-farthest-human-spaceflight/ |website=nasa.gov |publisher=NASA |access-date=7 April 2026}}</ref> The mission's re-entry capsule ''Integrity'' safely [[Splashdown|splashed down]] in the Pacific Ocean southwest of [[San Diego]] on 11 April 2026.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Artemis II crew 'happy and healthy' after completing historic mission to the Moon |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/live/c3dlnzv5r71t |access-date=2026-04-17 |website=BBC News |language=en-GB}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Mendenhall |first=Alison Klesman, Brooks |date=2026-04-10 |title=As it happened: Artemis 2 splashes down, 'a perfect mission' |url=https://www.astronomy.com/space-exploration/artemis-2-splashes-down/ |access-date=2026-04-17 |website=Astronomy Magazine |language=en}}</ref>

==== Tiangong space station ====
On 30 March, China launched a prototype of the new [[cargo spacecraft]] [[Qingzhou (spacecraft)|Qingzhou]] on the first flight of the [[Kinetica 2]] rocket.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Jones |first=Andrew |date=2026-03-30 |title=China's Kinetica-2 rocket debuts successfully, sending prototype cargo spacecraft to orbit |url=https://spacenews.com/chinas-kinetica-2-rocket-debuts-successfully-sending-prototype-cargo-spacecraft-to-orbit/ |access-date=2026-03-31 |work=SpaceNews |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Marín |first=Daniel |date=2026-03-30 |title=Éxito del primer lanzamiento del cohete chino Lijian 2 (Kinetica 2) con la nave de carga Qingzhou 1 |url=https://danielmarin.naukas.com/2026/03/31/exito-del-primer-lanzamiento-del-cohete-chini-lijian-2-kinetica-2-con-la-nave-de-carga-qingzhou-1/ |access-date=2026-03-31 |website=Eureka |language=es}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |author1=Andrew Jones |date=2025-12-22 |title=Meet Qingzhou, China's next-gen cargo craft for its Tiangong space station (video) |url=https://www.space.com/space-exploration/human-spaceflight/meet-qingzhou-chinas-next-gen-cargo-craft-for-its-tiangong-space-station-video |access-date=2026-01-05 |website=Space |language=en}}</ref> Once in orbit, the spacecraft conducted a series of rendezvous and proximity operations tests involving another satellite.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Jones |first=Andrew |date=17 April 2026 |title=Qingzhou prototype cargo spacecraft completes rendezvous tests in orbit |url=https://spacenews.com/qingzhou-prototype-cargo-spacecraft-completes-rendezvous-tests-in-orbit/ |work=spacenews.com}}</ref> 

On 11&nbsp;May, China launched its first [[Tiangong space station]] resupply mission of the year, [[Tianzhou 10]],<ref>{{Cite web |author1=Mike Wall |date=2026-05-11 |title=China's Tianzhou 10 freighter delivers 7 tons of cargo to Tiangong space station |url=https://www.space.com/space-exploration/launches-spacecraft/chinas-tianzhou-10-freighter-delivers-7-tons-of-cargo-to-tiangong-space-station |access-date=2026-05-11 |website=Space |language=en}}</ref> followed by the first Chinese crewed spaceflight of the year, [[Shenzhou 23]], on 24 May.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Jones |first=Andrew |date=2026-05-24 |title=Shenzhou-23 crew arrives at Tiangong as China maps path to 2030 lunar landing |url=https://spacenews.com/shenzhou-23-crew-arrives-at-tiangong-as-china-maps-path-to-2030-lunar-landing/ |access-date=2026-05-25 |work=SpaceNews |language=en-US}}</ref>

[[ISRO]] aims to launch [[Gaganyaan-1]], [[India]]'s first uncrewed orbital test flight to support human exploration missions.<ref>{{Cite web |last= |first= |date=2026-01-01 |title=How Isro's Gaganyaan and Nasa's Artemis-II launch will change the world in 2026 |url=https://www.indiatoday.in/science/story/how-isros-gaganyaan-and-nasas-artemis-ii-launch-will-change-the-world-in-2026-2844599-2026-01-01 |access-date=2026-01-01 |website=India Today |language=en}}</ref>

=== Rocket innovation ===
On 12 February, [[Arianespace]] launched 32 [[Amazon Leo]] satellites on the first flight of [[Ariane 6#Ariane 64|Ariane 64]], the 4-booster variant of [[Ariane 6]], marking the first successful orbital [[maiden flight]] of the year.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Parsonson |first=Andrew |date=2026-02-12 |title=Arianespace Launches First Four-Booster Ariane 6 Rocket |url=https://europeanspaceflight.com/arianespace-launches-first-four-booster-ariane-6-rocket/ |access-date=2026-02-12 |website=European Spaceflight |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Luinstra |first=Martijn |date=2026-02-12 |title=Inaugural Ariane 64 launches Amazon Leo satellites from Kourou |url=https://www.nasaspaceflight.com/2026/02/le-01-launch/ |access-date=2026-02-12 |website=NASASpaceFlight.com |language=en-US}}</ref> Other successful first flights to orbit were achieved by the Chinese [[Kinetica 2]], [[Long March 12B]], [[Long March 10B]], and [[Pallas-1]], the Russian [[Soyuz-5 (rocket)|Soyuz-5]], the Japanese [[H3 (rocket)#Variants|H3-30S]], and the Indian [[Vikram-1]].

On 10 July, China became the second nation to successfully recover a booster after orbital flight, when a [[Long March 10B]]'s first stage landed on a net-like structure on a ship at sea during its maiden flight.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Year |first=The End of the |date=2026-07-10 |title=Making history! Center|DLR]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Menon |first=Jay |date=2026-07-15 |title=JAXA's RV-X rocket demonstrates vertical take-off and landing On 18 July, Skyroot Aerospace launched [[Vikram-1|Vikram 1]], India's first commercially built rocket, with a successful flight carrying multiple payloads to Low Earth Orbit.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2026-07-17|title='The dawn of a new space era': Vikram-1, India's 1st private orbital rocket, aces debut launch|url=https://www.space.com/space-exploration/launches-spacecraft/skyroot-aerospace-india-first-private-orbital-launch-vikram-1|access-date=2026-07-18|website=Space|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Foust|first=Jeff|date=2026-07-18|title=Skyroot Aerospace reaches orbit on first Vikram-1 launch|url=https://spacenews.com/skyroot-aerospace-reaches-orbit-on-first-vikram-1-launch/|access-date=2026-07-18|website=SpaceNews|language=en-US}}</ref>

On 5 September, the [[Germany|German]] company [[Isar Aerospace]], supported by [[European Space Agency|ESA]], successfully launched its [[Spectrum (rocket)|Spectrum]] rocket from [[Andøya Space|Andøya]] Spaceport in [[Norway]], marking the first orbital launch from West European soil.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Parsonson |first=Andrew |date=2026-09-06 |title=Isar Aerospace Completes First Successful Spectrum Flight |url=https://europeanspaceflight.com/isar-aerospace-completes-first-successful-spectrum-flight/ |access-date=2026-09-10 |website=European Spaceflight |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Davenport |first=Justin |date=2026-09-05 |title=Isar Aerospace launches Spectrum rocket after months of delays |url=https://www.nasaspaceflight.com/2026/09/isar-onward-and-upward/ |access-date=2026-09-10 |website=NASASpaceFlight.com |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last1=Spectrum |first1=Mike Wall "This is right now making history-making history for |last2=Isar |first2=making history for |last3=Europe." |first3=making history for |date=2026-09-05 |title=Private German rocket makes history, reaches orbit from European soil |url=https://www.space.com/space-exploration/launches-spacecraft/isar-aerospace-second-launch-norway-andoya-spaceport-spectrum-rocket |access-date=2026-09-10 |website=Space |language=en}}</ref>

=== Satellite technology ===
In January, [[Hisdesat]] announced that the [[Spainsat NG]] II communications satellite launched in October 2025 for Spanish government and military use was struck by a “space particle" while on its way to [[Geostationary orbit]] and suffered non-recoverable damage.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Foust |first=Jeff |date=2026-01-03 |title=New Spanish communications satellite suffers 'space particle' impact |url=https://spacenews.com/new-spanish-communications-satellite-suffers-space-particle-impact/ |access-date=2026-02-04 |work=SpaceNews |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Parsonson |first=Andrew |date=2026-01-18 |title=Hisdesat Confirms Spanish Military Satellite Sustained "Non-Recoverable Damage" |url=https://europeanspaceflight.com/hisdesat-confirms-spanish-military-satellite-sustained-non-recoverable-damage/ |access-date=2026-02-04 |website=European Spaceflight |language=en-US}}</ref>

On 12 January, the Spanish [[space capsule]] company Orbital Paradigm, supported by [[European Space Agency|ESA]]'s [[Future Launchers Preparatory Programme|FLPP]], launched its first technology demonstration mission. The [[KID (spacecraft)|KID]] capsule was expected to [[Atmospheric entry|re-enter Earth atmosphere]] after reaching orbit on the [[PSLV-C62]] flight. The Indian [[Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle|PSLV]] rocket failed in flight but KID separated from the falling launch vehicle and managed to transmit flight data during its non-nominal suborbital flight, thus becoming the lone survivor of 2026's first launch failure.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The KID Survived - Mission Update #2 We've spent the last 24 hours reviewing all data received during the PSLV-C62 mission to understand what happened. On 27 January, the [[European Union|EU]] announced that the [[European Union Agency for the Space Programme|EUSPA]]'s [[IRIS²#GOVSATCOM|GOVSATCOM]] program for encrypted communications is now operational, integrating eight satellites from five EU member states.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Parsonson |first=Andrew |date=2026-01-29 |title=EU Brings GOVSATCOM Secure Communications Service Online |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |date=27 January 2026 |title=EU governments' satellite comms programme lifts off |url=https://www.euractiv.com/news/eu-governments-satellite-comms-programme-lifts-off/ |work=Euractiv}}</ref> The program serves as an operational bridge to the planned [[IRIS²|IRIS<sup>2</sup>]] constellation.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |last=Parsonson |first=Andrew |date=2026-03-11 |title=Cyprus First to Use EU GOVSATCOM Secure Communications Service [[IRIS²|IRIS<sup>2</sup>]] project entered its implementation phase in August.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Gorman |first=Douglas |date=2026-08-10 |title=Europe's IRIS2 Constellation Enters the Build Phase |url=https://payloadspace.com/europes-iris2-constellation-enters-the-build-phase/ |access-date=2026-09-04 |website=Payload |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Parsonson |first=Andrew |date=2026-08-31 |title=SES Awards OHB €1 billion for IRIS2 MEO Satellites |url=https://europeanspaceflight.com/ses-awards-ohb-e1-billion-for-iris2-meo-satellites/ |access-date=2026-09-04 In March 2026, the Chinese company Sustain Space demonstrated on-orbit operations of a flexible robotic arm for satellite servicing and refuelling on its Xiyuan-0 satellite launched on a [[Kuaizhou|Kuaizhou-11]] rocket on 16 March 2026.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Jones |first=Andrew |date=2026-04-01 |title=Chinese startup tests flexible robotic arm in space for on-orbit servicing |url=https://spacenews.com/chinese-startup-tests-flexible-robotic-arm-in-space-for-on-orbit-servicing/ |access-date=2026-04-11 |work=SpaceNews |language=en-US}}</ref>

On 28 March, [[European Space Agency|ESA]] launched the first two satellites of the [[GNSS augmentation]] constellation [[Celeste (LEO-PNT)]] on a [[Rocket Lab]]'s [[Rocket Lab Electron|Electron]] rocket.<ref>{{Cite web |title=European satellite navigation opens new chapter at ESA's Ministerial Council |url=https://www.esa.int/Applications/Satellite_navigation/European_satellite_navigation_opens_new_chapter_at_ESA_s_Ministerial_Council |access-date=2025-12-31 |website=www.esa.int |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=ESA's Celeste target launch date confirmed |url=https://www.esa.int/Applications/Satellite_navigation/ESA_s_Celeste_target_launch_date_confirmed |access-date=2026-02-19 |website=www.esa.int |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Watch live: First Celeste launch |url=https://www.esa.int/Applications/Satellite_navigation/Watch_live_First_Celeste_launch |access-date=2026-03-28 |website=www.esa.int |language=en}}</ref> The mission delivered its first navigation signals on 8 April 2026.<ref>{{Cite web |title=ESA's Celeste broadcasts first navigation signal from low Earth orbit |url=https://www.esa.int/Applications/Satellite_navigation/Celeste/ESA_s_Celeste_broadcasts_first_navigation_signal_from_low_Earth_orbit |access-date=2026-04-11 |website=www.esa.int |language=en}}</ref>

On 3 May, the German [[ICARUS Initiative]] launched its first operational satellite of the [[ICARUS Initiative#ICARUS 2.0 satellites|ICARUS 2.0 constellation]], built by the Bulgarian company [[EnduroSat]] and named RAVEN, for [[Animal migration tracking|tracking animal migrations]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Penev |first=Velin |date=2026-01-12 |title=TALOS and EnduroSat to Build "Internet of Animals" Satellite Constellation |url=https://www.endurosat.com/news/talos-and-endurosat-to-build-internet-of-animals-constellation/ |access-date=2026-01-21 |website=EnduroSat |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=CAS500-2 Mission|url=https://www.spacex.com/launches/cas500-2|access-date=2026-04-30|website=SpaceX|language=en}}</ref>

On 27 August, [[Ariane 6]] performed its first [[geostationary orbit]] mission, launching the European weather satellite [[MTG-I2]] (Meteosat-14), which completed the first trio of [[Meteosat#Third Generation ("MTG")|MTG]] satellites.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Poisson |first=Juliette |date=2026-07-20 |title=Arianespace to launch weather satellite MTG-I2 on Ariane 6's first mission to geostationary On 31 August and 1 September, [[European Space Agency|ESA]] sent a small airplane to observe the destructive [[Atmospheric entry|reentries]] of the last two satellites of the magnetospheric mission [[Cluster II (spacecraft)|Cluster II]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Samba's fiery farewell recorded |url=https://www.esa.int/Space_Safety/Space_Debris/Samba_s_fiery_farewell_recorded |access-date=2026-09-02 |website=www.esa.int |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2026-09-01 |title=Final Cluster reentries – Live blog – Rocket Science |url=https://blogs.esa.int/rocketscience/2026/08/30/final-cluster-reentries-live-blog/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260902064813/https://blogs.esa.int/rocketscience/2026/08/30/final-cluster-reentries-live-blog/ |archive-date=2026-09-02 |access-date=2026-09-02 |website=blogs.esa.int}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Cluster's encore for reentry science a success |url=https://www.esa.int/Space_Safety/Space_Debris/Cluster_s_encore_for_reentry_science_a_success |access-date=2026-09-02 |website=www.esa.int |language=en}}</ref> To better coordinate the aerial observation campaign, ESA commanded the satellites in late January 2026 to slightly alter their orbits so they would reenter closer to each other. This initiative was part of ESA [[Space Safety Programme]]'s efforts to reduce the risks of [[space debris]] and served as precursor to the ''[[Draco (space mission)|Draco]]'' mission planned for 2027.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Moving satellites to meet a plane for rare reentry data |url=https://www.esa.int/Space_Safety/Space_Debris/Moving_satellites_to_meet_a_plane_for_rare_reentry_data |access-date=2026-02-04 |website=www.esa.int |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=online |first=heise |date=2026-02-04 |title=ESA: Flugzeug soll Verglühen zweier Satelliten vor Ort beobachten |url=https://www.heise.de/news/ESA-Flugzeug-soll-Vergluehen-zweier-Satelliten-vor-Ort-beobachten-11164520.html |access-date=2026-02-04 |website=heise online |language=de}}</ref>

On 3 September, [[ISRO]] launched [[EOS-05]], India's first geostationary Earth observation satellite.<ref>{{Cite news |date=4 September 2026 |title=ISRO's EOS-05 EXPLAINED: What India's first geosynchronous imaging satellite can do |url=https://www.thestatesman.com/technology/science/isros-eos-05-explained-what-indias-first-geosynchronous-imaging-satellite-can-do-1503634621.html}}</ref> The satellite was launched on [[Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle|PSLV]]'s return-to-flight mission after the failed [[PSLV-C62]] in January 2026.<ref>{{Cite news |date=2026-09-04 |title=Why EOS-05 matters: Isro breaks Gisat jinx, returns to flight & gets 1st success of 2026 |url=https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/science/why-eos-05-matters-isro-breaks-gisat-jinx-returns-to-flight-gets-1st-success-of-2026/articleshow/133754361.cms |access-date=2026-09-04 |work=The Times of India |issn=0971-8257}}</ref>

On 1 October 2026, [[Ukraine]] launched the first satellite of [[UASAT]], its sovereign [[Satellite internet constellation]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=GomSpace and STETMAN Establish UASAT Joint Venture for Ukrainian Sovereign Communications – SatNews |url=https://satnews.com/2026/04/22/gomspace-and-stetman-establish-uasat-joint-venture-for-ukrainian-sovereign-communications/ |access-date=2026-08-25 |website=satnews.com}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Find UASAT-Nano |url=https://satellitemap.space/sat/100884}}</ref>

== Orbital launch statistics ==
=== By country ===
For the purposes of this section, the yearly tally of orbital launches by country assigns each flight to the country of origin of the rocket, not to the launch services provider or the spaceport.

== Suborbital launch statistics ==
=== By country ===
For the purposes of this section, the yearly tally of suborbital launches by country assigns each flight to the country of origin of the rocket, not to the launch services provider or the spaceport. Flights intended to fly below {{cvt|80|km}} are omitted. This includes suborbital flights for all purposes, including scientific and military application.

======================================================================
WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: Animals in space
======================================================================

{{Short description|none}} <!-- "none" is preferred when the title is sufficiently descriptive; see [[WP:SDNONE]] -->
{{pp-pc}}
{{Use American English|date=June 2023}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=May 2020}}
[[Image:Miss Baker, the squirrel monkey.jpg|right|thumb|300px|[[Miss Baker]], a [[squirrel monkey]], rode a [[PGM-19 Jupiter|Jupiter IRBM]] (scale model of rocket shown) into space in 1959.]]
{{Sidebar
| title = Landmarks for animals in space
| contentstyle = text-align: left;
| content1 = {{Plainlist|
* 1946: [[Fruit flies in space|First animals in space (fruit flies)]]
* 1949: [[Albert II (monkey)|First mammal and first primate in space]]
* 1950: First mouse in space
* 1951: [[Soviet space dogs|First dogs in space]]

* 1959: First rabbit in space
* 1960: [[Belka and Strelka|First animals to survive Earth orbit]]
* 1961: [[Ham (chimpanzee)|First ape in space]]
* 1961: [[Korabl-Sputnik 4|First guinea pig in space]]
* 1963: [[Félicette|First cat in space]]
* 1968: [[Zond 5|First reptiles in space, first animals in deep space, and first animals to circle the Moon]]
* 1970: [[Orbiting Frog Otolith|First adult frogs in space]]
* 1972: [[Fee, Fi, Fo, Fum, and Phooey|First mice to orbit the Moon]]
* 1973: [[Skylab 3|First fish in space]]
* 1973: [[Skylab 3|First spiders in space]]
* 2007: First animals, [[Tardigrades in space|tardigrades]], survive exposure to space
