The '''NASA Deep Space Network''' ('''DSN''') is a worldwide [[Telecommunications network|network]] of spacecraft communication [[ground segment]] facilities, located in the United States (California), Spain ([[Madrid]]), and Australia (Canberra), that supports [[NASA]]'s [[interplanetary spaceflight|interplanetary]] [[spacecraft]] missions. It also performs [[radio astronomy|radio]] and [[radar astronomy]] observations for the exploration of the [[Solar System]] and the [[universe]], and supports selected [[Earth]]-orbiting missions. DSN is part of the NASA [[Jet Propulsion Laboratory]] (JPL).

== General information ==
{{geoGroup|section=General information}}
[[File:deep-space-op.jpg|thumb|upright=1.565|Deep Space Network Operations Center at JPL, Pasadena, California, in 1993|right]]

DSN currently consists of three deep-space communications facilities located such that a distant spacecraft is always in view of at least one station.<ref name="NF-151/7-87">{{Cite book |last1=Haynes |first1=Robert |url=https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/19870020470/downloads/19870020470.pdf |title=How We Get Pictures From Space |publisher=[[NASA]] |year=1987 |edition=Revised |series=NASA Facts |access-date=September 19, 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220418072103/https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/19870020470/downloads/19870020470.pdf |archive-date=April 18, 2022 |url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="about">{{Cite web|url=http://deepspace.jpl.nasa.gov/dsn/|title=About the Deep Space Network|publisher=[[JPL]]|access-date=2012-06-08|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120608040231/http://deepspace.jpl.nasa.gov/dsn/|archive-date=2012-06-08}}</ref><ref name="ST">{{Cite journal|last=Latifiyan|first=Pouya|date=April 2021|title=Space Telecommunications, how?|journal=Take off|publisher=[[Civil Aviation Technology College]]|publication-place=[[Tehran]]|volume=1|pages=15|via=[[Persian language|Persian]]}}</ref> They are:

* the [[Goldstone Deep Space Communications Complex]] ({{coord|35|25|36|N|116|53|24|W|type:landmark_region:US-CA|display=inline|name=Goldstone}}) about {{convert|60|km}} north of [[Barstow, California|Barstow]], California. For details of Goldstone's contribution to the early days of space probe tracking, see [[Project Space Track (1957-1961)|Project Space Track]];
* the [[Madrid Deep Space Communications Complex]] ({{coord|40|25|53|N|4|14|53|W|region:ES_type:landmark_source:dewiki|display=inline|name=Madrid}}), {{convert|60|km}} west of [[Madrid]], Spain; and
* the [[Canberra Deep Space Communication Complex|Canberra Deep Space Communication Complex (CDSCC)]] in the [[Australian Capital Territory]] ({{Coord|35|24|05|S|148|58|54|E|region:AU-ACT_type:landmark|display=inline|name=Canberra}}), {{convert|40|km}} southwest of [[Canberra]], Australia near the [[Tidbinbilla Nature Reserve]].

Each facility is situated in semi-mountainous, bowl-shaped terrain to help shield against radio frequency interference.<ref name="antennas">{{cite web |url=http://deepspace.jpl.nasa.gov/dsn/antennas/index.html |title=DSN:antennas |publisher=JPL, NASA |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110411022826/http://deepspace.jpl.nasa.gov/dsn/antennas/index.html |archive-date=2011-04-11 }}</ref> The strategic placement of the stations permits constant observation of spacecraft as the Earth rotates, which helps to make the DSN the largest and most sensitive scientific telecommunications system in the world.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Bracing for an Interplanetary Traffic Jam |url=https://science.nasa.gov/science-news/science-at-nasa/2001/ast06jun_1 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170515173632/https://science.nasa.gov/science-news/science-at-nasa/2001/ast06jun_1 |archive-date=May 15, 2017 |access-date=May 17, 2018 |website=science.nasa.gov |publisher=[[NASA]] }}</ref>

The DSN supports [[NASA]]'s contribution to the [[Discovery and exploration of the Solar System|scientific investigation of the Solar System]]: It provides a two-way communications link that guides and controls various NASA [[uncrewed spacecraft|uncrewed]] interplanetary [[space probe]]s, and brings back the images and new scientific information these probes collect. All DSN antennas are steerable, high-gain, [[parabolic reflector]] antennas.<ref name="antennas"/>
The antennas and data delivery systems make it possible to:<ref name="about" />

* acquire [[telemetry]] data from spacecraft.
* transmit commands to spacecraft.
* upload software modifications to spacecraft.
* track spacecraft position and velocity.
* perform [[Very Long Baseline Interferometry]] observations.
* measure variations in radio waves for radio science experiments.
* gather science data.
* monitor and control the performance of the network.

Other countries and organizations also run deep space networks. The DSN operates according to the standards of the [[Consultative Committee for Space Data Systems]], as do most other deep space networks, and hence the DSN is able to inter-operate with the networks of other space agencies. These include the [[Soviet Deep Space Network]], the [[Chinese Deep Space Network]], the [[Indian Deep Space Network]], the [[Japanese Deep Space Network]], and the [[ESTRACK]] of the [[European Space Agency]]. These agencies often cooperate for better mission coverage.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://trs.jpl.nasa.gov/bitstream/handle/2014/44347/13-2005_A1b.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220418070859/https://trs.jpl.nasa.gov/bitstream/handle/2014/44347/13-2005_A1b.pdf |url-status=live |archive-date=2022-04-18 |title=Deep Space Network (DSN) Mission Services and Operations Interface for Small Deep Space Missions |first= Susan |last= Kurtik |date=23 April 2013 |publisher= Jet Propulsion Laboratory|s2cid=117882864 |hdl=2014/44347 }}</ref> In particular, DSN has a cross-support agreement with ESA that allows mutual use of both networks for more effectiveness and reduced risk.<ref>{{Cite press release |last1=Warhaut |first1=Manfred |last2=Braukus |first2=Michael |date=April 2, 2007 |title=ESA and NASA extend ties with major new cross-support agreement |url=https://www.esa.int/About_Us/ESOC/ESA_and_NASA_extend_ties_with_major_new_cross-support_agreement |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230205115402/https://www.esa.int/About_Us/ESOC/ESA_and_NASA_extend_ties_with_major_new_cross-support_agreement |archive-date=February 5, 2023 |access-date=July 5, 2020 |website=www.esa.int |publisher=[[ESA]] }}</ref> In addition, radio astronomy facilities, such as the [[Parkes Observatory]], the [[Green Bank Telescope]], and the [[Very Large Array]], are sometimes used to supplement the antennas of the DSN.

===Operations control center===
{{Main|Space Flight Operations Facility}}

The antennas at all three DSN Complexes communicate directly with the Deep Space Operations Center (also known as Deep Space Network operations control center) located at the JPL facilities in [[Pasadena, California]].<ref name="ST" />

In the early years, the operations control center did not have a permanent facility. It was a provisional setup with numerous desks and phones installed in a large room near the computers used to calculate orbits. In July 1961, NASA started the construction of the permanent facility, Space Flight Operations Facility (SFOF). The facility was completed in October 1963 and dedicated on May 14, 1964. In the initial setup of the SFOF, there were 31 consoles, 100 closed-circuit television cameras, and more than 200 television displays to support [[Ranger 6]] to [[Ranger 9]] and [[Mariner 4]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Deep Space Network Operations Control Center at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory, Pasadena, California |url=http://deepspace.jpl.nasa.gov/dsn/history/dsn43.html|work=Picture Album of the DEEP SPACE NETWORK|publisher=NASA/JPL|access-date=26 January 2014|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130217115700/http://deepspace.jpl.nasa.gov/dsn/history/dsn43.html|archive-date=17 February 2013}}</ref>

Currently, the operations center personnel at SFOF monitor and direct operations, and oversee the quality of spacecraft telemetry and navigation data delivered to network users. In addition to the DSN complexes and the operations center, a ground communications facility provides communications that link the three complexes to the operations center at JPL, to space flight control centers in the United States and overseas, and to scientists around the world.<ref>{{cite web |title=NASA Facts: Deep Space Network |url=http://www.jpl.nasa.gov/news/fact_sheets/DSN-0203.pdf |publisher=JPL |access-date=2011-03-25 |archive-date=2020-04-26 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200426202053/https://www.jpl.nasa.gov/news/fact_sheets/DSN-0203.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref>

==Deep space==
[[File:DSNantenna.svg|thumb|upright=1.7|left|View from the Earth's north pole, showing the field of view of the main DSN antenna locations. Once a mission gets more than {{cvt|30,000|km}} from Earth, it is al&shy;ways in view of at least one of the stations.]]

Tracking vehicles in deep space is quite different from tracking missions in [[low Earth orbit]] (LEO). Deep space missions are visible for long periods of time from a large portion of the Earth's surface, and so require few stations (the DSN has only three main sites). These few stations, however, require huge antennas, ultra-sensitive receivers, and powerful transmitters in order to transmit and receive over the vast distances involved.

Deep space is defined in several different ways. According to a 1975 NASA report, the DSN was designed to communicate with "spacecraft traveling approximately 16,000&nbsp;km (10,000 miles) from Earth to the farthest planets of the solar system."<ref>{{Cite tech report |last=Renzetti |first=N. |url=https://ipnpr.jpl.nasa.gov/progress_report2/42-28/28A.PDF |title=DSN Functions and Facilities |date=May 1975 |publisher=[[JPL]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230903162954/https://ipnpr.jpl.nasa.gov/progress_report2/42-28/28A.PDF |archive-date=September 3, 2023 |url-status=live }}</ref> JPL diagrams<ref>{{Cite conference |last=Deutsch |first=Les |date=June 24, 2012 |title=NASA's Deep Space Network: Big Antennas with a Big Job |url=https://dataverse.jpl.nasa.gov/api/access/datafile/48284 |conference=Anten Sympoisum, Toulouse Space Show |type=PDF |location=Toulouse, France |publisher=[[JPL]] |page=25 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240121192609/https://dataverse.jpl.nasa.gov/api/access/datafile/48284 |archive-date=January 21, 2024 |url-status=live |hdl=2014/42668 }}</ref> state that at an altitude of {{cvt|30,000|km}}, a spacecraft is always in the field of view of one of the tracking stations.  The [[International Telecommunication Union]], which sets aside [[deep space bands|various frequency bands for deep space and near Earth use]], defines "deep space" to start at a distance of {{convert|2|e6km|e6mi|abbr=unit}} from the Earth's surface.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://deepspace.jpl.nasa.gov/dsndocs/810-005/201/201B.pdf |title=201, Rev. B: Frequency and Channel Assignments |date=December 15, 2009 |access-date=July 13, 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140611094446/http://deepspace.jpl.nasa.gov/dsndocs/810-005/201/201B.pdf |archive-date=June 11, 2014 |url-status=dead |df=mdy-all}}</ref>

=== Frequency bands ===
The NASA Deep Space Network can both send and receive in all of the ITU deep space bands—[[S band|S-band]] (2 GHz), [[X band|X-band]] (8 GHz), and [[Ka band|Ka-band]] (32 GHz).  Frequency usage has in general moved upward over the life of the DSN, as higher frequencies have higher gain for the same size antenna, and the deep space bands are wider, so more data can be returned. However, higher frequencies also need more accurate pointing (on the spacecraft) and more precise antenna surfaces (on Earth), so improvements in both spacecraft and the DSN were required to move to higher bands.  Early missions used S-band for both uplink and downlink.  [[Viking program|Viking]] (1975) had X-band as an experiment,<ref>{{cite web |url=https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/19760023186 |title=Viking X-band telemetry experiment|date=September 1976 |last1=Weber |first1=W. J. |last2=Ackerknecht |first2=W. E. |last3=Kollar |first3=F. J. }}</ref> and [[Voyager program|Voyager]] (1977) was the first to use it operationally.<ref>{{cite web |title=Voyager Telecommunications |url=https://descanso.jpl.nasa.gov/DPSummary/Descanso4--Voyager_ed.pdf }}, p. 32</ref> Similarly, [[Mars Observer]] (1994) carried a Ka-band experiment,<ref>{{cite web |url=https://core.ac.uk/download/pdf/42785642.pdf |title=The Mars Observer Ka-Band Link Experiment}}</ref> [[Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter]] (2005) had a Ka-band demo,<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Shambayati |first1=S. |last2=Davarian |first2=F. |last3=Morabito |first3=D. |title=2005 IEEE Aerospace Conference |chapter=Link design and planning for Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (MRO) Ka-band (32 GHZ) telecom demonstration |date=March 12, 2005 |publisher=[[IEEE]] |pages=1559–1569 |doi=10.1109/AERO.2005.1559447 |isbn=0-7803-8870-4 |s2cid=20667200 }}</ref> and [[Kepler space telescope|Kepler]] (2009) was the first mission to use Ka-band as the primary downlink.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://personales.upv.es/thinkmind/dl/conferences/spacomm/spacomm_2016/spacomm_2016_2_30_20032.pdf |title=Performance Analysis of Operational Ka-band Link with Kepler}}</ref>

However, not all space missions can use these bands.  The Moon, the Earth-moon Lagrange points, and the Earth–Sun [[Lagrangian point]]s L<sub>1</sub> and L<sub>2</sub> are all closer than 2 million km from Earth (distances are [[Lagrange Point#Solar System values|here]]), so they are considered near space and cannot use the ITU's deep space bands.  Missions at these locations that need high data rates must therefore use the "near space" K band (27 GHz).  Since NASA has several such missions (such as the [[James Webb Space Telescope]] and the [[Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter]]), they have enhanced the Deep Space Network to receive (but not transmit) at these frequencies as well.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=LaBelle |first1=R. |last2=Rochblatt |first2=D. |year=2012 |title=Ka-band high-rate telemetry system upgrade for the NASA deep space network |journal=Acta Astronautica |language=en |volume=70 |issue=70 |pages=58–68 |bibcode=2012AcAau..70...58L |doi=10.1016/j.actaastro.2011.07.023}}</ref>

The DSN is also pursuing optical deep space communication, offering greater communication speeds at the cost of susceptibility to weather and the need for extremely precise pointing of the spacecraft.  This technology is working in prototype form.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.jpl.nasa.gov/news/nasas-new-experimental-antenna-tracks-deep-space-laser |title=NASA's New Experimental Antenna Tracks Deep Space Laser|website=[[Jet Propulsion Laboratory]] }}</ref>

== History ==
{{further|History of the Deep Space Network}}

The forerunner of the DSN was established in January 1958, when [[Jet Propulsion Laboratory|JPL]], then under contract to the [[U.S. Army|US Army]], deployed portable radio tracking stations in Nigeria, Singapore, and California to receive [[telemetry]] and plot the orbit of the Army-launched [[Explorer 1]], the first successful US [[satellite]].<ref name="sp-2001-4227">{{Cite book |last=Mudgway |first=Douglas J. |url=https://www.nasa.gov/wp-content/uploads/2023/04/sp-4227.pdf |title=Uplink-Downlink: A History of the Deep Space Network, 1957–1997 |publisher=National Aeronautics and Space Administration |year=2001 |series=The NASA History Series |page=5 |id=SP-2001-4227}}</ref> [[NASA]] was officially established on October 1, 1958, to consolidate the separately developing space-exploration programs of the US Army, [[US Navy]], and [[US Air Force]] into one civilian organization.<ref name="act1">{{Cite web|url=http://www.nasa.gov/offices/ogc/about/space_act1.html|title=The National Aeronautics and Space Act|access-date=November 9, 2007|publisher=NASA|date=2005|author=NASA}}</ref>

On December 3, 1958, JPL was transferred from the US Army to NASA and given responsibility for the design and execution of lunar and planetary exploration programs using remotely controlled spacecraft. Shortly after the transfer, NASA established the concept of the Deep Space Network as a separately managed and operated communications system that would accommodate all [[Deep space exploration|deep space]] missions, thereby avoiding the need for each flight project to acquire and operate its own specialized space communications network. The DSN was given responsibility for its own research, development, and operation in support of all of its users. Under this concept, it has become a world leader in the development of low-noise receivers; large parabolic-dish antennas; tracking, telemetry, and command systems; digital signal processing; and deep space navigation. The Deep Space Network formally announced its intention to send missions into deep space on Christmas Eve 1963; it has remained in continuous operation in one capacity or another ever since.<ref name="Christmas Eve 1963 Genesis">{{Cite web |last=Stirone |first=Shannon |date=March 2018 |title=Welcome to the Center of the Universe |url=https://longreads.com/2018/03/15/welcome-to-the-center-of-the-universe/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231202171405/https://longreads.com/2018/03/15/welcome-to-the-center-of-the-universe/ |archive-date=December 2, 2023 |access-date=March 17, 2018 |website=LongReads }}</ref>

The largest antennas of the DSN are often called on during spacecraft emergencies. Almost all spacecraft are designed so normal operation can be conducted on the smaller (and more economical) antennas of the DSN, but during an emergency the use of the largest antennas is crucial. This is because a troubled spacecraft may be forced to use less than its normal transmitter power, [[Attitude dynamics and control|attitude control]] problems may preclude the use of [[high-gain antenna]]s, and recovering every bit of telemetry is critical to assessing the health of the spacecraft and planning the recovery. The most famous example is the [[Apollo 13]] mission, where limited battery power and inability to use the spacecraft's high-gain antennas reduced signal levels below the capability of the [[Manned Space Flight Network]], and the use of the biggest DSN antennas (and the Australian [[Parkes Observatory]] [[radio telescope]]) was critical to saving the lives of the astronauts. While Apollo was also a US mission, DSN provides this emergency service to other space agencies as well, in a spirit of inter-agency and international cooperation. For example, the [[Solar and Heliospheric Observatory#Near loss of SOHO|recovery]] of the [[Solar and Heliospheric Observatory]] (SOHO) mission of the [[European Space Agency]] (ESA) would not have been possible without the use of the largest DSN facilities.

=== DSN and the Apollo program ===
Although normally tasked with tracking uncrewed spacecraft, the Deep Space Network (DSN) also contributed to the communication and tracking of [[Apollo program|Apollo mission]]s to the [[Moon]], although primary responsibility was held by the [[Manned Space Flight Network]] (MSFN). The DSN designed the MSFN stations for lunar communication and provided a second antenna at each MSFN site (the MSFN sites were near the DSN sites for just this reason). Two antennas at each site were needed both for redundancy and because the beam widths of the large antennas needed were too small to encompass both the lunar orbiter and the lander at the same time. DSN also supplied some larger antennas as needed, in particular for television broadcasts from the Moon, and emergency communications such as Apollo 13.<ref name="Mandal">{{Cite web|url=http://shunpike.mit.edu/writings/16.895J_Interview_Report_Soumyajit.pdf|title=Engineering Apollo, Interview Report: Deep Space Network Support for the Apollo Missions|first=Soumyajit|last=Mandal|access-date=July 2, 2008|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110720001947/http://shunpike.mit.edu/writings/16.895J_Interview_Report_Soumyajit.pdf|archive-date=July 20, 2011}}</ref>

Excerpt from a NASA report describing how the DSN and MSFN cooperated for Apollo:<ref>{{Cite report|title=NASA Technical report CR 140390, Histories of the Space Tracking and Data Acquisition Network (STADAN), the Manned Space Flight Network (MSFN), and the NASA Communications Network (NASCOM)|hdl=2060/19750002909|first=William|last=R. Corliss|publisher=NASA|date=June 1974 |url=https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/19750002909/downloads/19750002909.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220303084522/https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/19750002909/downloads/19750002909.pdf |archive-date=2022-03-03 |url-status=live }} 100MB PDF file. Explicitly non-copyrighted.</ref>

{{blockquote|Another critical step in the evolution of the Apollo Network came in 1965 with the advent of the DSN Wing concept. Originally, the participation of DSN 26-m antennas during an Apollo Mission was to be limited to a backup role. This was one reason why the MSFN 26-m sites were collocated with the DSN sites at Goldstone, Madrid, and Canberra. However, the presence of two, well-separated spacecraft during lunar operations stimulated the rethinking of the tracking and communication problem. One thought was to add a dual S-band RF system to each of the three 26-m MSFN antennas, leaving the nearby DSN 26-m antennas still in a backup role. Calculations showed, though, that a 26-m antenna pattern centered on the landed Lunar Module would suffer a 9-to-12 db loss at the lunar horizon, making tracking and data acquisition of the orbiting Command Service Module difficult, perhaps impossible. It made sense to use both the MSFN and DSN antennas simultaneously during the all-important lunar operations. JPL was naturally reluctant to compromise the objectives of its many uncrewed spacecraft by turning three of its DSN stations over to the MSFN for long periods. How could the goals of both Apollo and deep space exploration be achieved without building a third 26-m antenna at each of the three sites or undercutting planetary science missions?
}}
{{blockquote|The solution came in early 1965 at a meeting at NASA Headquarters, when [[Eberhardt Rechtin]] suggested what is now known as the "wing concept". The wing approach involves constructing a new section or "wing" to the main building at each of the three involved DSN sites. The wing would include a MSFN control room and the necessary interface equipment to accomplish the following:

# Permit tracking and two-way data transfer with either spacecraft during lunar operations.
# Permit tracking and two-way data transfer with the combined spacecraft during the flight to the Moon.
# Provide backup for the collocated MSFN site passive track (spacecraft to ground RF links) of the Apollo spacecraft during trans-lunar and trans-earth phases.

With this arrangement, the DSN station could be quickly switched from a deep-space mission to Apollo and back again. GSFC personnel would operate the MSFN equipment completely independently of DSN personnel. Deep space missions would not be compromised nearly as much as if the entire station's equipment and personnel were turned over to Apollo for several weeks.
}}

The details of this cooperation and operation are available in a two-volume technical report from JPL.<ref>{{Cite tech report |last1=Flanagan |first1=F. M. |last2=Goodwin |first2=P. S. |last3=Renzetti |first3=N. A. |url=https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/19710009001/downloads/19710009001.pdf |title=Deep Space Network Support of the Manned Space Flight Network for Apollo, 1962–1968 |date=July 15, 1970 |publisher=[[NASA]] |volume=1 |id=JPL-TM-33-452-VOL-1/NASA-CR-116801 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220521171150/https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/19710009001/downloads/19710009001.pdf |archive-date=May 21, 2022 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite tech report |last1=Flanagan |first1=F. M. |last2=Goodwin |first2=P. S. |last3=Renzetti |first3=N. A. |url=https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/19710015677/downloads/19710015677.pdf |title=Deep Space Network Support of the Manned Space Flight Network for Apollo, 1969–1970 |date=May 1971 |publisher=NASA |volume=2 |id=JPL-TM-33-452-VOL-2/NASA-CR-118325 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220418071912/https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/19710015677/downloads/19710015677.pdf |archive-date=April 18, 2022 |url-status=live }}</ref>

== Management ==
The network is a NASA facility and is managed and operated for NASA by JPL, which is part of the [[California Institute of Technology]] (Caltech). The Interplanetary Network Directorate (IND) manages the program within JPL and is charged with the development and operation of it. The IND is considered to be JPL's focal point for all matters relating to telecommunications, interplanetary navigation, information systems, information technology, computing, software engineering, and other relevant technologies. While the IND is best known for its duties relating to the Deep Space Network, the organization also maintains the JPL [[Advanced Multi-Mission Operations System]] (AMMOS) and JPL's [[Institutional Computing and Information Services]] (ICIS).<ref>{{cite web |url=http://tmot.jpl.nasa.gov/Program_Overview_Information/program_overview_information.html |title=IND Technology Program Overview |publisher=JPL |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090411171552/http://tmot.jpl.nasa.gov/Program_Overview_Information/program_overview_information.html |archive-date=2009-04-11 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite conference |last1=Weber |first1=William J. |date=May 27, 2004 |title=Interplanetary Network Directorate |url=https://dataverse.jpl.nasa.gov/api/access/datafile/5418 |conference=7th Briefing for Industry |type=PDF |location=Pasadena, California |publisher=[[JPL]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240121194509/https://dataverse.jpl.nasa.gov/api/access/datafile/5418 |archive-date=January 21, 2024 |hdl=2014/40704 |url-status=live }}</ref>

The facilities in Spain and Australia are jointly owned and operated in conjunction with that government's scientific institutions.  In Australia, "the [[CSIRO|Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organisation]] (CSIRO), an Australian Commonwealth Government Statutory Authority, established the CSIRO Astronomy and Space Science Division to manage the day-to-day operations, engineering, and maintenance activities of the Canberra Deep Space Communications Complex".<ref name="oig">{{Cite web |date=March 26, 2015 |title=NASA's Management of the Deep Space Network |url=https://oig.nasa.gov/docs/IG-15-013.pdf |website=NASA (Office of Inspector General) |id=IG-15-013}}</ref> Most of the staff at Tidbinbilla are Australian government employees; the land and buildings are owned by the Australian government; NASA provides the bulk of the funding, owns the movable property (such as dishes and electronic equipment) which it has paid for, and gets to decide where to point the dishes.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.austlii.edu.au/au/other/dfat/treaties/ATS/2018/4.html |title=Agreement between the Government of Australia and the Government of the United States of America for Space Vehicle Tracking and Communication Facilities}}</ref>  Similarly, in Spain, "Ingenieria de Sistemas para la Defensa de España S.A. (ISDEFE), a wholly owned subsidiary of the [[National Institute for Aerospace Technology|Instituto Nacional de Técnica Aeroespacial]] (INTA) and a part of the Spanish Department of Defense, operates and maintains the Madrid Deep Space Communications Complex (Madrid)".<ref name="oig" />

[[Peraton]] (formerly [[Harris Corporation]]) is under contract to JPL for the DSN's operations and maintenance. Peraton has responsibility for managing the Goldstone complex, operating the DSOC, and for DSN operations, mission planning, operations engineering, and logistics.<ref>{{Cite press release |last=Lackey |first=Leah |date=May 23, 2013 |title=ITT Exelis selected for NASA Deep Space Network subcontract by Jet Propulsion Laboratory |url=https://spaceref.com/press-release/itt-exelis-selected-for-nasa-deep-space-network-subcontract-by-jet-propulsion-laboratory/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://archive.today/20240121194929/https://spaceref.com/press-release/itt-exelis-selected-for-nasa-deep-space-network-subcontract-by-jet-propulsion-laboratory/ |archive-date=January 21, 2024 |access-date=July 5, 2016 |publisher=ITT Exelis |via=SpaceRef }}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Gelles |first=David |date=February 6, 2015 |title=Harris Corporation to Buy Defense Contractor Exelis for $4.7 Billion |url=https://archive.nytimes.com/dealbook.nytimes.com/2015/02/06/harris-corporation-to-buy-defense-and-aerospace-contractor-exelis-for-4-7-billion/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230326095835/https://archive.nytimes.com/dealbook.nytimes.com/2015/02/06/harris-corporation-to-buy-defense-and-aerospace-contractor-exelis-for-4-7-billion/ |archive-date=March 26, 2023 |access-date=October 31, 2016 |publisher=[[The New York Times]] |newspaper=DealBook }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=CONTRACT to PERATON INC. |url=https://www.usaspending.gov/award/CONT_AWD_80GSFC19C0063_8000_-NONE-_-NONE- |access-date=2023-05-15 |website=USAspending |language=en}}</ref>

== Antennas ==
{{Main|List of antennas in NASA's Deep Space Network}}
[[File:Goldstone DSN antenna.jpg|upright=1.5|thumb|70&nbsp;m antenna at [[Goldstone Deep Space Communications Complex|Goldstone]], [[California]]]]
Each complex consists of at least four deep space terminals equipped with ultra-sensitive receiving systems and large parabolic-dish antennas. There are:

* Three or more {{convert|34|m|adj=on|sp=us}} [[Beam waveguide antenna]]s (BWG)
* One {{convert|70|m|adj=on|sp=us}} antenna.

Five of the {{convert|34|m|adj=on|sp=us}} beam waveguide antennas were added to the system in the late 1990s. Three were located at Goldstone, and one each at Canberra and Madrid. A second {{convert|34|m|adj=on|sp=us}} beam waveguide antenna (the network's sixth) was completed at the Madrid complex in 2004.

In order to meet the current and future needs of deep space communication services, a number of new Deep Space Station antennas had to be built at the existing Deep Space Network sites. At the Canberra Deep Space Communication Complex the first of these was completed in October 2014 (DSS35), with a second becoming operational in October 2016 (DSS36).<ref>{{Cite web |title=Antennas |url=https://www.cdscc.nasa.gov/Pages/antennas.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230606161318/https://www.cdscc.nasa.gov/Pages/antennas.html |archive-date=June 6, 2023 |access-date=July 13, 2015 |publisher=[[NASA]] }}</ref> A new 34-meter dish (DSS53) became operational at the Madrid complex in February 2022.<ref>{{Cite press release |last1=O'Neill |first1=Ian J. |last2=Pamer |first2=Melissa |title=NASA Adds Giant New Dish to Communicate with Deep Space Network |url=https://www.jpl.nasa.gov/news/nasa-adds-giant-new-dish-to-communicate-with-deep-space-missions |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240117235554/https://www.jpl.nasa.gov/news/nasa-adds-giant-new-dish-to-communicate-with-deep-space-missions |archive-date=January 17, 2024 |access-date=November 17, 2022 |publisher=[[JPL]] }}</ref>

The 70 meter antennas are aging and more difficult to maintain than the modern BWG antennas.  Therefore in 2012 NASA announced a plan to decommission all three of them and replace them with arrayed 34-meter BWG antennas.  Each of these new antennas would be upgraded to have X-band uplink capabilities and both X and Ka-band downlink capabilities.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.nasa.gov/directorates/heo/scan/services/networks/txt_daep_transition.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150205110004/http://www.nasa.gov/directorates/heo/scan/services/networks/txt_daep_transition.html|url-status=dead|archive-date=February 5, 2015|title=Proposed DSN Aperture Enhancement Project Transition|date=May 16, 2018|website=nasa.gov|access-date=May 16, 2018}}</ref>  However by 2021, NASA decided instead to do a complete refurbishment of all 70-meter antennas, requiring taking them offline for months at a time.  These refurbished antennas were expected to serve for decades to come.<ref name="aging">{{cite web |title=NASA's Deep Space Network Looks to the Future |url=https://www.nasa.gov/technology/nasas-deep-space-network-looks-to-the-future/ |date=September 1, 2021}}</ref>

== Current signal processing capabilities ==
[[File:Canberra Deep Space Communication Complex - general view (2174403243).jpg|thumb|upright=1.5|The [[Canberra Deep Space Communication Complex]] in 2008]]
The general capabilities of the DSN have not substantially changed since the beginning of the [[Voyager program|Voyager]] Interstellar Mission in the early 1990s. However, many advancements in digital signal processing, arraying and error correction have been adopted by the DSN.
[[File:Deep Space Station 43 (DSS-43) Antenna.png|thumb|70 m antenna at [[Canberra]], Australia]]
The ability to array several antennas was incorporated to improve the data returned from the ''[[Voyager 2]]'' [[Neptune]] encounter, and extensively used for the [[Galileo spacecraft|''Galileo'']] mission, when the spacecraft's high-gain antenna failed to deploy and as a result ''Galileo'' was forced to resort to operating solely off its low-gain antennas.<ref>{{harvnb|Mudgway|2001|at=Chapter 5, The Galileo Era – 1986–1996}}</ref> 

The DSN array currently available since the ''Galileo'' mission can link the {{convert|70|m|adj=on|sp=us}} dish antenna at the Deep Space Network complex in Goldstone, California, with an identical antenna located in Australia, in addition to two {{convert|34|m|adj=on|sp=us}} antennas at the Canberra complex. The California and Australia sites were used concurrently to pick up communications with ''Galileo''.

Arraying of antennas within the three DSN locations is also used. For example, a {{convert|70|m|adj=on|sp=us}} dish antenna can be arrayed with a 34-meter dish. For especially vital missions, like ''Voyager 2'', non-DSN facilities normally used for radio astronomy can be added to the array.<ref>{{Cite tech report |last1=Brown |first1=D. W. |last2=Brundage |first2=W. D. |last3=Ulvestad |first3=J. S. |last4=Kent |first4=S. S. |last5=Bartos |first5=K. P. |url=https://ipnpr.jpl.nasa.gov/progress_report/42-102/102I.PDF |title=Interagency Telemetry Arraying for the Voyager-Neptune Encounter |date=August 15, 1990 |publisher=[[JPL]] |id=TDA Progress Report 42-102 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231117180555/http://ipnpr.jpl.nasa.gov/progress_report/42-102/102I.PDF |archive-date=November 17, 2023 |url-status=live }}</ref>  In particular, the Canberra {{convert|70|m|adj=on|sp=us}} dish can be arrayed with the [[Parkes Radio Telescope]] in Australia; and the Goldstone 70-meter dish can be arrayed with the [[Very Large Array]] of antennas in New Mexico.<ref>{{cite web |title=Antenna Arraying |date=30 March 2020 |url=https://deepspace.jpl.nasa.gov/about/complexes/antenna-arraying/ |publisher=JPL}}</ref> Also, two or more {{convert|34|m|adj=on|sp=us}} dishes at one DSN location are commonly arrayed together.

All the stations are remotely operated from a centralized Signal Processing Center at each complex. These Centers house the electronic subsystems that point and control the antennas, receive and process the telemetry data, transmit commands, and generate the spacecraft navigation data. Once the data are processed at the complexes, they are transmitted to JPL for further processing and for distribution to science teams over a modern communications network.

Especially at Mars, there are often many spacecraft within the beam width of an antenna.  For operational efficiency, a single antenna can receive signals from multiple spacecraft at the same time.  This capability is called '''Multiple Spacecraft Per Aperture''', or '''MSPA'''.  Currently, the DSN can receive up to 4 spacecraft signals at the same time, or MSPA-4.  However, apertures cannot currently be shared for uplink.  When two or more high-power carriers are used simultaneously, very high order intermodulation products fall in the receiver bands, causing interference to the much (25 orders of magnitude) weaker received signals.<ref>{{Cite tech report |last1=Conroy |first1=B. L. |last2=Hoppe |first2=D. J. |url=https://tmo.jpl.nasa.gov/progress_report/42-127/127E.pdf |title=Noise Bursts and Intermodulation Products Caused by Multiple Carriers at X-Band |date=November 15, 1996 |publisher=[[JPL]] |id=TDA Progress Report 42-127 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231206115444/http://tmo.jpl.nasa.gov/progress_report/42-127/127E.pdf |archive-date=December 6, 2023 |url-status=live }}</ref>  Therefore, only one spacecraft at a time can get an uplink, though up to 4 can be received.

== Network limitations and challenges ==
[[File:Madrid Deep Space Network Complex.jpg|thumb|upright=1.5|70 m antenna at [[Robledo de Chavela]], Spain]]
There are a number of limitations to the current DSN, and a number of challenges going forward.  Most of these are outlined in a 2023 Audit of NASA's Deep Space Network performed by NASA's Office of Inspector General.<ref name="NASA Audit">{{cite web |url=https://www.nasa.gov/wp-content/uploads/2023/08/ig-23-016.pdf |title=Audit of NASA's Deep Space Network |publisher=NASA's Office of Inspector General |year=2023}}{{source-attribution}}</ref>  Their main conclusions are:
* NASA's DSN is oversubscribed, leading to mission impacts and scheduling challenges
* Capacity limitations leading to mission impacts are expected to increase with the onset of crewed Artemis missions
* Capacity limitations, lack of readily available backups, and laborious process present challenges to scheduling time on DSN
* Upgrades to NASA's Deep Space Network are behind schedule and more costly than planned
* Challenges with international partners and project oversight<ref name="NASA Audit"/>

Other problems have been noted as well:
* The Deep Space Network nodes are all on Earth. Therefore, data transmission rates from/to  spacecraft and space probes are severely constrained due to the distances from Earth. For now it can connect with the Mars orbiters in the [[Mars Relay Network]] for faster and more flexible communications with spacecraft and landers on Mars.<ref>{{Cite press release |last1=O'Neill |first1=Ian J. |last2=Hautaluoma |first2=Grey |last3=Johnson |first3=Alana |date=February 16, 2021 |title=The Mars Relay Network Connects Us to NASA's Martian Explorers |url=https://mars.nasa.gov/news/8861/the-mars-relay-network-connects-us-to-nasas-martian-explorers/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240111141625/https://mars.nasa.gov/news/8861/the-mars-relay-network-connects-us-to-nasas-martian-explorers/ |archive-date=January 11, 2024 |access-date=March 10, 2021 |website=NASA's Mars Exploration Program |publisher=[[NASA]] }}</ref> Adding dedicated communication satellites elsewhere in space, to handle multiparty, multi-mission use, such as the planned [[Mars Telecommunications Network]], would increase flexibility towards some sort of [[Interplanetary Internet]]. 
* The need to support "legacy" missions that have remained operational beyond their original lifetimes but are still returning scientific data. Programs such as [[Voyager program|Voyager]] have been operating long past their original mission termination date. They also need some of the largest antennas.
* Replacing major components, and/or accidents,<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.nasa.gov/directorates/somd/space-communications-navigation-program/nasa-concludes-antenna-mishap-investigation-releases-report/ |title=NASA Concludes Antenna Mishap Investigation, Releases Report}}</ref> can leave an antenna out of service for months or years at a time.  
* Some DSN capabilities, such as the [[Goldstone Solar System Radar]], are only available on one antenna.  When that antenna is out of service or unavailable, the capability is lost.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://echo.jpl.nasa.gov/asteroids/goldstone_asteroid_schedule.html~ |title=Goldstone Asteroid Schedule}}</ref>
* The older 70&nbsp;m antennas are reaching the end of their lives, and at some point will need to be replaced.  NASA has so far extended their lives through major refurbishment.<ref name="aging"/>  The leading candidate for 70&nbsp;m replacement had been an array of smaller dishes,<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://dsnarray.jpl.nasa.gov/|title=The Future Deep Space Network: An Array of Many Small Antennas|publisher=JPL|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090714022934/http://dsnarray.jpl.nasa.gov/|archive-date=July 14, 2009}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Bagri |first1=Durgadas S. |last2=Statman |first2=Joseph I. |last3=Gatti |first3=Mark S. |name-list-style=amp |year=2007 |title=Proposed Array-Based Deep Space Network for NASA |journal=[[Proceedings of the IEEE]] |publisher=[[IEEE]] |volume=95 |issue=10 |pages=1916–1922 |doi=10.1109/JPROC.2007.905046 |issn=0018-9219 |s2cid=27224753}}</ref> but more recently the decision was taken to expand the provision of 34-meter (112&nbsp;ft) BWG antennas at each complex to a total of 4.<ref>{{Cite web |date=November 10, 2012 |title=DSN Aperature Enhancement Project |url=http://www.nasa.gov/content/deep-space-network-aperture-enhancement-project/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150205070546/http://www.nasa.gov/content/deep-space-network-aperture-enhancement-project/ |archive-date=February 5, 2015 |access-date=June 6, 2013 |publisher=[[NASA]] }}</ref> All the 34-meter HEF antennas have been replaced.

Because of capacity limits on the DSN, new spacecraft intended for missions beyond [[geocentric orbit]]s are being equipped to use the [[beacon mode service]], which allows such missions to operate without the DSN most of the time.<ref>{{Cite tech report |last1=Wyatt |first1=E. Jay |last2=Foster |first2=Mike |last3=Schlutsmeyer |first3=Alan |last4=Sherwood |first4=Rob |last5=Sue |first5=Miles K. |url=https://www.scss.tcd.ie/Stephen.Farrell/ipn/background/beacon-overview.pdf |title=An Overview of the Beacon Monitor Operations Technology |publisher=[[JPL]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230321091326/https://www.scss.tcd.ie/stephen.farrell/ipn/background/beacon-overview.pdf |archive-date=March 21, 2023 |url-status=live }}</ref>  In addition, NASA is creating a network of [[Lunar Exploration Ground Sites]] to offload much of the lunar and Artemis mission needs from the DSN.

==DSN and radio science==
[[File:Illustration of Juno spacecraft at Jupiter (PIA19639).jpg|thumb|upright|Illustration of ''Juno'' and Jupiter. ''Juno'' is in a polar orbit that takes it close to Jupiter as it passes from north to south, getting a view of both poles. During the GS experiment it must point its antenna at the Deep Space Network on Earth to pick up a special signal sent from DSN.]]
The DSN forms one portion of the radio sciences experiment included on most deep space missions, where radio links between spacecraft and Earth are used to investigate planetary science, space physics and fundamental physics.  The experiments include radio occultations, gravity field determination and celestial mechanics, bistatic scattering, doppler wind experiments, solar corona characterization, and tests of fundamental physics.<ref>{{cite web |title=Radio Science|url=https://scienceandtechnology.jpl.nasa.gov/research/research-topics-list/planetary-sciences/radio-science |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161203081603/http://scienceandtechnology.jpl.nasa.gov/research/research-topics-list/planetary-sciences/radio-science |url-status=dead |archive-date=2016-12-03 |publisher=JPL}}</ref>

For example, the Deep Space Network forms one component of the [[Gravity Science (Juno)|gravity science experiment on ''Juno'']].  This includes special communication hardware on Juno and uses its communication system.<ref name="europlanet-eu.org">{{Cite web | url=http://www.europlanet-eu.org/juno-europe/ | title=European Involvement in Juno – Europlanet Society}}</ref> The DSN radiates a Ka-band uplink, which is picked up by ''Juno''{{'}}s Ka-Band communication system and then processed by a special communication box called KaTS, and then this new signal is sent back the DSN.<ref name="europlanet-eu.org"/> This allows the velocity of the spacecraft over time to be determined with a level of precision that allows a more accurate determination of the gravity field at planet Jupiter.<ref name="europlanet-eu.org"/><ref>{{Cite news |last=Pearson |first=Ezzy |date=June 4, 2016 |title=What will we learn from the Juno mission? |url=https://www.sciencefocus.com/space/what-will-we-learn-from-the-juno-mission |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240121201239/https://www.sciencefocus.com/space/what-will-we-learn-from-the-juno-mission |archive-date=January 21, 2024 |work=Science Focus |publisher=[[BBC Online]] }}</ref>

Another radio science experiment is [[REX (New Horizons)|REX]] on the ''New Horizons'' spacecraft to Pluto-Charon. REX received a signal from Earth as it was occulted by Pluto, to take various measurements of that system of bodies.

WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: New Space Race
======================================================================

{{Short description|Renewed 21st-century competition in space exploration}}
{{About|the renewed competition in space exploration|attempts to land a human on Mars|Mars race|other space races|List of space races|other uses of the term|Space Race (disambiguation)}}

{{Spaceflight sidebar}}

The '''New Space Race'''<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |last=Riley |first=Patrick |title=The New Space Race |url=https://www.britannica.com/story/new-space-race-map-and-timeline-infographic |access-date=April 10, 2026 |website=[[Encyclopædia Britannica]]}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=April 8, 2026 |title=The New Space Race |url=https://aerospaceamerica.aiaa.org/the-new-space-race/ |access-date=April 10, 2026 |website=[[Aerospace America]] |language=en-US}}</ref><ref name=":3">{{Cite web |title=The New Space Race {{!}} Power & Politics in 21st Century |url=https://www.rmg.co.uk/stories/space-astronomy/new-space-race-astropolitics-power-21st-century |access-date=April 10, 2026 |website=Royal Museums Greenwich |language=en}}</ref> or '''Second Space Race'''<ref>Fawkes, Steven (October 2006), ''[https://www.researchgate.net/publication/259324441_The_Second_Space_Race The Second Space Race]'', [[Journal of the British Interplanetary Society]], vol. 59, p. 364–367</ref><ref name=":2">{{Cite web |last=Emerson |first=Andrew Michael |date=January 25, 2022 |title=The Second Space Race: Democratic Outcomes for the Future of Space |url=https://gjia.georgetown.edu/science-technology/the-second-space-race-democratic-outcomes-for-the-future-of-space/ |access-date=April 10, 2026 |website=[[Georgetown Journal of International Affairs]] |language=en}}</ref> describes the renewed competition in [[space exploration]] and [[Space technology|technological]] development in the 21st century, primarily between the [[space programs]] of [[Chinese space program|China]] and the [[Space policy of the United States|United States]], as well as other nations, and [[private spaceflight]]. This modern race is characterized by a broad range of objectives, including large [[satellite constellation]]s,<ref name=":5">{{cite web |date=June 10, 2019 |title=On the increasing number of satellite constellations |url=https://www.eso.org/public/announcements/ann19029/ |website=[[European Southern Observatory]] |access-date=April 10, 2026 |language=en}}</ref> advancements in [[Reusable launch vehicle|reusable launch vehicles]] and [[Reusable spacecraft|spacecraft]],<ref name=":2" /> a return to [[Moon landing|crewed Moon landings]], establishing a permanent [[moonbase]],<ref name=":3" /><ref name=":7">{{Cite web |last=Dangwal |first=Ashish |date=November 22, 2023 |title=1st Country With Lunar Outpost, Competition 'Heating-Up' Between US-Led Artemis & China's ILRS |url=https://www.eurasiantimes.com/new-artemis-or-china-led-international-lunar-research-station/ |access-date=April 10, 2026 |website=Latest Asian, Middle-East, EurAsian, Indian News |language=en-US}}</ref> and [[human mission to Mars|crewed missions to Mars]].<ref name=":8">{{Cite web |title=Moon to Mars {{!}} NASA's Artemis Program |url=https://www.nasa.gov/humans-in-space/artemis/ |access-date=April 10, 2026 |language=en-US|website=[[NASA]]}}</ref><ref name=":9">{{Cite web |last=Auslender |first=Viki |date=October 1, 2023 |title=The new space race: Mars, the Moon, and the new political frontier |url=https://www.calcalistech.com/ctechnews/article/ryjnpsiga |access-date=April 10, 2026 |website=ctech |language=en}}</ref> 

The [[Space Race]] was part of the [[Cold War]], a rivalry between the US and the [[Soviet Union]], and saw the realization of [[Satellite|satellites]], crewed Moon landings, [[Space station|space stations]], and [[interplanetary spaceflight]]. In the 21st century, the [[China Manned Space Program]] saw its [[Shenzhou 5|first crewed flight]], [[Tiangong program|two prototype space stations]], and a continuously-occupied modular space station, [[Tiangong space station|''Tiangong'']]; the [[China National Space Administration]] sent orbiters, landers, and rovers [[Chinese Lunar Exploration Program|to the Moon]] and [[Tianwen-1|to Mars]]. In the same period, NASA's human spaceflight centered on the [[International Space Station]]; crewed lunar hardware was consolidated under the [[Artemis program]] in 2017, centered on the [[Space Launch System]] and [[Orion (spacecraft)|Orion]] spacecraft; long-term NASA [[Space probe|probes]] [[Mars Exploration Program#Missions|explored the Martian surface]], [[Juno (spacecraft)|Jupiter]], and [[Cassini–Huygens|Saturn]]. Humans returned to [[cislunar space]] during NASA's [[Artemis II]] flight in 2026, for the first time [[Apollo 17|since 1972]]. The US currently targets a crewed lunar landing with [[Artemis IV]] in 2028. China plans a [[Long March 10]]-launched crewed lunar landing in 2029, and [[Tianwen-3|a robotic Mars sample return]] launch in 2028.

Some have argued that the New Space Race is part of a [[Second Cold War]] between China and the US.<ref name=":12">{{Cite web |last=King |first=Ryan Erik |date=2025-04-23 |title=U.S. Blocking Countries From Hitching Ride With Rival Moon Base Project, China Claims |url=https://www.jalopnik.com/1842246/us-blocks-countries-rival-moon-base-project-china-claim/ |access-date=2026-05-10 |website=Jalopnik |language=en-US}}</ref> The New Space Race is seen as more [[Polarity (international relations)|multipolar]] than the original. The US-led [[Artemis Accords]] involve 68 nations, including [[European Space Agency|space agencies of Europe]], [[Department of Space|India]], [[Japanese space program|Japan]], [[Canadian Space Agency|Canada]], and the [[Mohammed bin Rashid Space Centre|UAE]]. China and Russia's [[Roscosmos]] lead the [[International Lunar Research Station]] effort.<ref name=":6">{{Cite web |last=Jones |first=Andrew |date=2024-06-12 |title=ESA-China moon cooperation could end with Chang'e-6 |url=https://spacenews.com/esa-china-moon-cooperation-could-end-with-change-6/ |access-date=2026-05-07 |website=SpaceNews |language=en-US}}</ref> Collaborations include ESA's Orion [[European Service Module]], alongside other contributions made by five other space agencies in the cancelled NASA-led [[Lunar Gateway]] space station.

The concept also includes the "[[billionaire space race]]": increasing involvement of private [[aerospace]] companies, such as [[SpaceX]], [[Blue Origin]], and [[Virgin Galactic]]. These have transformed [[Space launch market competition|launch services]] via the [[Falcon 9]], the [[satellite internet constellation]] market with [[Starlink]], and [[space tourism]] via [[SpaceX Dragon 2|Dragon 2]], [[New Shepard]], and [[SpaceShipTwo]].

==Participants and objectives==
[[File:Artemis II launch (SLS MAF 20260401 ArtemisIILaunch 02) crop.jpg|thumb|[[Space Launch System]] with the [[Orion (spacecraft)|Orion spacecraft]] launching from [[Kennedy Space Center Launch Complex 39B]] for [[Artemis II]]]]

The primary race is between the [[Government space agency|government space agencies]] of the [[NASA|United States]] and [[China National Space Administration|China]].<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite news |last=Gebrekidan |first=Selam |date=April 2, 2026 |title=The Race for the Future of the Moon |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2026/04/02/world/space-artemis-us-china-trump-iran-pam-bondi.html |access-date=April 10, 2026 |work=[[The New York Times]] |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite news |last=Glasner |first=Eli |date=April 4, 2026 |title=The new space race: Why the U.S. and China are racing to the moon |url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/science/space-race-us-china-moon-9.7150635 |access-date=April 10, 2026 |work=[[CBC News]]}}</ref> The US uses its [[Artemis program]] and China uses its [[Chinese Lunar Exploration Program]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=October 1, 2023 |title=The new space race: Mars, the Moon, and the new political frontier |url=https://www.calcalistech.com/ctechnews/article/ryjnpsiga |access-date=April 12, 2026 |website=ctech |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Berger |first=Eric |date=May 3, 2024 |title=NASA hasn't landed on the Moon in decades—China just sent its third in six years |url=https://arstechnica.com/space/2024/05/china-just-launched-another-ambitious-lunar-mission-is-nasa-falling-behind/ |access-date=April 12, 2026 |website=Ars Technica |language=en-us}}</ref>

In the 2020s, both the US and China are engaged in an effort to establish a [[Moonbase|permanent presence on the Moon]], with an emphasis on the [[lunar south pole]]. Further objectives include large [[satellite constellation]]s,<ref name=":5" /> advancements in [[Reusable launch vehicle|reusable launch vehicles]] and [[Reusable spacecraft|spacecraft]],<ref name=":2" /> establishing a permanent a return to [[Moon landing|crewed Moon landings]], and [[human mission to Mars|crewed missions to Mars]].<ref name=":8" /><ref name=":9" />

Other nations, such as [[Roscosmos|Russia]], [[ISRO|India]],<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":4">{{Cite news |last1=Kumar |first1=Hari |last2=Travelli |first2=Alex |last3=Mashal |first3=Mujib |last4=Chang |first4=Kenneth |date=August 23, 2023 |title=India Moon Landing: In Latest Moon Race, India Lands First in Southern Polar Region |language=en-US |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/live/2023/08/23/science/india-moon-landing-chandrayaan-3 |url-status=live |access-date=April 10, 2026 |issn=0362-4331}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Bhattacharjee |first=Nivedita |date=January 22, 2025 |title=India File: Jostling for position in the space race |url=https://www.reuters.com/world/india/india-file-jostling-position-space-race-2025-01-22/ |access-date=April 10, 2026 |work=[[Reuters]]}}</ref> [[JAXA|Japan]],<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{cite news |last1=Cooper |first1=Chris |last2=Matsuda |first2=Kiyotaka |date=November 29, 2016 |title=The U.S. and China Are Fighting Over Mars, but Japan May Win the Space Race |url=https://www.bloomberg.com/graphics/2016-asia-space-race/japan.html |publisher=Bloomberg |access-date=April 10, 2026}}</ref> as well as [[European Space Agency|European countries]],<ref>{{Cite news |last=Desmarais |first=Anna |date=November 24, 2025 |title=The new space race: These are the different space strategies across Europe |url=https://www.euronews.com/next/2025/11/24/the-new-space-race-these-are-the-different-space-strategies-across-europe |access-date=April 10, 2026 |work=[[Euronews]]}}</ref> are also active participants.

==Primary missions==

===Lunar missions===
[[File:Artemis Base Camp.png|thumb|Concept art of [[Artemis Base Camp]] at the [[lunar south pole]]]]

Most missions associated with the New Space Race have focused on [[lunar exploration]]. A particular emphasis has been placed on the [[lunar south pole]], where a large fraction of [[Lunar water|lunar water ice]] may be accessible. These missions are intended to demonstrate technologies and capabilities for sustained lunar exploration in preparation for the eventual establishment of [[Moonbase|permanent human outposts]], as well as to serve as a proving ground and stepping stone for future [[human mission to Mars|crewed missions to Mars]].<ref name=":8" /><ref name=":9" />

In 2019, China became the first country to achieve a [[soft landing]] on the [[far side of the Moon]] with [[Chang'e 4]], which deployed [[Yutu-2|''Yutu''-2]], which remains operational as the longest-lived lunar rover ever.<ref>{{cite news|last=Lyons|first=Kate|title=Chang'e 4 landing: China probe makes historic touchdown on far side of the moon|url=https://www.theguardian.com/science/2019/jan/03/china-probe-change-4-land-far-side-moon-basin-crater|access-date=3 January 2019|newspaper=The Guardian|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190103043232/https://www.theguardian.com/science/2019/jan/03/china-probe-change-4-land-far-side-moon-basin-crater|archive-date=3 January 2019|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="planetary_success">{{cite web|url=http://www.planetary.org/blogs/jason-davis/change4-success.html|title=China successfully lands Chang'e-4 on far side of Moon|access-date=3 January 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190103133008/http://www.planetary.org/blogs/jason-davis/change4-success.html|archive-date=3 January 2019|url-status=live}}</ref>  In 2024, China became the first country to return lunar samples from the far side of the Moon with [[Chang'e 6]].<ref>{{Cite web |author1=Rahul Rao |date=2024-06-25 |title=China's Chang'e 6 probe will soon bring samples of the moon's far side to Earth — and scientists are getting excited |url=https://www.space.com/change-6-sample-return-science-investigations-scientists |access-date=2024-06-25 |website=Space.com |language=en |archive-date=25 June 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240625053616/https://www.space.com/change-6-sample-return-science-investigations-scientists |url-status=live }}</ref> China plans a [[Long March 10]]-launched crewed landing in 2029, likely late in the year.<ref>{{Cite web |last=C |first=Jack |title=Where and When Will China Land Taikonauts on the Moon? |url=https://www.china-in-space.com/p/where-and-when-will-china-land-taikonauts |access-date=2026-07-05 |website=www.china-in-space.com |language=en}}</ref>

In April 2026, NASA's [[Artemis II]] mission returned astronauts to the vicinity of the Moon for the first time since the [[Apollo program]], including the first non-American to travel beyond [[low Earth orbit]] ([[Canadian astronaut]] [[Jeremy Hansen]]), and broke the record previously set by [[Apollo 13]] for the farthest distance humans have ever traveled from Earth.<ref name="Graf 2026-04-06">{{Cite web |last=Graf |first=Abby |date=April 6, 2026 |title=Artemis II Flight Day 6: Lunar Flyby Updates |url=https://www.nasa.gov/blogs/missions/2026/04/06/artemis-ii-flight-day-6-lunar-flyby-updates/ |access-date=April 6, 2026 |website=NASA |language=en-US }}</ref><ref name="space.com timeline">{{cite web |website=space.com |title=NASA Artemis 2 astronauts to make historic moon flyby today. Here's what to expect hour by hour (timeline) |url=https://www.space.com/space-exploration/artemis/nasa-artemis-2-astronauts-to-make-historic-moon-flyby-today-heres-what-to-expect-hour-by-hour-timeline |access-date=April 6, 2026 |date=April 6, 2026|last=Malik|first=Tariq}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Wall |first=Mike |date=April 6, 2026 |title=Artemis 2 breaks humanity's all-time distance record during historic loop around the moon |url=https://www.space.com/space-exploration/artemis/artemis-2-breaks-humanitys-all-time-distance-record-during-historic-loop-around-the-moon }}</ref> The Artemis program's [[Human Landing System]], either a [[Blue Moon (spacecraft)|Blue Moon Mark 2]] or [[Starship HLS]], will be selected following orbital testing during [[Artemis III]] in 2027, while [[Artemis IV]] is planned to land a crew on the surface in 2028.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Foust |first=Jeff |date=2022-10-30 |title=Lunar landing restored for Artemis 4 mission |url=https://spacenews.com/lunar-landing-restored-for-artemis-4-mission/ |access-date=2026-07-05 |website=SpaceNews |language=en-US}}</ref>

India has already made significant progress with missions such as [[Chandrayaan-3]], which successfully landed near the lunar south polar region on 23 August 2023, making it one of the few nations to achieve a soft landing on the Moon and the first to land near the lunar south pole.<ref name=":4" />

===Martian missions===
[[File:Mars sample returnjpl.jpg|thumb|Launch concept of an interplanetary [[Mars sample-return mission]]]]

Mars remains a longer-term objective of the New Space Race. Unlike the Moon, Mars has not yet been visited by humans, and its greater distance makes crewed missions substantially more difficult. Robotic exploration has therefore continued to serve as a precursor to potential crewed missions.

In 2021, China became only the second country (after the United States) to successfully operate a lander and rover on Mars with [[Tianwen-1|''Tianwen''-1]] and [[Zhurong (rover)|''Zhurong'']].<ref>{{cite web|url= https://www.nbcnews.com/science/space/china-becomes-only-second-nation-history-land-rover-mars-n1267410 |title= China becomes only second nation in history to land a rover on Mars |website=NBC News |date=15 May 2021 |first= Tim |last=Fitzsimons }}</ref>

Robotic [[Mars sample-return mission|Mars sample-return missions]] have been planned [[Tianwen-3|by China]], as well as [[NASA-ESA Mars Sample Return|by NASA and the European Space Agency]]. However, as of August 2026, following [[2026 United States federal budget#January 2026 negotiations |US congressional budget cuts]] and ESA member proposals to cancel the Earth Return Orbiter (ERO)—a key element of the sample return<ref>{{Cite web |title=Appropriators Release Three-Bill Minibus {{!}} United States Senate Committee on Appropriations |url=https://www.appropriations.senate.gov/news/minority/appropriators-release-three-bill-minibus |access-date=September 1, 2026 |website=www.appropriations.senate.gov |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Parsonson |first=Andrew |date=March 28, 2026 |title=ESA Member States Call for Cancellation of Earth Return Orbiter |url=https://europeanspaceflight.com/esa-member-states-call-for-cancellation-of-earth-return-orbiter/ |access-date=September 1, 2026 |website=European Spaceflight |language=en-US}}</ref>—the joint mission is considered virtually cancelled.<ref>{{Cite web |title=NASA's Mars Sample Return mission is dead |url=https://www.science.org/content/article/nasa-s-mars-sample-return-mission-dead |access-date=September 1, 2026 |website=www.science.org |language=en}}</ref>

===Space stations===
[[File:Chinese Tiangong Space Station.jpg|thumb|Rendering of China's [[Tiangong space station|''Tiangong'' space station]] with a [[Tianzhou spacecraft|''Tianzhou'' spacecraft]] docked aft and two [[Shenzhou spacecraft|''Shenzhou'' spacecraft]] docked to the forward and nadir (Earth facing) ports]]

The New Space Race has also expanded into the development of space stations and commercial destinations in low Earth orbit.

Since 2021, China has operated [[Tiangong space station|''Tiangong'']], the only space station in orbit alongside the [[International Space Station]], and the third to use [[Modular design#In space stations|modular design]] following ''[[Mir]]'' and the ISS.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Tiangong, China’s space station |url=https://www.planetary.org/space-missions/chinese-space-station |access-date=September 1, 2026 |website=The Planetary Society |language=en}}</ref>

==Governance==
{{See also|Space law}}
[[File:The growth of all tracked objects in space over time (space debris and satellites).png|thumb|The growth of all tracked objects in space over time showing a recent increase of active satellites<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Lawrence |first1=Andy |last2=Rawls |first2=Meredith L. |last3=Jah |first3=Moriba |last4=Boley |first4=Aaron |last5=Di Vruno |first5=Federico |last6=Garrington |first6=Simon |last7=Kramer |first7=Michael |last8=Lawler |first8=Samantha |last9=Lowenthal |first9=James |last10=McDowell |first10=Jonathan |last11=McCaughrean |first11=Mark |title=The case for space environmentalism |journal=Nature Astronomy |date=April 2022 |volume=6 |issue=4 |pages=428–435 |doi=10.1038/s41550-022-01655-6 |arxiv=2204.10025 |bibcode=2022NatAs...6..428L |s2cid=248300127 |language=en |issn=2397-3366}}</ref>]]

Some have argued the New Space Race is a component of the [[Second Cold War]] concept,<ref name=":12" /> pointing to the alignment under the US-led [[Artemis Accords]] with Europe, India, and Japan, contrasted with the China and Russia-led [[International Lunar Research Station]] (ILRS).<ref name=":6" /> {{As of|2026|5}}, 67 nations have joined the Artemis Accords, predominantly in the [[Global North]] and [[Latin America]], while 13 nations have joined the ILRS, predominantly in the [[Global South]]. China and Russia initially hoped to attract major European states to the project, but the [[2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine]] was seen as ending these efforts.<ref name=":62">{{Cite web |last=Jones |first=Andrew |date=2024-06-12 |title=ESA-China moon cooperation could end with Chang'e-6 |url=https://spacenews.com/esa-china-moon-cooperation-could-end-with-change-6/ |access-date=2026-05-07 |website=SpaceNews |language=en-US}}</ref>

Some scholars have argued the substance of the Accords is "uncontentious" and represent a "significant political attempt to codify key principles of space law" for governing nations' space activities.<ref name="Newman 2020">{{cite web |last=Newman |first=Christopher |date=October 19, 2020 |title=Artemis Accords: why many countries are refusing to sign Moon exploration agreement |url=http://theconversation.com/artemis-accords-why-many-countries-are-refusing-to-sign-moon-exploration-agreement-148134 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220625095410/https://theconversation.com/artemis-accords-why-many-countries-are-refusing-to-sign-moon-exploration-agreement-148134 |archive-date=June 25, 2022 |access-date=June 17, 2021 |website=[[The Conversation (website)|The Conversation]]}}</ref> China and Russia have criticized the Accords' framework for [[lunar mining]] as too favorable to US interests, with China describing them as "akin to European colonial [[enclosure]] land-taking methods."<ref name="The Diplomat 2020">{{cite web |last1=Ji |first1=Elliot |last2=Cerny |first2=Michael B |last3=Piliero |first3=Raphael J |date=September 17, 2020 |title=What Does China Think About NASA's Artemis Accords? |url=https://thediplomat.com/2020/09/what-does-china-think-about-nasas-artemis-accords/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220202143759/https://thediplomat.com/2020/09/what-does-china-think-about-nasas-artemis-accords/ |archive-date=February 2, 2022 |access-date= |website=[[The Diplomat (magazine)|The Diplomat]]}}</ref><ref name="pmid33033208">{{cite journal |vauthors=Boley A, Byers M |year=2020 |title=U.S. policy puts the safe development of space at risk |journal=[[Science (journal)|Science]] |volume=370 |issue=6513 |pages=174–175 |bibcode=2020Sci...370..174B |doi=10.1126/science.abd3402 |pmid=33033208 |s2cid=222211122}}</ref> 

==Private sector involvement==
{{Main|Private spaceflight|Billionaire space race}}
[[File:NASA 2 HLS.webp|thumb|Renderings of the [[Human Landing System]] spacecraft: [[SpaceX]]'s [[Starship HLS]] (''left'') and [[Blue Origin]]'s [[Blue Moon Mark 2]] (''right'')]]

Unlike the original [[Space Race]] during the [[Cold War]] era, private [[aerospace]] companies play a massive role in the New Space Race, with [[SpaceX]] and [[Blue Origin]] developing [[Launch vehicle|launch technology]] and services.<ref name=":3" /><ref name=":1" /> This [[private spaceflight]] race involves sending privately developed rockets and vehicles to various destinations in space, often in response to government programs or even to develop the [[space tourism]] sector.<ref>{{cite book |author=Guthrie |first=Julian |title=How to Make a Spaceship: A Band of Renegades, an Epic Race, and the Birth of Private Spaceflight |date=2016 |publisher=Penguin Press |isbn=978-1-59420-672-6}}</ref>

SpaceX's [[Falcon 9]] has the [[Comparison of orbital launch systems|most total launches of an active vehicle]] worldwide,<ref>{{Cite web |last=Berger |first=Eric |date=2022-02-03 |title=The Falcon 9 may now be the safest rocket ever launched |url=https://arstechnica.com/science/2022/02/spacexs-falcon-9-rocket-has-set-a-record-for-most-consecutive-successes/ |access-date=2026-07-05 |website=Ars Technica |language=en}}</ref> its in-development [[SpaceX Starship|Starship]] is the [[Super heavy-lift launch vehicle|most powerful rocket flown]],<ref>{{Cite web |last=Berger |first=Eric |date=2024-04-08 |title=Elon Musk just gave another Mars speech—this time the vision seems tangible |url=https://arstechnica.com/space/2024/04/elon-musk-just-gave-another-mars-speech-this-time-the-vision-seems-tangible/ |access-date=2026-07-05 |website=Ars Technica |language=en}}</ref> [[Starlink]] comprises 75% of active maneuverable satellites in orbit as of March 2026;<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Bennett |first=Mia M. |last2=Cudney |first2=Zachary |date=2026-01-09 |title=Holding up the skies: is Starlink occupying low Earth orbit? |url=https://doi.org/10.1080/21622671.2025.2594491 |journal=Territory, Politics, Governance |volume=0 |issue=0 |pages=1–19 |doi=10.1080/21622671.2025.2594491 |issn=2162-2671|url-access=subscription |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref name="S-1">{{Cite web |date=May 20, 2026 |title=FORM S-1: Space Exploration Technologies Corp. |url=https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1181412/000162828026036936/spaceexplorationtechnologi.htm |access-date=May 21, 2026}}</ref> Blue Origin's [[New Glenn]] is the most powerful reusable rocket to reach orbit.<ref>{{Cite web |title=New Glenn {{!}} Blue Origin |url=https://www.blueorigin.com/new-glenn |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260317064435/https://www.blueorigin.com/new-glenn |archive-date=2026-03-17 |access-date=2026-07-05 |website=Blue Origin |language=en-US}}</ref>

In October 2025, NASA announced that it would reopen competition to develop its [[Human Landing System]] for the [[Artemis III]] mission, planning to use Space X's [[Starship HLS]] or Blue Origin's [[Blue Moon Mark 2]], or both, depending on which was ready. NASA's acting administrator [[Sean Duffy]] said, "SpaceX has the contract to build the HLS which will get U.S. astronauts there on Artemis III. But, competition and innovation are the keys to our dominance in space so NASA is opening up HLS production to Blue Origin and other great American companies."<ref>{{cite web |last=Edwards |first=Brook |date=October 20, 2025 |title=NASA reopens competition for Artemis lunar lander contract |url=https://www.floridatoday.com/story/tech/science/space/spacex/2025/10/20/with-spacex-starship-slow-to-progress-nasa-reopens-artemis-iii-contract-blue-origin/86802546007/ |publisher=[[Florida Today]]|access-date=May 30, 2026}}</ref>

======================================================================
WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: Orbital spaceflight
======================================================================

{{short description|Spaceflight where spacecraft orbits an astronomical body}}
{{More citations needed|date=March 2008}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=April 2020}}
[[File:Animation of AMC-8 trajectory around Earth.gif|300px|thumb|right|Orbit of [[AMC-8]] satellite around the Earth in 2000, transferring from a [[geostationary transfer orbit]] to a [[geostationary orbit]]]]An '''orbital spaceflight''' (or '''orbital flight''') is a [[spaceflight]] in which a [[spacecraft]] is placed on a trajectory where it could remain in [[outer space|space]] for at least one [[orbit]]. To do this [[Geocentric orbit|around the Earth]], it must be on a free trajectory which has an [[altitude]] at [[Apsis|perigee]] (altitude at closest approach) around {{convert|80|km|mi|sp=us}}; this is the [[Outer space#Boundary|boundary of space]] as defined by [[NASA]], the [[United States Air Force|US Air Force]] and the [[Federal Aviation Administration|FAA]]. To remain in orbit at this altitude requires an [[orbital speed]] of ~7.8&nbsp;km/s. Orbital speed is slower for higher orbits, but attaining them requires greater [[delta-v]]. The [[Fédération Aéronautique Internationale]] has established the [[Kármán line]] at an altitude of {{convert|100|km|mi|abbr=on}} as a working definition for the boundary between aeronautics and astronautics. This is used because at an altitude of about {{Convert|100|km|mi|abbr=on}}, as [[Theodore von Kármán]] calculated, a vehicle would have to travel faster than [[Orbital speed|orbital velocity]] to derive sufficient [[aerodynamic lift]] from the atmosphere to support itself.<ref>{{cite book| last=O'Leary | first=Beth Laura | date=2009 | title=Handbook of space engineering, archaeology, and heritage | series=Advances in engineering | editor1-first=Ann Garrison | editor1-last=Darrin | publisher=CRC Press | isbn=978-1-4200-8431-3 | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=dTwIDun4MroC&pg=PA84 }}</ref>{{rp|84}}<ref name=space_begin>{{cite web|title = Where does space begin? – Aerospace Engineering, Aviation News, Salary, Jobs and Museums |url = http://aerospaceengineering.aero/where-does-space-begin/ |website = Aerospace Engineering, Aviation News, Salary, Jobs and Museums |access-date = 2015-11-10 |language = en-US |url-status=live |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20151117034012/http://aerospaceengineering.aero/where-does-space-begin/ |archive-date = 2015-11-17}}</ref>

Due to [[Aerodynamic drag|atmospheric drag]], the lowest altitude at which an object in a circular orbit can complete at least one full revolution without propulsion is approximately {{convert|150|km|mi}}.

The expression "orbital spaceflight" is mostly used to distinguish from [[sub-orbital spaceflight]]s, which are flights where the [[Apsis|apogee]] of a spacecraft reaches space, but the perigee is too low.<ref>{{Cite web|last=February 2020|first=Adam Mann 10|title=What's the difference between orbital and suborbital spaceflight?|url=https://www.space.com/suborbital-orbital-flight.html|access-date=2020-07-13|website=Space.com|date=10 February 2020|language=en|archive-date=16 June 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200616022726/https://www.space.com/suborbital-orbital-flight.html|url-status=live}}</ref>

==Trajectory==
{{main|Geocentric orbit}}
There are three main "bands" of [[orbit]] around the Earth: [[low Earth orbit]] (LEO), [[medium Earth orbit]] (MEO), and [[geostationary orbit]] (GEO).

According to [[orbital mechanics]], an orbit lies in a particular, largely fixed plane around the Earth, which coincides with the center of the Earth, and may be inclined with respect to the equator. The relative motion of the spacecraft and the movement of the Earth's surface, as the Earth rotates on its axis, determine the position that the spacecraft appears in the sky from the ground, and which parts of the Earth are visible from the spacecraft.

It is possible to calculate a [[ground track]] that shows which part of the Earth a spacecraft is immediately above; this is useful for helping to visualise the orbit.

==Launch==
{| class=wikitable style="text-align:center; float:right; margin:2px"
