The '''Space Launch System''' ('''SLS''') is an American [[Two-stage-to-orbit|two-stage]] [[Super heavy-lift launch vehicle|super heavy-lift]] [[Expendable launch system|expendable launch vehicle]] used by [[NASA]]. The primary launch vehicle for the [[Artemis program]], SLS is designed to launch the four-person [[Orion (spacecraft)|Orion spacecraft]]. The rocket first launched in November 2022, carrying the uncrewed [[Artemis&nbsp;I]] mission. Its only crewed launch has been for the [[Artemis&nbsp;II]] lunar [[Flyby (spaceflight)|flyby]] in April 2026, becoming the second launch vehicle to carry humans beyond [[low Earth orbit]] (LEO), after NASA's [[Saturn V]] of the [[Apollo program]].

Development of SLS began in 2011 as a congressionally mandated replacement for the retiring [[Space Shuttle]] program and the cancelled [[Ares&nbsp;I]] and [[Ares&nbsp;V]] launch vehicles of the [[Constellation program]],<!--<ref name="senatebill" /><ref name="SFN20110331" /><ref name="SR-20131125" /> --> incorporating some hardware from both programs. Costing US$31.6 billion as of 2025, the project has been criticized for mismanagement, budget overruns, and delays, but ultimately [[Artemis II|succeeded in human spaceflight in 2026]].<!--<ref name="PL-111-267" /> -->

All SLS launches take place from [[Kennedy Space Center Launch Complex 39B|Launch Complex 39B]] at the [[Kennedy Space Center]] in Florida. The new [[Boeing]]-built [[Space Launch System core stage|core stage]] is powered by four ex-Shuttle [[RS-25]] engines. [[Booster (rocketry)|Attached to the core]] are two [[Northrop Grumman]] [[Space Shuttle Solid Rocket Booster#Five-segment booster|five-segment Solid Rocket Boosters]], built for the Ares vehicles, tested on [[Ares I-X]], developed from the Shuttle's [[Space Shuttle Solid Rocket Booster|four-segment SRB]]. SLS currently uses the [[Delta Cryogenic Second Stage#Interim Cryogenic Propulsion Stage|Interim Cryogenic Propulsion Stage]] (ICPS) as its second stage, for the [[Orbit insertion|insertions]] to low Earth orbit and trans-lunar injection. ICPS uses the [[RL10]] engine, and was derived from the [[Delta Cryogenic Second Stage]] designed by [[National Space Development Agency of Japan|Japan's space agency]]. [[Aerojet Rocketdyne]] builds the RS-25 and RL10 engines.

Starting from Artemis&nbsp;IV, SLS will use the [[Centaur V]] upper stage, developed for the [[Vulcan Centaur]], instead of ICPS. NASA previously planned to upgrade SLS from its current Block 1 configuration to a Block 1B and Block 2, but cancelled these plans in February 2026, aiming to standardize on Block&nbsp;1.<ref name="Berger 2026" /><ref name=":6" /> Block&nbsp;1B was to use the [[Exploration Upper Stage]], and Block&nbsp;2 would have used new solid rocket boosters. There plans were included in Section 10812 the most recent NASA Authorization Act and have not been rescinded by Congress.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Rep. Ryan |first=Tim [D-OH-13 |date=2022-08-09 |title=Text - H.R.4346 - 117th Congress (2021-2022): CHIPS and Science Act |url=https://www.congress.gov/bill/117th-congress/house-bill/4346/text |access-date=2026-10-24 |website=www.congress.gov}}</ref>

While SLS has the highest liftoff thrust of any rocket to ever carry humans, {{Convert|39|MN|lk=on|abbr=off}},{{Efn|The Soviet [[N-1 rocket]] produced 45.7 MN and was also designed to carry humans to the Moon, but was never flown manned. [[SpaceX Starship]] is also planned to carry humans, and has demonstrated liftoff thrust exceeding 70 MN.{{citation needed|date=April 2026}}}}<ref>{{Cite web |last=Sauers |first=Elisha |date=2026-01-17 |title=Is SLS still the most powerful rocket? 5 facts as Artemis 2 rolls out |url=https://mashable.com/article/nasa-sls-artemis-2-rollout-facts |access-date=2026-04-15 |website=Mashable |language=en}}</ref> SLS's payload capacity to [[trans-lunar injection]] of {{Convert|27|MT|lb|0}} is only around half that of the Saturn V's {{Convert|48.6|MT|lb|0}} payload.<ref name="NASA-SLS">{{cite web |title=Space Launch System (SLS) Fact Sheet |url=https://www.nasa.gov/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/sls-4960-sls-fact-sheet-oct2024-508.pdf |publisher=NASA |access-date=2026-04-07}}</ref><ref name="NASA-SLS-secondary">{{cite web |title=SLS Space Launch System Secondary Payloads |url=https://www.nasa.gov/reference/sls-space-launch-system-secondary-payloads/ |publisher=NASA |access-date=2026-04-07}}</ref><ref name="NASA-SaturnV">{{cite report |title=Heavy-Lift Launch Vehicle Capability |url=https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/20100021048/downloads/20100021048.pdf |publisher=NASA |access-date=2026-04-07}}</ref><ref name="a">{{Cite conference |title=Progress on Enabling Unprecedented Payloads for Space in the 21st Century |conference=2010 IEEE Aerospace Conference |last=Creech |first=Steve |date=2010-01-01 |url=https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20100017341}}</ref> Thus for Artemis lunar landings, beginning with [[Artemis IV]] targeted early 2028, Orion is planned to dock with the [[Human Landing System]] (HLS) in lunar orbit or low Earth orbit, separately launched on a non-SLS rocket;<ref>{{Cite web |last=Foust |first=Jeff |date=2026-06-13 |title=Revised Artemis lunar lander plans take shape |url=https://spacenews.com/revised-artemis-lunar-lander-plans-take-shape/ |access-date=2026-06-15 |website=SpaceNews |language=en-US}}</ref> SpaceX's [[Starship HLS]] and [[Blue Origin]]'s [[Blue Moon (spacecraft)|Blue Moon]] are under development as HLS vehicles.<ref>{{cite web|title="Artemis mission plan"|url=https://www.nasa.gov/reference/human-landing-systems-2/}}</ref>

Its next scheduled flight is [[Artemis III]], a 2027 [[low Earth orbit]] docking test between Orion and HLS vehicles. Beginning with Artemis V, NASA will transfer SLS operations to the [[Deep Space Transport LLC]], a [[Private spaceflight|commercial launch provider]] consortium of Boeing and Northrop Grumman.

== Components ==
{{See also|Super heavy-lift launch vehicle#Comparison|l1=Comparison of super heavy-lift launch vehicles}}

The SLS is a [[Shuttle-derived vehicle|Space Shuttle-derived launch vehicle]]. Its first stage consists of a central core stage powered by four engines, flanked by two space shuttle-derived solid rocket boosters.<ref name="NSFTrades" /><ref name="NSFDual" /><ref name="NSF20110616" /><ref name="nsf-20120223" />

NASA had planned to introduce upgraded variants of the rocket. The Block&nbsp;1B configuration was to incorporate a larger, purpose-built upper stage, while the Block&nbsp;2 configuration was to feature newly developed solid rocket boosters. On February 26, 2026, NASA announced that it would standardize the Block&nbsp;1 configuration and pursue alternative upper-stage options.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Grush |first=Loren |date=February 27, 2026 |title=NASA Overhauls Moon Mission in Effort to Cut Risks and Costs |url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-02-27/nasa-overhauls-moon-mission-in-effort-to-cut-risks-and-costs |access-date=March 2, 2026 |work=[[Bloomberg News]]}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Wattles |first=Jackie |date=February 27, 2026 |title=NASA abruptly changes its roadmap to putting boots back on the moon |url=https://www.cnn.com/2026/02/27/science/nasa-moon-landing-artemis-schedule |access-date=March 2, 2026 |website=CNN |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=NASA Adds Mission to Artemis Lunar Program, Updates Architecture - NASA |url=https://www.nasa.gov/news-release/nasa-adds-mission-to-artemis-lunar-program-updates-architecture/ |access-date=March 2, 2026 |language=en-US}}</ref>

=== Core stage ===
{{main|Space Launch System core stage}}

[[File:Spacelaunchsystem-enginesection-jan2020.jpg|thumb|The SLS core stage rolling out of the [[Michoud Assembly Facility]]|left]]

The SLS core stage is built by [[Boeing]] at NASA's [[Michoud Assembly Facility]] in [[New Orleans]]. It measures {{Convert|65|m|sp=us}} in length and {{Convert|8.4|m|sp=us}} in diameter, matching the diameter of the [[Space Shuttle external tank]] to allow NASA to leverage Shuttle-era experience. The stage is visually similar to the Shuttle tank due to its rust-colored spray-on insulation.<ref name="SFN20110331" /><ref name="NSFAnnounce" />

The stage contains [[liquid hydrogen]] and [[liquid oxygen]] propellant tanks, the attach points for the solid rocket boosters, avionics, equipment for [[autogenous pressurization]] of the tanks, and the Main Propulsion System (MPS), an assembly of four [[RS-25]] engines with associated plumbing and hydraulic [[Gimbaled thrust|gimbal actuators]]. The first core stages reused MPS plumbing removed from the three remaining Space Shuttle orbiters following their decommissioning. The core stage, when combined with the solid rocket boosters, is capable of propelling the Orion spacecraft into a [[highly elliptical orbit]] without the upper stage firing, though the upper stage is required for trans-lunar injection.<ref name="NSFTrades" /><ref name="ArtDay" /><ref name="NASA_Fact-Sht" />

The core stage structure is primarily made of [[2219 aluminium alloy|2219 aluminum alloy]], and compared to the Space Shuttle external tank, several manufacturing improvements were incorporated.<ref name="NSF-20130218" /><ref name="NASA-20160602" /><ref name="NASA-20141115" /> Production began in 2014, but delays in manufacturing, testing, and integration postponed the readiness of the first flight article by several years. It uses ten barrel-shaped main sections, four domes, and seven rings.<ref name="SLS_CORE_FACT_SHEET"/>

The first four SLS missions will each use four of the remaining fourteen RS-25D engines left over from the Space Shuttle program. The final two engines needed were assembled from existing RS-25D spare parts.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Clark |first=Stephen |date=April 30, 2025 |title=NASA just swapped a 10-year-old Artemis II engine with one nearly twice its age |url=https://arstechnica.com/space/2025/04/nasa-just-swapped-a-10-year-old-artemis-ii-engine-with-one-nearly-twice-its-age/ |access-date=March 4, 2026 |work=[[Ars Technica]] |language=en}}</ref> [[Aerojet Rocketdyne]] refurbished these engines with modernized controllers, expanded throttle capability, and additional insulation to handle the higher thermal environment caused by proximity to the solid rocket boosters.<ref name="NASA-RS25-CS" /> Later flights will transition to the RS-25E, optimized for expendable use, being faster to build and costing 30% less.<ref name="NSFStennis012015" /><ref name="rocket20210329" /> Thrust for the refurbished RS-25D engines has been increased from {{cvt|2188 to 2281|kN|lb-f|lk=on|order=flip}}, while the RS-25E is rated at {{cvt|2321|kN|lb-f|order=flip}} per engine.<ref name="nsf-20201231" /><ref name="ntrs-2017" />  The first test firing of an RS-25E occurred in June 2025 and was declared successful.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Dean |first=LaToya |date=June 23, 2025 |title=NASA Tests New RS-25 Engine |url=https://www.nasa.gov/image-article/new-rs-25-engine/ |access-date=June 28, 2025 |website=NASA |language=en-US}}</ref>

The SLS uses a conical [[frustum]]-shaped [[Adapter (rocketry)|interstage]] known as the Launch Vehicle Stage Adapter (LVSA) between the core stage and the narrower diameter upper stage. The LVSA consists of sixteen [[aluminum-lithium]] panels made of [[2195 aluminium alloy|2195 aluminum alloy]] and is built by [[Teledyne Technologies|Teledyne Brown Engineering]].<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.tbe.com/en-us/news-and-media/Pages/teledyne-to-build-nasa-60-million-launch-vehicle-stage-adapter.aspx | title=Teledyne to Build NASA's $60 Million Launch Vehicle Stage Adapter | access-date=April 1, 2023 | archive-date=April 1, 2023 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230401232054/https://www.tbe.com/en-us/news-and-media/Pages/teledyne-to-build-nasa-60-million-launch-vehicle-stage-adapter.aspx | url-status=live}}</ref> The first unit cost approximately $60 million, with the next two costing $85 million combined.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.teledyne.com/en-us/news/Pages/Teledyne-Brown-Engineering-Awarded-$85-Million-NASA-Contract-to-Provide-Key-Stage-of-NASA%27s-Space-Launch-System-Vehicle-Ret.aspx|title=Teledyne Brown Engineering Awarded $85 Million NASA Contract to Provide Key Stage of NASA's Space Launch System Vehicle Returning Astronauts to the Moon|website=www.teledyne.com|access-date=May 31, 2023|archive-date=April 1, 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230401232059/https://www.teledyne.com/en-us/news/Pages/Teledyne-Brown-Engineering-Awarded-%2485-Million-NASA-Contract-to-Provide-Key-Stage-of-NASA%27s-Space-Launch-System-Vehicle-Ret.aspx|url-status=live}}</ref>

=== Solid rocket boosters ===
====Shuttle-derived====
[[File:Artemis II Preflight (NHQ202603300013).jpg|thumb|upright|SLS of [[Artemis&nbsp;II]], with side view showing one of the two boosters]]
The first eight SLS flights are planned to use two [[Space Shuttle Solid Rocket Booster#Five-segment booster|five-segment]] solid rocket boosters derived from the four-segment [[Space Shuttle Solid Rocket Booster]] manufactured by [[Northrop Grumman]]. The booster for the SLS incorporates casing segments previously flown as part of the Shuttle program, with the addition of a center segment to increase performance. The boosters feature updated avionics and lighter insulation but do not include a parachute recovery system, as they are expended after launch.<ref name="SFI-20160110" />

The boosters are filled with an [[ammonium perchlorate composite propellant]], consisting of [[Aluminium powder|aluminum powder]] (fuel) and [[ammonium perchlorate]] (oxidizer), bound together with [[polybutadiene acrylonitrile]]. The mixture has a rubber eraser-like consistency and is cast into each segment.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Perry |first1=Beverly |title=We've Got (Rocket) Chemistry, Part 2 |url=https://blogs.nasa.gov/Rocketology/2016/04/21/weve-got-rocket-chemistry-part-2/ |website=Rocketology: NASA's Space Launch System |publisher=National Aeronautics and Space Administration |access-date=September 30, 2022 |date=April 21, 2016 |archive-date=September 30, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220930181736/https://blogs.nasa.gov/Rocketology/2016/04/21/weve-got-rocket-chemistry-part-2/ |url-status=dead }}</ref>

At liftoff, the two boosters together produce more than 75 percent of the total thrust required to propel SLS. The five-segment configuration provides approximately 25 percent greater total impulse than the Shuttle-era boosters.<ref name="NTRS-20120507" /><ref name="NSFHowToLaunch022012" />

The available inventory of Shuttle-era booster casing segments limits use of this configuration to eight SLS flights.<ref name="NSFBoosters" />

====BOLE====
[[File:NASA, Northrop Grumman Test Fire SLS BOLE Booster (C0180 00 01 41 23 Still002 Edit).jpg|thumb|Test fire of BOLE prototype, June{{Spaces}}2025]]
The Booster Obsolescence and Life Extension (BOLE) program was announced in 2019 to develop replacement solid rocket boosters for SLS once the supply of Shuttle-derived hardware is exhausted. In 2021, NASA awarded Northrop Grumman a $3.2 billion contract to produce Shuttle-derived boosters for five missions (Artemis&nbsp;IV–VIII) and to design, develop, and test the new BOLE booster.<ref name=":4">{{Cite web |last=Clark |first=Stephen |date=June 26, 2025 |title=NASA tested a new SLS booster that may never fly, and the end of it blew off |url=https://arstechnica.com/space/2025/06/nasa-tested-a-new-sls-booster-that-may-never-fly-and-the-end-of-it-blew-off/ |access-date=June 28, 2025 |website=Ars Technica |language=en}}</ref>

The BOLE design replaces Shuttle-era steel motor cases with [[carbon-fiber composite]] cases, which are lighter and stronger. It also substitutes the hydraulic thrust vector control system with an electronic system and uses a different propellant formulation derived from Northrop Grumman's commercial solid rocket motors.<ref name=":4" />

Each BOLE booster is designed to produce approximately {{Convert|3.9|e6lb-f|MN|abbr=unit}} of thrust,<ref name=":4" /> about 19&nbsp;percent greater than the five-segment Shuttle-derived boosters, thereby increasing overall payload capability.<ref name="NSF-20210712" /><ref name="BOLEProgram" /><ref name="BOLEProgram2020" />

{{As of|2025|post=,}} BOLE remains in development. A prototype was test-fired in June 2025 but experienced a nozzle failure approximately 15 seconds before the end of the motor firing. However, the long-term future of the program is uncertain: SLS was authorized for only five flights at that time, and no funding has been provided for production of operational BOLE boosters.<ref name=":4" />

=== Upper stage ===
====Interim Cryogenic Propulsion Stage====
{{anchor|upper-stage-block-1}}
[[File:Interim Cryogenic Propulsion Stage.jpg|thumb|The [[Artemis&nbsp;I]] ICPS under construction]]

The [[Interim Cryogenic Propulsion Stage]] (ICPS) is the upper stage used on the initial Block&nbsp;1 configuration of the SLS. Three ICPS units were built by [[United Launch Alliance]] (ULA), a joint venture of Boeing and [[Lockheed Martin]]. The ICPS is derived from the [[Delta Cryogenic Second Stage]] (DCSS), incorporating minimal modifications for integration with SLS. Following the discontinuation of the DCSS, further ICPS production is no longer available as an option.

The ICPS flown on Artemis&nbsp;I was powered by a single [[RL10]]B-2 engine, also built by Aerojet Rocketdyne. The ICPS units flown on Artemis&nbsp;II and planned for use on Artemis&nbsp;IV use a single RL10C-2.<ref name="askins-20205000944" /><ref>Rosenberg, Zach. [http://www.flightglobal.com/news/articles/delta-second-stage-chosen-as-sls-interim-371581/ "Delta second stage chosen as SLS interim"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120727084044/http://www.flightglobal.com/news/articles/delta-second-stage-chosen-as-sls-interim-371581/ |date=July 27, 2012}}. ''Flight International'', May 8, 2012.</ref><ref name="NASA-20141030" />

Artemis III will have no ICPS, as it is only a mission to low Earth orbit (LEO), and instead its ICPS will be used for Artemis&nbsp;IV.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2026-05-13 |title=NASA Outlines Preliminary Artemis III Mission Plans - NASA |url=https://www.nasa.gov/missions/artemis/artemis-3/nasa-outlines-preliminary-artemis-iii-mission-plans/ |access-date=2026-06-18 |language=en-US}}</ref>

====Exploration Upper Stage (cancelled)====
The [[Exploration Upper Stage]] (EUS) was originally planned to debut on [[Artemis&nbsp;IV]] as the upper stage for the Block&nbsp;1B configuration.<ref name="NSFPDR032015" /> It would have shared the {{Convert|8.4|m|sp=us|adj=on}} diameter of the SLS core stage and be powered by four RL10C-3 engines,<ref name="NSFEUS" /> with a later upgrade to improved RL10C-X engines.<ref name="NSF-20210304" /> Although the EUS progressed through [[Design review (U.S. government)|design review]], it did not enter full-scale hardware production and was ultimately canceled in February 2026, prior to flight.<ref name="Berger 2026">{{cite web |last=Berger |first=Eric |date=February 27, 2026 |title=NASA shakes up its Artemis program to speed up lunar return |url=https://arstechnica.com/staff/2026/02/nasa-shakes-up-its-artemis-program-to-speed-up-lunar-return/ |access-date=February 2, 2026 |work=Ars Technica}}</ref>

==== Centaur V (future) ====
In February 2026, NASA announced plans to standardize the SLS on the Block&nbsp;1 configuration and discontinue development of the EUS. With production of the DCSS ended, NASA selected an existing commercially developed upper stage for missions following depletion of the ICPS stock: ULA's [[Centaur V]], which uses a pair of RL10 engines and is expected to provide modestly improved performance over the ICPS.<ref name="Berger 2026" /><ref name=":6">{{Cite web |last=Boyer |first=Charles |date=March 6, 2026 |title=NASA Formally Selects ULA's Centaur V For Artemis IV and V |url=https://talkoftitusville.com/2026/03/06/nasa-formally-selects-ulas-centaur-v-for-artemis-iv-and-v/ |access-date=March 24, 2026 |website=TalkOfTitusville.com |language=en}}</ref>

== Development ==
=== Funding ===
During the joint Senate-NASA presentation in September 2011, it was stated that the SLS program had a projected development cost of [[United States dollar|US$]]18 billion through 2017, with $10 billion for the SLS rocket, $6 billion for the [[Orion spacecraft]], and $2 billion for upgrades to the launch pad and other facilities at [[Kennedy Space Center]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.spacepolicyonline.com/news/new-nasa-crew-transportation-system-to-cost-18-billion-through-2017|title=New NASA Crew Transportation System to Cost US$18 Billion Through 2017|publisher=Space Policy Online|date=September 14, 2011|access-date=September 15, 2011|first=Marcia |last=Smith|archive-date=April 2, 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150402133411/http://www.spacepolicyonline.com/news/new-nasa-crew-transportation-system-to-cost-18-billion-through-2017|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite AV media |url=http://www.c-span.org/video/?301537-1/future-nasa-space-program |title=Future of NASA Space Program |date=September 14, 2011 |language=en-us |publisher=Cspan.org |location=Washington, D.C. |people=Bill Nelson, Kay Bailey Hutchison, Charles F. Bolden |access-date=March 25, 2015 |archive-date=April 2, 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150402124545/http://www.c-span.org/video/?301537-1/future-nasa-space-program |url-status=live}}</ref> These costs and schedules were considered optimistic in an independent 2011 cost assessment report by [[Booz Allen Hamilton]] for NASA.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nasa.gov/pdf/581582main_BAH_Executive_Summary.pdf|title=Independent Cost Assessment of the Space Launch System, Multi-purpose Crew Vehicle and 21st Century Ground Systems Programs: Executive Summary of Final Report|publisher=Booz Allen Hamilton|date=August 19, 2011|access-date=March 3, 2012|archive-date=March 2, 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120302191457/http://www.nasa.gov/pdf/581582main_BAH_Executive_Summary.pdf|url-status=live}} {{PD-notice}}</ref> An internal 2011 NASA document estimated the cost of the program through 2025 to total at least $41 billion for four {{cvt|95|order=flip|t|lb}} launches (1 uncrewed, 3 crewed),<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/SB10001424053111903648204576555010831469864|title=White House Experiences Sticker Shock Over NASA's Plans|newspaper=The Wall Street Journal|date=September 7, 2011|access-date=February 22, 2015|first=Andy |last=Paszior|archive-date=December 9, 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171209152249/https://www.wsj.com/articles/SB10001424053111903648204576555010831469864|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://spacepolicyonline.com/pages/images/stories/SLS_budget_Integration_2011-08.pdf|title=ESD Integration, Budget Availability Scenarios|publisher=Space Policy Online |date=August 19, 2011|access-date=September 15, 2011|archive-date=December 9, 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111209072917/http://spacepolicyonline.com/pages/images/stories/SLS_budget_Integration_2011-08.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref> with the {{cvt|130|order=flip|t|lb}} version ready no earlier than 2030.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.spacepolicyonline.com/news/the-nasa-numbers-behind-that-wsj-article|title=The NASA Numbers Behind That WSJ Article|first=Marcia |last=Smith|publisher=Space Policy Online|date=September 9, 2011|access-date=September 15, 2011|archive-date=January 4, 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130104184900/http://www.spacepolicyonline.com/news/the-nasa-numbers-behind-that-wsj-article|url-status=live}}</ref> The Human Exploration Framework Team estimated unit costs for 'Block&nbsp;0' at $1.6 billion and Block&nbsp;1 at $1.86&nbsp;billion in 2010.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.nasawatch.com/images/heft.presentation.pdf|title=HEFT Phase I Closeout|page=69|website=nasawatch.com|date=September 2010|access-date=March 25, 2012|archive-date=September 30, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210930001735/http://www.nasawatch.com/images/heft.presentation.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref> However, since these estimates were made, the Block 0 SLS vehicle was dropped in late 2011, and the design was not completed.<ref name="NSFTrades" />

In September 2012, an SLS deputy project manager stated that $500 million is a reasonable target average cost per flight for the SLS program.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.nbcnews.com/id/49019843|title=NASA's huge new rocket may cost US$500 million per launch|publisher=NBC News|date=September 12, 2012|access-date=November 13, 2019|archive-date=August 12, 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200812001859/http://www.nbcnews.com/id/49019843|url-status=dead}}</ref> In 2013, the Space Review estimated the cost per launch at $5 billion, depending on the rate of launches.<ref>{{cite web |author=Roop |first=Lee |date=July 29, 2013 |title=NASA defends Space Launch System against charge it 'is draining the lifeblood' of space program |url=http://blog.al.com/breaking/2013/07/nasa_defends_space_launch_syst.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150218232702/http://blog.al.com/breaking/2013/07/nasa_defends_space_launch_syst.html |archive-date=February 18, 2015 |access-date=February 18, 2015 |website=al.com}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.thespacereview.com/article/2330/1|title=Revisiting SLS/Orion launch costs|publisher=The Space Review|date=July 15, 2013 |first=John |last=Strickland|access-date=February 18, 2015|archive-date=February 18, 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150218224343/http://www.thespacereview.com/article/2330/1|url-status=live}}</ref> NASA announced in 2013 that the [[European Space Agency]] will build the [[Orion service module]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nasa.gov/exploration/systems/mpcv/orion_feature_011613.html|title=NASA Signs Agreement for a European-Provided Orion Service Module|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130118034139/https://www.nasa.gov/exploration/systems/mpcv/orion_feature_011613.html|publisher=NASA|url-status=dead|archive-date=January 18, 2013|orig-year=2013|date=April 12, 2015}} {{PD-notice}}</ref> In August 2014, as the SLS program passed its Key Decision Point C review and was deemed ready to enter full development, costs from February 2014 until its planned launch in September 2018 were estimated at $7.021 billion.<ref name="SNDebut082014" /> Ground systems modifications and construction would require an additional $1.8 billion over the same time.<ref>{{cite web|last1=Davis|first1=Jason|title=NASA Budget Lists Timelines, Costs and Risks for First SLS Flight|url=http://www.planetary.org/blogs/jason-davis/2015/20150203-budget-maiden-sls-flight.html|archive-date=March 12, 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150312012014/http://www.planetary.org/blogs/jason-davis/2015/20150203-budget-maiden-sls-flight.html|url-status=live|publisher=The Planetary Society|access-date=March 11, 2015}}</ref>

In October 2018, NASA's [[NASA Office of Inspector General|Inspector General]] reported that the [[Boeing]] core stage contract had made up 40% of the $11.9 billion spent on the SLS as of August 2018. By 2021, development of the core stage was expected to have cost $8.9 billion, twice the initially planned amount.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://oig.nasa.gov/docs/IG-19-001.pdf|title=NASA's Management of the Space Launch System Stages Contract |date=October 10, 2018 |website=oig.nasa.gov|publisher=NASA Office of Inspector General Office of Audits|access-date=October 14, 2018|archive-date=October 10, 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181010172919/https://oig.nasa.gov/docs/IG-19-001.pdf|url-status=live}} {{PD-notice}}</ref> In December 2018, NASA estimated that yearly budgets for the SLS will range from $2.1 to $2.3 billion between 2019 and 2023.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nasa.gov/sites/default/files/atoms/files/fy19_nasa_budget_estimates.pdf|title=NASA FY 2019 Budget Estimates|website=nasa.gov |page=BUD-2|archive-date=December 24, 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181224004339/https://www.nasa.gov/sites/default/files/atoms/files/fy19_nasa_budget_estimates.pdf|url-status=live|access-date=December 16, 2018}} {{PD-notice}}</ref>

In March 2019, the [[First presidency of Donald Trump|Trump administration]] released its [[United States budget|fiscal year 2020 budget request]] for NASA, which notably proposed dropped funding for the Block&nbsp;1B and 2 variants of SLS. Congressional action ultimately included the funding in the passed budget.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.fool.com/investing/2019/03/26/is-nasa-preparing-to-cancel-its-space-launch-syste.aspx|title=Is NASA Preparing to Cancel Its Space Launch System?|last=Smith|first=Rich|date=March 26, 2019 |website=The Motley Fool|access-date=May 15, 2019 |archive-date=June 23, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190623203841/https://www.fool.com/investing/2019/03/26/is-nasa-preparing-to-cancel-its-space-launch-syste.aspx|url-status=live}}</ref>

On May 1, 2020, NASA awarded a contract extension to [[Aerojet Rocketdyne]] to manufacture 18 additional RS-25 engines with associated services for $1.79 billion, bringing the total RS-25 contract value to almost $3.5 billion.<ref name="nasa-20200501" /><ref name="rocket20210329" />

==== Budget ====
{{anchor|SLS-total-budget-table}}NASA has spent $31.5 billion on SLS development from 2011 through 2025, in nominal dollars. This is equivalent to $38.7 billion in 2026 dollars using the NASA New Start Inflation Indices.<ref name="NASAInflationCalculator2020" />

Included in the above SLS costs above are the $412 million contract for the Interim Cryogenic Propulsion Stage (ICPS),<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://govtribe.com/award/federal-contract-award/definitive-contract-nnm12aa82c|title=Definitive Contract NNM12AA82C|website=govtribe.com|access-date=December 16, 2018|archive-date=September 30, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210930001739/https://govtribe.com/award/federal-contract-award/definitive-contract-nnm12aa82c|url-status=live}} {{PD-notice}}</ref> and the costs of developing the Exploration Upper Stage (EUS), which are detailed in the table below. Excluded from the SLS cost above are the costs to assemble, integrate, prepare and launch the SLS and its payloads, funded separately in the NASA [[Exploration Ground Systems]] program, running about $600 million per year in 2021,<ref name="budget-FY2021" /><ref name="gsd-pdr-2016" /> and rising to $910 million for 2025.<ref name=":14" />

Also excluded are payloads that launch on the SLS, such as the [[Orion (spacecraft)|Orion]] crew capsule, the predecessor programs that contributed to the development of the SLS, such as the [[Ares&nbsp;V]] cargo launch vehicle project, funded from 2008 to 2010 for a total of $70 million,<ref name="auto" /> and the [[Ares&nbsp;I]] crew launch vehicle, funded from 2006 to 2010 for a total of $4.8 billion<ref name="auto" /><ref>{{Cite web |title=FY 2008 Budget Estimates |url=http://www.nasa.gov/pdf/168652main_NASA_FY08_Budget_Request.pdf |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160603152901/http://www.nasa.gov/pdf/168652main_NASA_FY08_Budget_Request.pdf |archive-date=June 3, 2016 |access-date=June 23, 2016 |publisher=NASA |page=ESMD-14}} {{PD-notice}}</ref> in development, including the 5-segment Solid Rocket Boosters used on the SLS.<ref name="NSFAdvBooster022015" />

Despite calls from the [[Second presidency of Donald Trump|Trump administration]] to terminate the SLS program after Artemis&nbsp;III, the 2025 [[One Big Beautiful Bill Act]] included $4.1 billion to fund SLS rockets for the Artemis&nbsp;IV and V missions, with mandated minimum spending of $1.025 billion per year from FY 2026 through 29.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |last=Mendenhall |first=Brooks |date=July 9, 2025 |title="One Big Beautiful Bill" sets stage for NASA's return to the Moon |url=https://www.astronomy.com/space-exploration/trumps-one-big-beautiful-bill-sets-the-stage-for-nasas-return-to-the-moon/ |access-date=September 12, 2025 |website=Astronomy Magazine |language=en-US}}</ref> However, as a compromise, lawmakers suggested eliminating the EUS, and directed NASA to evaluate alternatives such as the Centaur V or [[New Glenn]]'s GS2 upper stage. In early 2026 this change was implemented with the Centaur V being selected as the future SLS upper stage, replacing the EUS.<ref name=":3">{{Cite web |last=Berger |first=Eric |date=September 8, 2025 |title=Congress and Trump may compromise on the SLS rocket by axing its costly upper stage |url=https://arstechnica.com/space/2025/09/congress-and-trump-may-compromise-on-the-sls-rocket-by-axing-its-costly-upper-stage/ |access-date=September 12, 2025 |website=Ars Technica |language=en}}</ref><ref name=":6" />

=== Early plans ===
[[File:Space Launch System Booster Passes Major Ground Test.webm|thumb|Test fire of Shuttle-derived booster, March 2015]]The SLS was created by an act of the U.S. Congress in the [[NASA Authorization Act of 2010]], Public Law 111–267, in which NASA was directed to create a system for launching payloads and crew into space that would replace the capabilities lost with the retirement of the [[Space Shuttle]].<ref name="PL-111-267" /> The act set out certain goals, such as being able to lift 70–100 tons into low earth orbit with evolvability to 130 tons, a target date of December 31, 2016, for the system to be fully operational, and a directive to use "to the extent practicable" existing components, hardware, and workforce from the Space Shuttle and from [[Ares&nbsp;I]].<ref name="PL-111-267" />{{rp|12}}

On September 14, 2011, NASA announced their plan to meet these requirements: the design for the SLS, with the [[Orion spacecraft]] as payload.<ref name="SLSAnnounce" /><ref>{{Cite web|date=May 24, 2011|title=NASA Announces Key Decision For Next Deep Space Transportation System|url=http://www.nasa.gov/home/hqnews/2011/may/HQ_11-164_MPCV_Decision.html|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160915182112/http://www.nasa.gov/home/hqnews/2011/may/HQ_11-164_MPCV_Decision.html|archive-date=September 15, 2016|access-date=January 26, 2012|publisher=NASA}} {{PD-notice}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.c-span.org/Events/Press-Conference-on-the-Future-of-NASA-Space-Program/10737424158/|title=Press Conference on the Future of NASA Space Program|publisher=C-Span|date=September 14, 2011|access-date=September 14, 2011|archive-date=February 8, 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120208145214/http://www.c-span.org/Events/Press-Conference-on-the-Future-of-NASA-Space-Program/10737424158/|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |author=Chang |first=Kenneth |date=September 14, 2011 |title=NASA Unveils New Rocket Design |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2011/09/15/science/space/15nasa.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170221195020/http://www.nytimes.com/2011/09/15/science/space/15nasa.html |archive-date=February 21, 2017 |access-date=September 14, 2011 |newspaper=The New York Times}}</ref>
[[File:Artemis_II_Core_Stage_Move_to_VAB_High_Bay_2_(KSC-20241211-PH-KLS01_0054).jpg|thumb|[[SLS core stage]] for Artemis&nbsp;II lifted into High Bay 2 of the [[Vehicle Assembly Building]] shortly after stacking operations began in December 2024]]
The SLS has considered several future development routes of potential launch configurations, with the planned evolution of the blocks of the rocket having been modified many times.<ref name="NSFAdvBooster022015" /> Many options, all of which just needed to meet the congressionally mandated payload minimums,<ref name="NSFAdvBooster022015" /> were considered, including a Block 0 variant with three main engines,<ref name="NSFTrades" /> a variant with five main engines,<ref name="NSFAdvBooster022015" /> a Block&nbsp;1A variant with upgraded boosters instead of the improved second stage,<ref name="NSFTrades" /> and a Block 2 with five main engines plus the [[Earth Departure Stage]], with up to three [[J-2X]] engines.<ref name="nsf-20120223" />

In the initial announcement of the design of the SLS, NASA also announced an "Advanced Booster Competition", to select which boosters would be used on Block 2 of the SLS.<ref name="SLSAnnounce" /><ref>{{Cite web |author=Cowing |first=Keith |date=September 14, 2011 |title=NASA's New Space Launch System Announced – Destination TBD |url=http://www.spaceref.com/news/viewnews.html?id=1567 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://archive.today/20120604021003/http://www.spaceref.com/news/viewnews.html?id=1567 |archive-date=June 4, 2012 |access-date=January 26, 2012 |publisher=SpaceRef}}</ref><ref name="NASA_Fact-Sht" /><ref>{{Cite web |author=Morring |first=Frank |date=June 17, 2011 |title=NASA Will Compete Space Launch System Boosters |url=http://www.aviationweek.com/aw/generic/story_channel.jsp?channel=space&id=news/awx/2011/06/16/awx_06_16_2011_p0-337088.xml&headline=NASA%20Will%20Compete%20Space%20Launch%20System%20Boosters |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111011122336/http://www.aviationweek.com/aw/generic/story_channel.jsp?channel=space&id=news%2Fawx%2F2011%2F06%2F16%2Fawx_06_16_2011_p0-337088.xml&headline=NASA%20Will%20Compete%20Space%20Launch%20System%20Boosters |archive-date=October 11, 2011 |access-date=June 20, 2011 |publisher=Aviation Week}}</ref> Several companies proposed boosters for this competition, all of which were indicated as viable:<ref>{{Cite web|date=January 14, 2013|title=SLS Block II drives hydrocarbon engine research|url=http://www.thespacereview.com/article/2217/1|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130902024820/http://www.thespacereview.com/article/2217/1|archive-date=September 2, 2013|access-date=September 13, 2013|work=thespacereview.com}}</ref> [[Aerojet]] and [[Teledyne Technologies|Teledyne Brown]] proposed three booster engines each with dual combustion chambers,<ref>{{Cite web|title=NASA's Space Launch System: Partnering For Tomorrow|url=http://www.asee.org/Crumbly_ASEE_Final.pdf|publisher=NASA|access-date=March 12, 2013|archive-date=April 2, 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150402114152/http://www.asee.org/Crumbly_ASEE_Final.pdf|url-status=live}} {{PD-notice}}</ref> [[Alliant Techsystems]] proposed a modified solid rocket booster with lighter casing, more energetic propellant, and four segments instead of five,<ref>{{Cite news|url=http://www.nasaspaceflight.com/2013/01/the-dark-knights-atks-advanced-booster-revealed-for-sls/|title=The Dark Knights – ATK's Advanced Boosters for SLS revealed|publisher=NASASpaceFlight.com|date=January 14, 2013|access-date=September 10, 2013|archive-date=September 12, 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130912223133/http://www.nasaspaceflight.com/2013/01/the-dark-knights-atks-advanced-booster-revealed-for-sls/|url-status=live}}</ref> and [[Pratt & Whitney Rocketdyne]] and [[Dynetics]] proposed a liquid-fueled booster named [[Saturn C-3#Pyrios|Pyrios]].<ref>{{Cite news |author=Hutchinson |first=Lee |date=April 15, 2013 |title=New F-1B rocket engine upgrades Apollo-era design with 1.8M lbs of thrust |url=https://arstechnica.com/science/2013/04/new-f-1b-rocket-engine-upgrades-apollo-era-deisgn-with-1-8m-lbs-of-thrust/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171202064940/https://arstechnica.com/science/2013/04/new-f-1b-rocket-engine-upgrades-apollo-era-deisgn-with-1-8m-lbs-of-thrust/ |archive-date=December 2, 2017 |access-date=April 15, 2013 |publisher=Ars Technica}}</ref> However, this competition was planned for a development plan in which Block&nbsp;1A would be followed by Block 2A, with upgraded boosters. NASA canceled Block&nbsp;1A and the planned competition in April 2014, in favor of simply remaining with the [[Ares&nbsp;I]]'s five-segment solid rocket boosters, themselves modified from the [[Space Shuttle]]'s solid rocket boosters, until at least the late 2020s.<ref name="NSFAdvBooster022015" /><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.spacenews.com/article/civil-space/40647news-from-the-30th-space-symposium-second-sls-mission-might-not-carry-crew|archive-url=https://archive.today/20140727043122/http://www.spacenews.com/article/civil-space/40647news-from-the-30th-space-symposium-second-sls-mission-might-not-carry-crew|url-status=dead|archive-date=July 27, 2014|title=Second SLS Mission Might Not Carry Crew|date=May 21, 2014|publisher=SpaceNews|access-date=July 25, 2014}}</ref> The overly powerful advanced booster would have resulted in unsuitably high acceleration, and would need modifications to [[Kennedy Space Center Launch Complex 39B|Launch Complex 39B]], its flame trench, and [[Mobile launcher platform#Space Launch System|Mobile Launcher]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nasaspaceflight.com/2012/07/wind-tunnel-testing-sls-configurations-block-1b/|title=Wind Tunnel testing conducted on SLS configurations, including Block 1B |date=July 2012|publisher=NASASpaceFlight.com|access-date=November 13, 2012|archive-date=October 24, 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121024215052/http://www.nasaspaceflight.com/2012/07/wind-tunnel-testing-sls-configurations-block-1b/|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="NSFAdvBooster022015" />

On July 31, 2013, the SLS passed Preliminary Design Review. The review included not only the rocket and boosters but also ground support and logistical arrangements.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.nasa.gov/exploration/systems/sls/sls-pdr.html|publisher=NASA|date=August 1, 2013|title=NASA's Space Launch System Program PDR: Answers to the Acronym|access-date=August 3, 2013|archive-date=August 4, 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130804050311/http://www.nasa.gov/exploration/systems/sls/sls-pdr.html|url-status=live}} {{PD-notice}}</ref>

On August 7, 2014, the SLS Block&nbsp;1 passed a milestone known as Key Decision Point C and entered full-scale development, with an estimated launch date of November 2018.<ref name="SNDebut082014" /><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.nasa.gov/press/2014/august/nasa-completes-key-review-of-world-s-most-powerful-rocket-in-support-of-journey-to/#.U_5UAfl7Eeg|title=NASA Completes Key Review of World's Most Powerful Rocket in Support|date=April 15, 2015 |publisher=NASA|access-date=October 26, 2015|archive-date=May 27, 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160527051013/http://www.nasa.gov/press/2014/august/nasa-completes-key-review-of-world-s-most-powerful-rocket-in-support-of-journey-to/#.U_5UAfl7Eeg|url-status=live}} {{PD-notice}}</ref>

==== EUS options ====
In 2013, NASA and Boeing analyzed the performance of several Exploration Upper Stage (EUS) engine options. The analysis was based on a second-stage usable propellant load of 105 metric tons, and compared stages with four [[RL10]] engines, two [[MARC-60]] engines, or one [[J-2X]] engine.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.nasaspaceflight.com/2013/11/sls-us-proposals-increasing-payload-destination-options/|title=SLS upper stage proposals reveal increasing payload-to-destination options|date=November 13, 2013|publisher=NASASpaceFlight.com|first=Chris |last=Gebhardt|access-date=November 18, 2013|archive-date=November 18, 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131118144209/http://www.nasaspaceflight.com/2013/11/sls-us-proposals-increasing-payload-destination-options/|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://seradata.com/SSI/2013/06/sls-may-change-upper-stage-eng/|title=SLS design may ditch J-2X upper stage engine for four RL-10 engines|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304043940/http://seradata.com/SSI/2013/06/sls-may-change-upper-stage-eng/|archive-date=March 4, 2016|first=David |last=Todd|date=June 3, 2013|publisher=Seradata}}</ref> In 2014, NASA also considered using the European [[Vinci (rocket engine)|Vinci]] instead of the [[RL10]], which offered the same specific impulse but with 64% greater thrust, which would allow for the same performance at a lower cost.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://seradata.com/SSI/2014/11/next-steps-for-sls-europes-vinci-is-a-contender-for-exploration-upper-stage-engine/|title=Next Steps for SLS: Europe's Vinci is a contender for Exploration Upper-Stage Engine|first=David |last=Todd|date=November 7, 2014|publisher=Seradata|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304023658/http://seradata.com/SSI/2014/11/next-steps-for-sls-europes-vinci-is-a-contender-for-exploration-upper-stage-engine/|archive-date=March 4, 2016}}</ref>

In 2018, [[Blue Origin]] submitted a proposal to replace the EUS with a cheaper alternative to be designed and fabricated by the company, but it was rejected by NASA in November 2019 on multiple grounds; these included lower performance compared to the existing EUS design, incompatibility of the proposal with the height of the door of the [[Vehicle Assembly Building]] being only {{convert|390|ft|m}}, and unacceptable acceleration of Orion components such as its solar panels due to the higher thrust of the engines being used for the fuel tank.<ref>{{Cite news |last1=Berger|first1=Eric|title=NASA rejects Blue Origin's offer of a cheaper upper stage for the SLS rocket|url=https://arstechnica.com/science/2019/11/nasa-rejects-blue-origins-offer-of-a-cheaper-upper-stage-for-the-sls-rocket/|work = Ars Technica|access-date=December 19, 2019|date=November 5, 2019|archive-date=December 19, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191219042903/https://arstechnica.com/science/2019/11/nasa-rejects-blue-origins-offer-of-a-cheaper-upper-stage-for-the-sls-rocket/|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Redacted_EUS.pdf |url=https://sam.gov/opp/957d857a579a9c13c26c64825f82a5d5/view |website=sam.gov |access-date=October 6, 2021 |date=October 31, 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211006030858/https://iae-fbo-attachments.s3.amazonaws.com/fbo/files/b3a/b3a26357ad9cd1ca8bf7e370e7459804.pdf?response-content-disposition=attachment%3B%20filename%3DRedacted_EUS.pdf&X-Amz-Algorithm=AWS4-HMAC-SHA256&X-Amz-Date=20211006T030858Z&X-Amz-SignedHeaders=host&X-Amz-Expires=9&X-Amz-Credential=AKIA_SAMPLE_CREDENTIAL_KEY%2F20211006%2Fus-east-1%2Fs3%2Faws4_request&X-Amz-Signature=1697246eac19e0b7f799a6d9a048d3c583cecf12e1ee7213e4e5a254fae3a876 |url-status=live |archive-date=October 6, 2021}}<!-- Original was at https://web.archive.org/web/20191108003127/https://www.fbo.gov/index?s=opportunity&mode=form&tab=core&id=957d857a579a9c13c26c64825f82a5d5 Direct link is https://sam.gov/api/prod/opps/v3/opportunities/resources/files/b3a26357ad9cd1ca8bf7e370e7459804/download?&status=archived&token= --></ref>{{rp|7–8}}

In February 2026, NASA administrator [[Jared Isaacman]] announced the cancellation of EUS.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Berger |first=Eric |date=February 27, 2026 |title=NASA shakes up its Artemis program to speed up lunar return |url=https://arstechnica.com/space/2026/02/nasa-shakes-up-its-artemis-program-to-speed-up-lunar-return/ |access-date=March 28, 2026 |website=Ars Technica |language=en}}</ref>

==== SRB tests ====
From 2009 to 2011, three full-duration static fire tests of five-segment solid rocket boosters were conducted under the [[Constellation Program]], including tests at low and high core temperatures, to validate performance at extreme temperatures.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.nasa.gov/mission_pages/constellation/ares/dm1_success.html|title=NASA and ATK Successfully Test Ares First Stage Motor|publisher=NASA|date=September 10, 2009|access-date=January 30, 2012|archive-date=December 24, 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181224004602/https://www.nasa.gov/mission_pages/constellation/ares/dm1_success.html|url-status=live}} {{PD-notice}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.nasa.gov/mission_pages/constellation/ares/10-202.html|title=NASA and ATK Successfully Test Five-Segment Solid Rocket Motor|publisher=NASA|date=August 31, 2010|access-date=January 30, 2012|archive-date=December 19, 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111219022208/http://www.nasa.gov/mission_pages/constellation/ares/10-202.html|url-status=live}} {{PD-notice}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.nasa.gov/exploration/features/dm3.html|title=NASA Successfully Tests Five-Segment Solid Rocket Motor|publisher=NASA|date=August 31, 2010|access-date=September 8, 2011|archive-date=September 24, 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110924091505/http://www.nasa.gov/exploration/features/dm3.html|url-status=live}} {{PD-notice}}</ref> The 5-segment solid rocket booster would be carried over to SLS.<ref name="NSFAdvBooster022015" /> [[Northrop Grumman Innovation Systems]] has completed full-duration static fire tests of the five-segment solid rocket boosters. Qualification Motor 1 was tested on March 10, 2015.<ref>{{Cite news|last1=Bergin|first1=Chris|title=QM-1 shakes Utah with two minutes of thunder|url=http://www.nasaspaceflight.com/2015/03/qm-1-shake-utah-two-minutes-thunder/|access-date=March 10, 2015|publisher=NASASpaceFlight.com|date=March 10, 2015|archive-date=March 13, 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150313223625/http://www.nasaspaceflight.com/2015/03/qm-1-shake-utah-two-minutes-thunder/|url-status=live}}</ref> Qualification Motor 2 was successfully tested on June 28, 2016.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://news.northropgrumman.com/news/features/orbital-atk-successfully-tests-the-world-s-largest-solid-rocket-motor |title=Orbital ATK Successfully Tests the World's Largest Solid Rocket Motor |publisher=Northrop Grumman |date=June 28, 2016 |access-date=October 11, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210615100406/https://news.northropgrumman.com/news/features/orbital-atk-successfully-tests-the-world-s-largest-solid-rocket-motor |archive-date=June 15, 2021 |url-status=live}}</ref>

=== Proposed cancellation ===
On February 7, 2025, Boeing, the primary contractor for the SLS, informed its employees working on the rocket program that they may face layoffs when the company's contract expires in March. The announcement coincided with the anticipated release of the presidential budget, suggesting the [[Second presidency of Donald Trump|Trump administration]] might propose canceling the SLS program.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Berger |first=Eric |author-link=Eric Berger (journalist) |date=February 7, 2025 |title=Boeing has informed its employees that NASA may cancel SLS contracts |url=https://arstechnica.com/space/2025/02/boeing-has-informed-its-employees-that-nasa-may-cancel-sls-contracts/ |access-date=February 7, 2025 |work=[[Ars Technica]] |language=en-US}}</ref>

On May 2, 2025, the Trump administration released its fiscal year 2026 budget proposal for NASA, which calls for terminating the SLS and Orion spacecraft programs after [[Artemis&nbsp;III]].<ref>{{Cite news |last=Berger |first=Eric |author-link=Eric Berger (journalist) |date=May 2, 2025 |title=White House budget seeks to end SLS, Orion, and Lunar Gateway programs |url=https://arstechnica.com/space/2025/05/white-house-budget-seeks-to-end-sls-orion-and-lunar-gateway-programs/ |access-date=May 2, 2025 |work=[[Ars Technica]]}}</ref><ref>{{Cite press release |title=President Trump's FY26 Budget Revitalizes Human Space Exploration |date=May 2, 2025 |publisher=NASA |url=https://www.nasa.gov/news-release/president-trumps-fy26-budget-revitalizes-human-space-exploration/ |last1=Dooren |first1=Jennifer M. |last2=Stevens |first2=Bethany |access-date=May 2, 2025 |id=25-035}}</ref> The budget proposal described the SLS as "grossly expensive", noting that it costs $4 billion per launch and has exceeded its budget by 140 percent. The budget allocates funding for a program to transition to "more cost-effective commercial systems", a move projected by the [[White House Office of Management and Budget]] to save NASA $879 million.<ref name="FY2026DBR">{{Cite web |date=May 2, 2025 |title=Fiscal Year 2026 Discretionary Budget Request |url=https://www.whitehouse.gov/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/Fiscal-Year-2026-Discretionary-Budget-Request.pdf |access-date=May 2, 2025 |website=United States Office of Management and Budget |page=37}}</ref>

The 2025 [[One Big Beautiful Bill Act]] included funding for SLS rockets for the Artemis&nbsp;IV and V missions, but a clause directed NASA to evaluate alternatives to the EUS.<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":3" />

== Launch costs ==
[[File:Artemis II launch (KSC - SLS 03302026 Artemis II Launch wide 3).jpg|thumb|The SLS taking off for [[Artemis II]].]]
NASA has been reluctant to provide an official per-flight cost estimate for the SLS.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://arstechnica.com/science/2017/10/nasa-chooses-to-not-tell-congress-how-much-deep-space-missions-cost/|title=NASA chooses not to tell Congress how much deep space missions cost |last=Berger|first=Eric|date=October 20, 2017|website=arstechnica.com|access-date=December 16, 2018|archive-date=December 17, 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181217062648/https://arstechnica.com/science/2017/10/nasa-chooses-to-not-tell-congress-how-much-deep-space-missions-cost/|url-status=live}}</ref> However, independent agencies, such as the [[Office of Management and Budget|White House Office of Management and Budget]] and the [[NASA Office of Inspector General]], have offered their own estimates.

A White House Office of Management and Budget letter to the Senate Appropriations Committee in October 2019 estimated that SLS's total cost to the taxpayer was estimated at "over $2 billion" per launch.<ref name="whitehouse" />{{refn|name=totalcost|group=note|See the [[#SLS-total-budget-table|budget table]] for yearly inflation-adjusted figures.}} When questioned by a journalist, a NASA spokesperson did not deny this per-flight cost estimate.<ref name="doesnotdeny" />

The NASA Office of Inspector General has conducted several audits of the SLS program. A November 2021 report estimated that, at least for the first four launches of Artemis program, the per-launch production and operating costs would be $2.2 billion for SLS, plus $568 million for [[Exploration Ground Systems]]. Additionally, the payload would cost $1 billion for [[Orion (spacecraft)|Orion]] and $300 million for the [[European Service Module]].<ref name="OIG-22-023" />{{rp|23}} An October 2023 report found that recurring production costs for SLS, excluding development and integration costs, are estimated to be at least $2.5 billion per launch.<ref name=":5" /> In 2025, [[Sean Duffy]], the then acting [[NASA administrator]], said that, "Artemis&nbsp;I, Artemis&nbsp;II, and Artemis&nbsp;III are all $4 billion a launch".<ref name=":3" />

NASA has said that it is working with Boeing to bring down the cost of SLS launches and that a higher launch frequency could potentially lead to economies of scale, and would allow fixed costs to be spread out over more launches.<ref name="doesnotdeny" /> However, the NASA Office of Inspector General has called NASA's cost savings goals highly unrealistic and other potential government customers have made it clear they have no interest in using SLS.<ref name=":5" /><ref name="Reuters 20230608" />

== Operation ==
=== Construction ===
[[File:NASA Readies Artemis II Liquid Hydrogen Tank for Next Phase of Manufacturing.jpg|thumb|[[Liquid hydrogen]] tank for [[Artemis&nbsp;II]] under construction, August 2020]]
[[File:MAF 20210609 CS2 BoatTail2CellA09.jpg|thumb|"Boat-tail" engine [[Aircraft fairing|fairing]] for [[Artemis&nbsp;II]] under construction, June 2021]]
[[File:NASA Readies Artemis III (MAF 20210401 ARTIII ESLift14).jpg|thumb|Engine section shroud structure for [[Artemis&nbsp;III]] under construction, April 2021]]

{{as of|2020}}, three SLS versions were planned: Block&nbsp;1, Block&nbsp;1B, and Block&nbsp;2. Each would use the same core stage with its four main engines, but Block&nbsp;1B will feature the [[Exploration Upper Stage]] (EUS), and Block&nbsp;2 will combine the EUS with upgraded boosters.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://commerce.senate.gov/public/index.cfm?p=Legislation&ContentRecord_id=8d7c1465-f852-4835-ba84-25faf56bbb36&ContentType_id=03ab50f5-55cd-4934-a074-d6928b9dd24c&Group_id=6eaa2a03-6e69-4e43-8597-bb12f4f5aede|work=Featured Legislation|title=The NASA Authorization Act of 2010|date=July 15, 2010 |publisher=U.S. Senate|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110410161657/https://www.commerce.senate.gov/public/index.cfm?p=Legislation&ContentRecord_id=8d7c1465-f852-4835-ba84-25faf56bbb36&ContentType_id=03ab50f5-55cd-4934-a074-d6928b9dd24c&Group_id=6eaa2a03-6e69-4e43-8597-bb12f4f5aede|archive-date=April 10, 2011|url-status=dead|access-date=May 26, 2011}} {{PD-notice}}</ref><ref name="slsfact-20171011" /><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.space.com/12957-nasa-giant-rocket-space-launch-system-infographic.html|title=Space Launch System: NASA's Giant Rocket Explained|first=Karl |last=Tate|date=September 16, 2011|publisher=Space.com|access-date=January 26, 2012|archive-date=January 27, 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120127120812/http://www.space.com/12957-nasa-giant-rocket-space-launch-system-infographic.html|url-status=live}}</ref>

The ICPS for Artemis&nbsp;1 was delivered by [[United Launch Alliance|ULA]] to NASA about July 2017<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nasaspaceflight.com/2017/07/sls-upper-stage-residency-former-home-iss-modules/|title=''SLS Upper Stage set to take up residence in the former home of ISS modules'' July 2017|date=July 11, 2017 |access-date=February 15, 2020|archive-date=August 7, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200807132155/https://www.nasaspaceflight.com/2017/07/sls-upper-stage-residency-former-home-iss-modules/|url-status=live}}</ref> and was housed at Kennedy Space Center as of November 2018.<ref>{{cite web|title=Meet the Interim Cryogenic Propulsion Stage for SLS |url=http://www.nasa.gov/exploration/systems/sls/interim-cryogenic-propulsion-stage-infographic-for-sls.html|url-status=dead|last=Harbaugh|first=Jennifer|date=November 8, 2018|publisher=NASA|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200807130817/https://www.nasa.gov/exploration/systems/sls/interim-cryogenic-propulsion-stage-infographic-for-sls.html|archive-date=August 7, 2020}} {{PD-notice}}</ref>

==== Construction of core stage ====
In mid-November 2014, construction of the first core stage hardware began using a new friction stir welding system in the South Vertical Assembly Building at NASA's [[Michoud Assembly Facility]].<ref name="NASA-20141115" /><ref name="NSF-20130218" /><ref name="NASA-20160602" /> Between 2015 and 2017, NASA test fired RS-25 engines in preparation for use on SLS.<ref name="NSFStennis012015" />

The core stage for the first SLS, built at Michoud Assembly Facility by Boeing,<ref name="ST20121227" /> had all four engines attached in November 2019,<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.nasa.gov/exploration/systems/sls/multimedia/four-engines-attached-to-sls-core-stage-for-artemis-I-mission.html|title=All Four Engines Are Attached to the SLS Core Stage for Artemis I Mission |date=November 8, 2019 |publisher=NASA|access-date=November 12, 2019|archive-date=November 12, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191112214328/https://www.nasa.gov/exploration/systems/sls/multimedia/four-engines-attached-to-sls-core-stage-for-artemis-I-mission.html|url-status=live}} {{PD-notice}}</ref> and it was declared finished by NASA in December 2019.<ref>{{cite web|last1=Clark|first1=Stephen|title=NASA declares first SLS core stage complete|url=https://spaceflightnow.com/2019/12/15/nasa-declares-first-sls-core-stage-complete/|publisher=Spaceflight Now|access-date=October 7, 2021|date=December 15, 2019|archive-date=May 11, 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220511091912/https://spaceflightnow.com/2019/12/15/nasa-declares-first-sls-core-stage-complete/|url-status=live}}</ref>

The first core stage left Michoud Assembly Facility for comprehensive testing at [[Stennis Space Center]] in January 2020.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.bbc.com/news/science-environment-51048986|title=Nasa Moon rocket core leaves for testing|last=Rincon|first=Paul|publisher=BBC News|date=January 9, 2020|access-date=January 9, 2020|archive-date=January 9, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200109151551/https://www.bbc.com/news/science-environment-51048986|url-status=live}}</ref> The static firing test program at Stennis Space Center, known as the Green Run, operated all the core stage systems simultaneously for the first time.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nasaspaceflight.com/2019/12/boeing-nasa-sls-core-stage-green-run-campaign-stennis/|title=Boeing, NASA getting ready for SLS Core Stage Green Run campaign ahead of Stennis arrival|date=December 14, 2019|publisher=NASASpaceFlight.com|access-date=January 9, 2020|archive-date=September 30, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210930001752/https://www.nasaspaceflight.com/2019/12/boeing-nasa-sls-core-stage-green-run-campaign-stennis/|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.nextbigfuture.com/2019/08/nasa-will-have-8-minute-hold-down-test-in-2020.html|title=NASA Will Have 8 Minute Hold Down Test in 2020|publisher=Next Big Future|access-date=August 2, 2019|archive-date=August 2, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190802192558/https://www.nextbigfuture.com/2019/08/nasa-will-have-8-minute-hold-down-test-in-2020.html|url-status=live}}</ref> Test 7 (of 8), the wet dress rehearsal, was carried out in December 2020 and the fire (test 8) took place on January 16, 2021, but shut down earlier than expected,<ref>{{cite web|last1=Foust|first1=Jeff|title=Green Run hotfire test ends early|url=https://spacenews.com/green-run-hotfire-test-ends-early/|publisher=SpaceNews|access-date=January 17, 2021|date=January 16, 2021|archive-date=October 3, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211003032149/https://spacenews.com/green-run-hotfire-test-ends-early/|url-status=live}}</ref> about 67 seconds in total rather than the desired eight minutes. The reason for the early shutdown was later reported to be because of conservative test commit criteria on the thrust vector control system, specific only for ground testing and not for flight. If this scenario occurred during a flight, the rocket would have continued to fly normally. There was no sign of damage to the core stage or the engines, contrary to initial concerns.<ref>{{Cite web|last1=Rincon|first1=Paul|title=SLS: NASA finds cause of 'megarocket' test shutdown|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/science-environment-55727686|publisher=BBC News|access-date=January 20, 2021|date=January 20, 2021|archive-date=January 20, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210120041016/https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/science-environment-55727686|url-status=live}}</ref>

The second fire test was completed on March 18, 2021, with all four engines igniting, throttling down as expected to simulate in-flight conditions, and gimballing profiles. The core stage was shipped to Kennedy Space Center to be mated with the rest of the rocket for Artemis&nbsp;I. It left Stennis on April 24 and arrived at Kennedy on April 27.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nasa.gov/image-feature/space-launch-system-core-stage-arrives-at-the-kennedy-space-center|title=Space Launch System Core Stage Arrives at the Kennedy Space Center|first=Brian|last=Dunbar|date=April 29, 2021|publisher=NASA|access-date=June 1, 2021|archive-date=May 7, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210507205846/http://www.nasa.gov/image-feature/space-launch-system-core-stage-arrives-at-the-kennedy-space-center/|url-status=live}} {{PD-notice}}</ref> It was refurbished there in preparation for stacking.<ref>{{cite web|title=SLS Core Stage thermal protection system refurbishment in work at Kennedy for Artemis 1|url=https://www.nasaspaceflight.com/2021/05/tps-repairs-core-stage-work-updatei/|last=Sloss|first=Philip|publisher=NASASpaceFlight.com|archive-date=May 26, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210526143900/https://www.nasaspaceflight.com/2021/05/tps-repairs-core-stage-work-updatei/|url-status=live|date=May 20, 2021|access-date=May 26, 2021}}</ref> On June 12, 2021, NASA announced the assembly of the first SLS rocket was completed at the Kennedy Space Center. The assembled SLS was used for the uncrewed Artemis&nbsp;I mission in 2022.<ref name="NSF-20210929" />

The first SLS, for Artemis&nbsp;I, launched an Orion spacecraft into a lunar orbit on a test flight in fall 2022,<ref>{{cite news |title=Former NASA Official: Moon launch this month may be "embarrassing" |url=https://futurism.com/the-byte/lori-garver-sls-moon-launch |work=The Byte |date=August 25, 2022 |access-date=September 15, 2022 |archive-date=September 16, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220916001826/https://futurism.com/the-byte/lori-garver-sls-moon-launch |url-status=live}}</ref> and NASA and Boeing are constructing the next three rockets for [[Artemis&nbsp;II]], [[Artemis&nbsp;III]], and [[Artemis&nbsp;IV]].<ref name="nsf-20210719" /> Boeing stated in July 2021 that while the [[COVID-19 pandemic]] had affected their suppliers and schedules, such as delaying parts needed for hydraulics, they would still be able to provide the Artemis&nbsp;II SLS core stage per NASA's schedule, with months to spare.<ref name="nsf-20210719" /> The spray-on foam insulation process for Artemis&nbsp;II was automated for most sections of the core stage, saving 12 days in the schedule.<ref name="boeing-20210714" /><ref name="nsf-20210719" /> The Artemis&nbsp;II forward skirt, the foremost component of the core stage, was affixed on the liquid oxygen tank in late May 2021.<ref name="nsf-20210719" /> By September 25, 2023, the core stage was functionally complete, as all sections were assembled and the four RS-25 engines had been installed.<ref>{{cite web | last=Mohon | first=Lee | title=All Engines Added to NASA's Artemis II Moon Rocket Core Stage – Artemis | website=NASA Blogs | date=September 25, 2023 | url=https://blogs.nasa.gov/artemis/2023/09/25/all-engines-added-to-nasas-artemis-ii-moon-rocket-core-stage/ | access-date=September 25, 2023 | archive-date=September 25, 2023 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230925202615/https://blogs.nasa.gov/artemis/2023/09/25/all-engines-added-to-nasas-artemis-ii-moon-rocket-core-stage/ | url-status=live}}</ref> The complete core stage was set to ship to NASA in late fall 2023,<ref>{{cite web | last=Clark | first=Stephen | title=Rocket Report: Iran launches satellite; Artemis II boosters get train ride | website=Ars Technica | date=September 29, 2023 | url=https://arstechnica.com/space/2023/09/rocket-report-iran-launches-satellite-artemis-ii-boosters-get-train-ride/ | access-date=October 2, 2023 | archive-date=September 29, 2023 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230929111259/https://arstechnica.com/space/2023/09/rocket-report-iran-launches-satellite-artemis-ii-boosters-get-train-ride/ | url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | last=Sloss | first=Philip | title=Artemis II Moon mission transitioning from planning to preparation | website=NASASpaceFlight.com | date=May 2, 2023 | url=https://www.nasaspaceflight.com/2023/05/artemis-ii-update/ | access-date=June 6, 2023 | archive-date=May 2, 2023 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230502201704/https://www.nasaspaceflight.com/2023/05/artemis-ii-update/ | url-status=live}}</ref> eight months later than was predicted originally.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Sloss |first=Philip |date=July 25, 2022 |title=Boeing aiming to deliver second SLS Core Stage to NASA in March |url=https://www.nasaspaceflight.com/2022/07/boeing-second-sls-core-march/ |access-date=July 30, 2022 |website=NASASpaceFlight.com |language=en-US |archive-date=August 31, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220831222158/https://www.nasaspaceflight.com/2022/07/boeing-second-sls-core-march/ |url-status=live}}</ref> The complete core stage was delivered in July 2024.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/boeing-delivers-second-stage-of-sls-rocket-to-nasa/ | title=Boeing delivers second stage of SLS rocket to NASA - AGN Boeing delivers second stage of SLS rocket to NASA | date=July 17, 2024 }}</ref> For Artemis&nbsp;III, assembly of elements of the thrust structure began at Michoud Assembly Facility in early 2021.<ref name="nsf-20210719" /> By August 2025, the thrust structure was completed and moved to storage in the [[Vehicle Assembly Building]] at Kennedy, to await the rest of the stage's arrival in mid-2026.<ref name="NASA 2025-08-18">{{cite web |author=NASA Communications team| title=NASA Begins Processing Artemis III Moon Rocket at Kennedy | website=NASA | date=August 18, 2025 | url=https://www.nasa.gov/blogs/missions/2025/08/18/nasa-begins-processing-artemis-iii-moon-rocket-at-kennedy/ | access-date=August 18, 2025}}</ref> The liquid hydrogen tank for Artemis&nbsp;III was originally planned to be the Artemis&nbsp;I tank, but it was set aside as the welds were found to be faulty.<ref name="highlights-202002" />{{rp|2}} Repair techniques were developed, and the tank re-entered production and will be proof tested for strength, for use on Artemis&nbsp;III.<ref name="highlights-202002" />{{rp|2}}

the next launch option was at first a period in late<ref name="NASA Ian Update Sept26" /><ref name="SN-20220927" /> October and then a launch in mid-November, due to unfavorable weather during [[Hurricane Ian (2022)|Hurricane Ian]].<ref name="NASA Ian Update 0924" /><ref>{{cite web | title=Artemis I Launch Attempt Scrubbed | last=Kraft | first=Rachel | website=NASA Blogs | date=September 3, 2022 | url=https://blogs.nasa.gov/artemis/2022/09/03/artemis-i-launch-attempt-scrubbed/ | access-date=September 3, 2022 | archive-date=December 28, 2022 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221228161944/https://blogs.nasa.gov/artemis/2022/09/03/artemis-i-launch-attempt-scrubbed/ | url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="NSF-20220908" /> It launched on November 16.<ref>{{Cite web |date=November 16, 2022 |title=SLS Artemis I Mission |url=https://rocketlaunch.org/mission-sls-block-1-artemis-i |website=RocketLaunch.org |access-date=March 27, 2024 |archive-date=September 1, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240901012834/https://rocketlaunch.org/mission-sls-block-1-artemis-i |url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last1=Roulette |first1=Joey |last2=Gorman |first2=Steve |date=November 16, 2022 |title=NASA's next-generation Artemis mission heads to moon on debut test flight |language=en |work=Reuters |url=https://www.reuters.com/lifestyle/science/nasas-artemis-moon-rocket-begins-fueling-debut-launch-2022-11-15/ |access-date=November 16, 2022 |archive-date=November 16, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221116115602/https://www.reuters.com/lifestyle/science/nasas-artemis-moon-rocket-begins-fueling-debut-launch-2022-11-15/ |url-status=live}}</ref>

NASA originally limited the amount of time the solid rocket boosters can remain stacked to "about a year" from the time two segments are joined.<ref name="nsf-20201204" /> The first and second segments of the Artemis&nbsp;I boosters were joined on January 7, 2021.<ref name="SFN-20210309" /> NASA could choose to extend the time limit based on an engineering review.<ref name="SFN-20210115" /> On September 29, 2021, Northrop Grumman indicated that the limit could be extended to eighteen months for Artemis&nbsp;I, based on an analysis of the data collected when the boosters were being stacked;<ref name="NSF-20210929" /> an analysis weeks before the actual launch date later extended that to December 2022 for the boosters of Artemis&nbsp;I, almost two years after stacking.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://spacenews.com/sls-returns-to-the-pad-for-next-artemis-launch-attempt/|title=SLS returns to the pad for next Artemis launch attempt|date=November 4, 2022|access-date=November 16, 2022}}</ref>

In late 2015, the SLS program was stated to have a 70% confidence level for the [[Artemis 2|first Orion flight that carries crew]], the second SLS flight overall, to happen by 2023;<ref>{{cite web |url=http://spacenews.com/first-crewed-orion-mission-may-slip-to-2023/|title=First Crewed Orion Mission May Slip to 2023|last=Foust|first=Jeff|date=September 16, 2015|publisher=SpaceNews|access-date=June 23, 2016|archive-date=September 30, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210930001748/https://spacenews.com/first-crewed-orion-mission-may-slip-to-2023/|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://spaceflightnow.com/2015/09/16/orion-spacecraft-may-not-fly-with-astronauts-until-2023/|title=Orion spacecraft may not fly with astronauts until 2023|last=Clark|first=Stephen|publisher=Spaceflight Now|date=September 16, 2015|access-date=June 23, 2016|archive-date=July 1, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160701155403/https://spaceflightnow.com/2015/09/16/orion-spacecraft-may-not-fly-with-astronauts-until-2023/|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.spacepolicyonline.com/news/mikulski-deeply-troubled-by-nasas-budget-request-sls-wont-use-70-percent-jcl|title=Mikulski "Deeply Troubled" by NASA's Budget Request; SLS Won't Use 70 Percent JCL|last=Clark|first=Smith|date=May 1, 2014|website=spacepolicyonline.com|access-date=June 23, 2016|archive-date=August 5, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160805085633/http://www.spacepolicyonline.com/news/mikulski-deeply-troubled-by-nasas-budget-request-sls-wont-use-70-percent-jcl|url-status=live}}</ref> however, the flight did not take place until 2026.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Harwood |first1=William |title=NASA launches Artemis II crew on flight around the moon. Here's everything to know about the mission. |url=https://www.cbsnews.com/news/nasa-artemis-ii-moon-launch-astronauts-flight-plan/ |website=[[CBS News]] |access-date=April 4, 2026}}</ref>
{{SLS launches/future}}

==== Usage beyond Artemis ====
{{main|List of Space Launch System launches#Proposed launches}}

Efforts have been made to expand the [[Artemis program|Artemis]] missions to launching NASA's robotic [[Space probes|space probes and observatories]]. However, SLS program officials have noted that between the launch cadence of Artemis missions and supply chain constraints, it is unlikely that rockets could be built to support science missions before the late 2020s or early 2030s.<ref name="Foust20210708">{{Cite web |last=Foust |first=Jeff |date=July 8, 2021 |title=Supply chain, Artemis program limit SLS use for science missions |url=https://spacenews.com/supply-chain-artemis-program-limits-sls-use-for-science-missions/ |access-date=November 27, 2024 |publisher=[[SpaceNews]]}}</ref>

Another challenge is that the large solid-rocket boosters produce significant vibrations, which can damage sensitive scientific instruments. During wind-tunnel testing, torsional load values (a measurement of twisting and vibration) were nearly double initial estimates.<ref name="Berger20210623">{{cite news |last=Berger |first=Eric |author-link=Eric Berger (journalist) |date=July 23, 2021 |title=SpaceX to launch the Europa Clipper mission for a bargain price |url=https://arstechnica.com/science/2021/07/spacex-to-launch-the-europa-clipper-mission-for-a-bargain-price/ |access-date=November 28, 2021 |work=[[Ars Technica]]}}</ref> Although program officials later acknowledged the issue, they expressed confidence in their ability to mitigate it.<ref name="Foust20210708" />
