======================================================================
WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: Third-party evidence for Apollo Moon landings
======================================================================

{{short description|Independent confirmations of Apollo Moon landings}}
[[Image:Apollo12ConradSurveyor.jpg|right|thumb|300px|Photograph AS12-48-7134: [[Apollo 12]] astronaut [[Pete Conrad]] with the uncrewed [[Surveyor 3]], which had landed on the [[Moon]] in 1967. Parts of Surveyor were brought back to Earth by Apollo 12. The camera (near Conrad's right hand) is on display at the [[National Air and Space Museum]]]]

'''Third-party evidence for the Apollo Moon landings''' is evidence or analysis of evidence about the [[Apollo mission|Apollo]] [[Moon landing]]s that does not come from the [[U.S. government]] (the first party) or from [[Moon landing conspiracy theories|Moon landing hoax theorists]] (the second party). This evidence provides independent confirmation of [[NASA]]'s account of the six lunar missions carried out between 1969 and 1972.

==Independent evidence==
In this section are only those observations that are completely independent of NASA—no NASA facilities were used, and there was no NASA funding. Each of the countries mentioned in this section ([[Soviet Union]], [[Japan]], [[China]], and [[India]]) has its own [[Space exploration|space program]], builds its own [[space probe]]s which are launched on their own [[launch vehicle]]s, and has its own deep space communication network.<ref>See, for example, the references in the articles [[Indian Deep Space Network]], [[Chinese Deep Space Network]], [[Soviet Deep Space Network]], [[ESTRACK]] (European Deep Space Network), and [[Japanese Deep Space Network]].</ref>

===SELENE photographs===
In 2008, the [[Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency]] (JAXA) [[SELENE]] lunar probe obtained several photographs showing evidence of Moon landings.<ref>{{cite press release |title=The "halo" area around Apollo 15 landing site observed by Terrain Camera on SELENE (KAGUYA) |date=May 20, 2008 |publisher=Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency |location=Chōfu, Tokyo |url=https://global.jaxa.jp/press/2008/05/20080520_kaguya_e.html |access-date=May 20, 2008 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220314183644/https://global.jaxa.jp/press/2008/05/20080520_kaguya_e.html |archive-date=14 March 2022 |url-status=live }}</ref> On the left are two photographs taken on the lunar surface by astronauts on August 2, 1971 during the third [[Apollo 15]] moonwalk at station 9A near Hadley Rille. On the right is a 2008 reconstruction from images taken by the SELENE terrain camera and [[3D computer graphics|3D]] projected to the same vantage point as the surface photos. The terrain is a close match within the SELENE camera resolution of 10 metres.{{citation needed|date=September 2023}}

<gallery mode=packed>
File:Apollo 15 with lunar rover.jpg|AS15-82-11121: Apollo 15 [[Lunar Roving Vehicle]]
file:Apollo15_Moon_photo.jpg|AS15-82-11122: Apollo 15 photo
file:JAXA_Moon_photo.jpg|[[3D computer graphics|3D]] SELENE reconstructed photo
</gallery>

The light-colored area of blown lunar surface dust created by the Lunar Module ''Falcon'' engine blast at the Apollo 15 landing site was photographed and confirmed by comparative analysis of photographs in May 2008. They correspond well to photographs taken from the Apollo 15 [[Apollo Command/Service Module|Command/Service Module]] showing a change in surface reflectivity due to the plume. This was the first visible trace of crewed landings on the Moon seen from space since the close of the Apollo program.{{citation needed|date=September 2023}}

===Chandrayaan-1===

As with SELENE, the Terrain Mapping Camera of India's [[Chandrayaan-1]] probe did not have enough [[angular resolution#Explanation|resolution]] to record Apollo hardware. Nevertheless, as with SELENE, Chandrayaan-1 independently recorded evidence of [[Space weathering#Effects on spectral properties|lighter, disturbed soil]] around the Apollo 15 site.<ref name="badsci">{{cite web |url=http://depletedcranium.com/apollo-15-confirmed-times-three/ |title=Apollo 15: Confirmed Times Three |last=drbuzz0 |date=November 7, 2009 |website=Depleted Cranium |publisher=Steve Packard |type=Blog |access-date=May 2, 2013 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120917234008/http://depletedcranium.com/apollo-15-confirmed-times-three/ |archive-date=September 17, 2012 }}</ref><ref name="isro">{{cite journal |last1=Chauhan |first1=Prakash |last2=Kirankumar |first2=A. S. |date=September 10, 2009 |title=Chandrayaan-1 captures Halo around Apollo-15 landing site using stereoscopic views from Terrain Mapping Camera |journal=[[Current Science]] |volume=97 |issue=5 |pages=630–31 |publisher=Current Science Association in collaboration with the [[Indian Academy of Sciences]] |issn=0011-3891 |url=http://www.currentscience.ac.in/Downloads/article_id_097_05_0630_0631_0.pdf}}</ref>

=== Chandrayaan-2 ===
[[File:Chandrayaan-2 Apollo.jpg|alt=Chandrayaan-2 image of the Lunar Module Eagle descent stage|thumb|[[Chandrayaan-2]] image of the [[Lunar Module Eagle|Lunar Module ''Eagle'']] descent stage at [[Tranquility Base]]]]
In April 2021 the [[ISRO]] [[Chandrayaan-2]] orbiter captured an image of the [[Apollo 11]] [[Lunar Module Eagle|Lunar Module ''Eagle'']] descent stage. The orbiter's image of [[Tranquility Base]], the Apollo 11 landing site, was released to the public in a presentation on September 3, 2021.<ref>{{Citation|title=GUJCOST Celebrates Vigyan Utsav (STI Ecosystem for Atmanirbhar Bharat) {{!}} 3rd September 2021| date=3 September 2021 |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=T8oV-Kx26no|language=en|access-date=2021-10-25}}</ref>

===Chang'e 2===
China's second lunar probe, [[Chang'e 2]], which was launched in 2010 is capable of capturing lunar surface images with a resolution of up to 1.3 metres. It claims to have spotted traces of the Apollo landings and the lunar Rover, though the relevant imagery has not been publicly identified.<ref>{{cite news |title=China publishes high-resolution full moon Map |editor-last=Zhang |editor-first=Nannan |url=https://english.cas.cn/newsroom/archive/china_archive/cn2012/201202/t20120207_81106.shtml |publisher=[[Chinese Academy of Sciences]] |location=Beijing |date=February 7, 2012 |access-date=January 9, 2024 }}</ref>

===Danuri===
South Korea's lunar probe, [[Danuri]], which was launched in 2022 is capable of capturing lunar surface images. It imaged both Apollo 11 and Apollo 17 landing sites in 2023, with a good enough resolution to spot the landers.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.kari.re.kr/kplo/danuri/multi/multiMediaView.do?idx=44 |title=[고해상도카메라] 아폴로 11호 착륙지점('23.3.30., 5.10.) |trans-title=[High-resolution camera] Apollo 11 landing site |website=Korean Areospace Research Institute |location=South Korea |language=Korean |date=2023-09-27 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241224095300/https://www.kari.re.kr/kplo/danuri/multi/multiMediaView.do?idx=44 |url-status=dead |archive-date=2024-12-24 |access-date=2025-12-05}}</ref>

=== Apollo missions tracked by independent parties ===
Aside from NASA, a number of entities and individuals observed, through various means, the Apollo missions as they took place. On later missions, NASA released information to the public explaining where third party observers could expect to see the various craft at specific times according to scheduled launch times and planned trajectories.<ref name="astr.ua.edu" />

==== Observers of all missions ====
The Soviet Union monitored the missions at their Space Transmissions Corps, which was "fully equipped with the latest intelligence-gathering and surveillance equipment".<ref>[[#Scott & Leonov|Scott & Leonov 2004]], p. 247</ref> [[Vasily Mishin]], in an interview for the article "The Moon Programme That Faltered", describes how the Soviet Moon programme dwindled after the Apollo landing.<ref>{{cite journal |date=March 1991 |title=The Moon Programme That Faltered |journal=[[Spaceflight (magazine)|Spaceflight]] |volume=33 |pages=2–3 |location=London |publisher=[[British Interplanetary Society]]|bibcode=1991SpFl...33....2. }}</ref>

The missions were tracked by radar from several countries on the way to the Moon and back.<ref>[[#Hansen|Hansen 2005]], p. 639</ref>

====Kettering Grammar School====
A group at [[Kettering Grammar School]], using simple radio equipment, monitored Soviet and U.S. [[spacecraft]] and calculated their orbits.<ref>{{cite journal |author=Perry, G. E. |title=A school satellite tracking station as an aid to the teaching of physics |journal=Physics Education |volume=3 |issue=6 |date=1968 |page=281 |url=http://www.phys.unsw.edu.au/~map/weather/notes/buildyourown/perry_1968.pdf |doi=10.1088/0031-9120/3/6/301|bibcode=1968PhyEd...3..281P }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |author=Roberts, G. |title=The Amateur and Artificial Satellites |journal=Monthly Notes of the Astronomical Society of South Africa |volume=45 |date=1986 |page=5 |bibcode=1986MNSSA..45....5R}}</ref> According to the group, in December 1972 a member "picks up Apollo 17 on its way to the Moon".<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.zarya.info/Kettering/Archive/Chronology1.php |title=Kettering Group Timeline |last=Christy |first=Robert D. |website=zarya.info |access-date=May 9, 2013}}</ref>

==== Apollo 8 ====
{{main|Apollo 8}}
Apollo 8 was the first crewed mission to orbit the Moon, but did not land.
* On December 21, 1968, at 18:00 UT, [[amateur astronomers]] (H. R. Hatfield, M. J. Hendrie, F. Kent, Alan Heath, and M. J. Oates) in the [[United Kingdom|UK]] photographed a fuel dump from the jettisoned [[S-IVB]] third rocket stage.<ref name="astr.ua.edu">{{cite web | url = http://www.astr.ua.edu/keel/space/apollo.html | title = Telescopic Tracking of the Apollo Lunar Missions | work = Bill Keel's Space History Bits |date=August 2008 | first = Bill | last = Keel}}</ref>
* [[Pic du Midi de Bigorre|Pic du Midi Observatory]] (in the [[French Pyrenees]]); the [[Catalina Station]] of the [[Lunar and Planetary Laboratory]] ([[University of Arizona]]); [[Corralitos Observatory]], [[New Mexico]], then operated by [[Northwestern University]]; [[McDonald Observatory]] of the [[University of Texas]]; and [[Lick Observatory]] of the [[University of California]] all filed reports of observations.<ref name="astr.ua.edu"/>
* Dr. Michael Moutsoulas at Pic du Midi Observatory reported an initial sighting around 17:10 UT on December 21 with the 1.1-metre reflector as an object ([[Apparent magnitude|magnitude]] near 10, through clouds) moving eastward near the predicted location of Apollo 8. He used a 60&nbsp;cm [[Refracting telescope|refractor telescope]] to observe a cluster of objects which were obscured by the appearance of a nebulous cloud at a time which matches a firing of the service module engine to assure adequate separation from the [[S-IVB]]. This event can be traced with the Apollo 8 Flight Journal, noting that launch was at 0751 EST or 12:51 UT on December 21.<ref name="astr.ua.edu"/>
* Justus Dunlap and others at Corralitos Observatory (then operated by Northwestern University) obtained over 400 short-exposure intensified images, giving very accurate locations for the spacecraft.<ref name="astr.ua.edu"/>
* The 2.1&nbsp;m [[Otto Struve Telescope]] at McDonald Observatory, from 01:50 to 2:37 UT on December 23, observed the brightest object flashing as bright as magnitude 15, with the flash pattern recurring about once a minute.<ref name="astr.ua.edu"/>
* The Lick Observatory observations during the return coast to Earth produced live television pictures broadcast to United States west coast viewers via [[KQED-TV]] in San Francisco.<ref name="astr.ua.edu"/>
* An article in the March 1969 issue of ''[[Sky & Telescope]]'' contained many reports of optical tracking of Apollo 8.<ref name="astr.ua.edu" /><ref>{{cite magazine |magazine=Sky and Telescope |year=1969 |issue=3 |pages=156 |title=Feature Optical Observations of Apollo 8 |last=Liemohn |first=Harold B.}}</ref>
* The first post-launch sightings were from the [[Smithsonian Astrophysical Observatory]] (SAO) station on [[Maui]].<ref name="astr.ua.edu" /> Many in [[Hawaii]] observed the trans-lunar injection burn near 15:44 UT on December 21.<ref>{{cite news |title=Apollo 8 Mission Leaves Earth on Historic Voyage |first=Dave |last=Swaim |url=https://newspaperarchive.com/independent-star-news/1968-12-22 |newspaper=Independent Star News |location=Pasadena, California |page=1 |date=December 22, 1968 |access-date=May 9, 2013 |quote=The TLI firing was begun at 7:41 a.m. (PST) while the craft was over Hawaii, and it was reported there that the burn was visible from the ground.}}</ref>

==== Apollo 10 ====
{{main|Apollo 10}}
Like Apollo 8, Apollo 10 orbited the Moon but did not land.
* A list of sightings of Apollo 10 were reported in "Apollo 10 Optical Tracking" by ''Sky & Telescope'' magazine, July 1969, pp.&nbsp;62–63.<ref>{{cite magazine |magazine=Sky and Telescope |year=1969 |issue=7 |pages=62–63 |title=Apollo 10 Optical Tracking }}</ref>
* During the Apollo 10 mission The Corralitos Observatory was linked with the CBS news network. Images of the spacecraft going to the Moon were broadcast live.<ref name="NASA1">{{cite journal |url=http://naca.larc.nasa.gov/search.jsp?R=19760016037&qs=Ns%3DLoaded-Date%7C0%26N%3D4294707799 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130509075111/http://naca.larc.nasa.gov/search.jsp?R=19760016037&qs=Ns%3DLoaded-Date%7C0%26N%3D4294707799 |url-status=dead |archive-date=2013-05-09 |title=The Corralitos Observatory Program for the Detection of Lunar Transient Phenomena |volume=76 |pages=23125 |last=Hynek |first=J. Allen |author-link=J. Allen Hynek |date=April 1976 |journal=NASA Technical Reports Server |publisher=NASA|bibcode=1976STIN...7623125H }}</ref> {{rp|p. 17}}

==== Apollo 11 ====
{{main|Apollo 11}}
* The [[Bochum Observatory]] director (Professor [[Heinz Kaminski]]) was able to provide confirmation of events and data independent of both the [[Russia]]n and U.S. space agencies.<ref name="Bochum">{{cite web | url = http://www.honeysucklecreek.net/other_stations/bochum/index.html | work = A Tribute to Honeysuckle Creek Tracking Station | title = Bochum}}</ref>
* A compilation of sightings appeared in "Observations of Apollo 11" by ''Sky and Telescope'' magazine, November 1969.<ref>{{cite magazine |magazine=Sky and Telescope |year=1969 |issue=11 |pages=358–359 |title=Observations of Apollo 11 }}</ref>
* At [[Jodrell Bank Observatory]] in the UK, the telescope was used to observe the mission, as it was used years previously for [[Sputnik]].<ref name="open2">{{cite web | url=http://www.open.edu/openlearn/history-the-arts/history/the-other-space-race-transcript | title=The other space race: Transcript | access-date=February 6, 2006 | work=[[OpenLearn]] | first=Michael | last=Portillo | date=June 2, 2005}}</ref><!-- Also see http://www.mikepeel.net/site/Jodrell_Bank_stories --> At the same time, Jodrell Bank scientists [https://web.archive.org/web/20090717021523/http://www.jodrellbank.manchester.ac.uk/multimedia/audio/luna15-apollo11.html were tracking] the uncrewed Soviet spacecraft [[Luna 15]], which was trying to land on the Moon.<ref>{{cite web | url = http://www.jb.man.ac.uk/news/2009/luna15-apollo11/ | title = Recording of Russia's lunar gatecrash attempt released | date = 3 July 2009 | publisher = [[Jodrell Bank Centre for Astrophysics]] | access-date = July 20, 2009}}</ref> In July 2009, Jodrell released some recordings they made.<ref>{{cite news | url = https://www.independent.co.uk/news/science/recording-tracks-russias-moon-gatecrash-attempt-1730851.html | title = Recording tracks Russia's Moon gatecrash attempt | first = Jonathan | last = Brown | date = 3 July 2009 | work = [[The Independent]] | location = London | access-date = July 20, 2009}}</ref>
* Larry Baysinger, a [[radio amateur]] (W4EJA) and a technician for [[WHAS (AM)|WHAS radio]] in [[Louisville, Kentucky]], independently detected and recorded transmissions between the Apollo 11 astronauts on the lunar surface and the Lunar Module.<ref>{{cite news |title=Lunar Eavesdropping: Louisvillians Hear Moon Walk Talk on Homemade Equipment |last=Rutherford |first=Glenn |url=http://observatory.jctcfaculty.org/APOLLO11/Default.htm |work=[[The Courier-Journal]] |location=Louisville, KY |date=23 July 1969 |page= B1 |access-date=May 14, 2013}}</ref> Recordings made by Baysinger share certain characteristics with recordings made at Bochum Observatory by Kaminski, in that both Kaminski's and Baysinger's recordings do not include the [[Flight controller#Spacecraft communicator (CAPCOM)|Capsule Communicator]] (CAPCOM) in [[Houston]], [[Texas]], and the associated [[Quindar tones]] heard in NASA audio and seen on NASA Apollo 11 transcripts. Kaminski and Baysinger could only hear the transmissions from the Moon, and not transmissions to the Moon from the Earth.<ref name="Bochum"/><ref>{{cite web | url = http://observatory.jctcfaculty.org/APOLLO11/Default.htm  | work = Lunar Eavesdropping in Louisville, Kentucky | title = Otter Creek-South Harrison Observatory}}</ref>
*The [[Arcetri Observatory]] near [[Florence]], [[Italy]], also detected transmissions coming from the mission<ref>{{Cite web|last=Bucciantini|first=Niccolò|date=2019-07-16|title=Così da Arcetri captarono lo sbarco sulla Luna|url=https://www.media.inaf.it/2019/07/16/sbarco-luna-arcetri-20-luglio/|access-date=2021-11-11|website=MEDIA INAF|language=it-IT}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|date=2019-07-16|title=La notte che da Arcetri ascoltarono gli astronauti parlare sulla luna|url=https://firenze.repubblica.it/tempo-libero/articoli/cultura/2019/07/16/news/luna_allunaggio_firenze-231312069/|access-date=2021-11-11|website=la Repubblica|language=it}}</ref> using a 10-meter dish.<ref>{{Cite journal|title=1967MmSAI..38..539C Page 539|url=http://articles.adsabs.harvard.edu//full/1967MmSAI..38..539C/0000539.000.html|access-date=2021-11-11|journal=Memorie della Societa Astronomica Italiana|bibcode=1967MmSAI..38..539C |last1=Cantù |first1=A. M. |last2=Felli |first2=M. |last3=Landini |first3=M. |last4=Tofani |first4=G. |year=1967 |volume=38 |page=539 }}</ref><!-- Also see https://lunasicisiamoandati.blogspot.com/2018/02/35-la-conferma-italiana-astronauti.html -->

==== Apollo 12 ====
{{main|Apollo 12}}

Paul Maley reports several sightings of the Apollo 12 Command Module.<ref name="astr.ua.edu" />

''Sky and Telescope'' magazine published reports of the optical sighting of this mission.<ref>{{cite magazine |magazine=Sky and Telescope |year=1970 |issue=2 |pages=127 |title=Optical Observations of Apollo 12}}</ref>

==== Apollo 13 ====
{{main|Apollo 13}}
Apollo 13 was intended to land on the Moon, but an oxygen tank explosion resulted in the mission being aborted after trans-lunar injection. It flew by the Moon but did not orbit or land.

[[Chabot Observatory]] calendar records an application of optical tracking during the final phases of Apollo 13, on April 17, 1970:

{{blockquote|Rachel, Chabot Observatory's 20-inch refracting telescope, helps bring Apollo 13 and its crew home. One last burn of the lunar lander engines was needed before the crippled spacecraft's re-entry into the Earth's atmosphere. In order to compute that last burn, NASA needed a precise position of the spacecraft, obtainable only by telescopic observation. All the observatories that could have done this were clouded over, except Oakland's Chabot Observatory, where members of the Eastbay Astronomical Society had been tracking the Moon flights. EAS members received an urgent call from NASA Ames Research Station, which had ties with Chabot's educational program since the 60s, and they put the Observatory's historic 20-inch refractor to work. They were able to send the needed data to Ames, and the Apollo crew was able to make the needed correction and to return safely to Earth on this date in 1970.<ref name="astr.ua.edu"/>}}

==== Apollo 14 ====
{{main|Apollo 14}}
Corralitos Observatory photographed Apollo 14.<ref name="astr.ua.edu" /><ref>{{cite journal|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=IgsAAAAAMBAJ&pg=PA33|title=The Relevance of Space (inset Apollo 14) |journal=Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists|first=Arthur|last=Kantrowitz|date=1 April 1971|publisher=Educational Foundation for Nuclear Science, Inc.|page=33|access-date=January 25, 2023}}</ref>

''Sky and Telescope'' magazine published reports of the optical sighting of this mission.<ref>{{cite magazine |magazine=Sky and Telescope |year=1971 |issue=4 |pages=251 |title=Some Optical Observations of Apollo 14}}</ref>

==== Apollo 15 ====
{{main|Apollo 15}}

Paul Wilson and Richard T. Knadle, Jr. received voice transmissions from the Command/Service Module in lunar orbit on the morning of August 1, 1971. In an article for ''[[QST]]'' magazine they provide a detailed description of their work, with photographs.<ref>{{cite journal |first1=P. M. |last1=Wilson |first2=R. T. |last2=Knadle |title=Houston, This is Apollo... |date=June 1972 |journal=[[QST]] |pages=60–65 |location=Newington, Connecticut |publisher=[[American Radio Relay League]]}}</ref>

==== Apollo 16 ====
{{main|Apollo 16}}
[[Jewett Observatory]] at [[Washington State University]] reported sightings of Apollo 16.<ref name="astr.ua.edu" />

At least two different radio amateurs, W4HHK and K2RIW, reported reception of Apollo 16 signals with home-built equipment.<ref>{{cite news |title=432 Record, W4HHK Apollo 16 Reception |work=QST |publisher=American Radio Relay League |location=Newington, Connecticut |date=June 1971 |pages=93–94}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=K2RIW Apollo 16 Reception & 2300 EME |work=QST |publisher=American Radio Relay League |location=Newington, Connecticut |date=July 1971 |pages=90–91}}</ref>

Bochum Observatory tracked the astronauts and intercepted the television signals from Apollo 16. The image was re-recorded in black and white in the [[576i|625 lines, 25 frames/s television standard]] onto 2-inch [[videotape]] using their sole quad machine. The transmissions are only of the astronauts and do not contain any voice from Houston, as the signal received came from the Moon only. The videotapes are held in storage at the observatory.<ref>{{cite news |title=Sternwarte Bochum beobachtet US-Apollo-Mondexperimente |last=Kaminski |first=H. |author-link=Heinz Kaminski |url=http://www.classicbroadcast.de/stories/stories_sternwarte_bochum.pdf |date=October–November 1972 |work=Neues von Rohde & Schwarz |publisher=[[Rohde & Schwarz]] |location=Munich |volume=57 |pages=24–27 |language=de |trans-title=Bochum Observatory Observed U.S. Apollo Moon Experiments |access-date=April 25, 2011}}</ref>

==== Apollo 17 ====
{{main|Apollo 17}}
Sven Grahn of the [[Swedish National Space Board|Swedish space program]] has described several amateur sightings of Apollo 17.<ref>{{cite web | url = https://planet4589.org/space/archive/sven/trackind/Apollo17/APOLLO17.htm | title = Tracking Apollo-17 from Florida | first = Sven | last = Grahn | work = Sven's Space Place}}</ref>

==Independent research consistent with NASA claims==

In this section is evidence, by independent researchers, that NASA's account is correct. However, at least somewhere in the investigation, there was some NASA involvement, or use of US government resources.

===Existence and age of Moon rocks===
A total of {{convert|382|kg|lb}} of [[Moon rock]]s and dust were collected during the Apollo 11, 12, 14, 15, 16 and 17 missions.<ref name="Papike98">{{cite journal | author = James Papike | author2 = Grahm Ryder| author3 = Charles Shearer  | name-list-style = amp| title = Lunar Samples | journal = Reviews in Mineralogy and Geochemistry | volume = 36 | pages = 5.1–5.234 | date = 1998 }}</ref> Some {{convert|10|kg|lb|abbr=on}} of the Moon rocks have been used in hundreds of experiments performed by both NASA researchers and planetary scientists at research institutions unaffiliated with NASA. These experiments have confirmed the age and origin of the rocks as lunar, and were used to identify lunar meteorites collected later from [[Antarctica]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.space.com/news/spaceagencies/apollo_moonrock_000927.html |title=House Passes Bill to Award Apollo Astronauts Moon Rocks |first=Robert |last=Pearlman |author-link=Robert Pearlman |date=September 27, 2000 |work=[[Space.com]] |publisher=[[TechMediaNetwork, Inc.]] |location=New York |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20001017185913/http://www.space.com/news/spaceagencies/apollo_moonrock_000927.html |archive-date=October 17, 2000 |access-date=May 14, 2013}}</ref> The oldest Moon rocks are up to 4.5 billion years old,<ref name="Papike98" /> making them 200 million years older than the [[Oldest rock|oldest Earth rocks]], which are from the [[Hadean]] eon and dated 3.8 to 4.3 billion years ago. The rocks returned by Apollo are very close in composition to the samples returned by the independent Soviet [[Luna programme]].<ref>{{cite journal |title=Chemical composition of Luna 20 rocks and soil and Apollo 16 soils |last1=Laul |first1=JC |last2=Schmitt |first2=RA |journal=Geochim. Cosmochim. Acta |volume=37 |issue=4 |date=1973 |bibcode=1973GeCoA..37..927L |doi=10.1016/0016-7037(73)90190-7 |pages=927–942}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |title=Geochemistry of rare elements in different types of lunar rocks (based on μXFA-SR data) |last1=Baryshev |first1=VB |last2=Kudryashova |first2=AF |last3=Tarasov |first3=LS |last4=Ulyanov |first4=AA |last5=Zolotarev |first5=KV |journal=Nucl. Instrum. Methods A |volume=470 |issue=1–2 |date=2001 |doi=10.1016/S0168-9002(01)01089-0 |pages=422–425|bibcode=2001NIMPA.470..422B }}</ref> A rock brought back by Apollo 17 was dated to be 4.417 billion years old, with a [[margin of error]] of plus or minus 6 million years. The test was done by a group of researchers headed by Alexander Nemchin at [[Curtin University of Technology]]  in [[Bentley, Western Australia|Bentley, Australia]].<ref>{{cite journal |last=Pendick |first=Daniel |date=June 2009 |title=Apollo sample pinpoints lunar crust's age |journal=[[Astronomy (magazine)|Astronomy]] |location=Waukesha, WI |publisher=[[Kalmbach Publishing]] |volume=37 |issue=6 |pages=16}}</ref>

===Retroreflectors===
[[Image:Apollo 11 Lunar Laser Ranging Experiment.jpg|thumb|200px|AS11-40-5952: Lunar Laser Ranging Experiment as left on the Moon by [[Apollo 11]]]]
[[Image:LunarPhotons.png|thumb|left|Plot of arrival time of photons (Y axis) for each of many [[laser]] pulses sent to the Moon (X axis). This data, along with similar data from the other landing sites, shows there are man-made objects on the Moon in the locations of the Apollo landings. Credit: The [[Apache Point Observatory Lunar Laser-ranging Operation|APOLLO]] (Lunar Laser Ranging) Collaboration]]
The detection on Earth of reflections from [[retroreflectors|laser ranging retro-reflector]]s (LRRRs, or arrays of corner-cube prisms used as targets for Earth-based tracking [[laser]]s) on [[Lunar Laser Ranging experiment]]s left on the Moon is evidence of landings.<ref>{{cite web | url = https://science.nasa.gov/headlines/y2004/21jul_llr.htm | title = What Neil & Buzz Left on the Moon | date = July 20, 2004 | work = Science@NASA | first = Tony | last = Phillips | url-status = dead | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20100405080014/http://science.nasa.gov/headlines/y2004/21jul_llr.htm | archive-date = April 5, 2010 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Laser Ranging Retroreflector |work=NSSDC Master Catalog |publisher=[[National Space Science Data Center]] |url=https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/nmc/experiment/display.action?id=1971-063C-08 |id=NSSDC ID: 1971-063C-08 |access-date=July 8, 2009}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last=Anderson |first=John D. |author-link=John D. Anderson |date=March 2009 |title=Is there something we don't know about gravity? |journal=Astronomy |location=Waukesha, WI |publisher=Kalmbach Publishing |volume=37 |issue=3 |pages=22–27}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last=Dorminey |first=Bruce |author-link=Bruce Dorminey |title=Secrets beneath the Moon's surface |date=March 2011 |journal=Astronomy |location=Waukesha, WI |publisher=Kalmbach Publishing |volume=39 |issue=3 |pages=24–29}}</ref>
[[File:ALSEP AS14-67-9386.jpg|thumb|200px|AS14-67-9386: Retroflector left on the Moon by [[Apollo 14]]]]

Quoting from James Hansen's 2005 biography of [[Neil Armstrong]], ''[[First Man: The Life of Neil A. Armstrong]]'':

<blockquote>For those few misguided souls who still cling to the belief that the Moon landings never happened, examination of the results of five decades of [[Lunar Laser Ranging experiment|LRRR experiments]] should evidence how delusional their rejection of the Moon landing really is.<ref>[[#Hansen|Hansen 2005]], pp. 515–516</ref></blockquote>

The NASA-independent [[Côte d'Azur Observatory|''Observatoire de la Côte d'Azur'']], [[McDonald Observatory|McDonald]], [[Apache Point Observatory Lunar Laser-ranging Operation|Apache Point]], and [[Haleakala Observatory|Haleakalā]] observatories regularly use the Apollo LRRR.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://syrte.obspm.fr/jsr/journees2005/pdf/s1_20_Bouquillon.pdf|title=Contribution of SLR Results to LLR Analysis |first1=S. |last1=Bouquillon |first2=J. |last2=Chapront |first3=G. |last3=Francou |publisher=[[Paris Observatory|Observatoire de Paris]] |location=Paris |access-date=July 26, 2007}} Paper presented at the Proceedings of the "Journées 2005 Systèmes de référence spatio-temporels," held at the [[Space Research Centre]] of the [[Polish Academy of Sciences]], Warsaw, Poland, September 19–21, 2005.</ref> Lick Observatory attempted to detect from Apollo 11's retroreflector while Armstrong and Aldrin were still on the Moon but did not succeed until August 1, 1969.<ref>[[#Hansen|Hansen 2005]], p. 515</ref> The Apollo 14 astronauts deployed a retroreflector on February 5, 1971, and McDonald Observatory detected it the same day. The Apollo 15 retroreflector was deployed on July 31, 1971, and was detected by McDonald Observatory within a few days.<ref>{{cite journal |author1=Bender, P. L. |author2=Currie, D. G. |author3=Dicke, R. H. |author4=Eckhardt, D. H. |author5=Faller, J. E. |author6=Kaula, W. M. |author7=Mullholland, J. D. |author8=Plotkin, H. H. |author9=Silverberg, E. C. |author10=Wilkinson, D. T. |author11=Williams, J. G. |author12=Alley, C. O. |date=October 19, 1973 |title=The Lunar Laser Ranging Experiment |journal=[[Science (journal)|Science]] |volume=182 |issue=4109 |pmid=17749298 |bibcode=1973Sci...182..229B |doi=10.1126/science.182.4109.229 |pages=229–238 |location=Washington, D.C. |publisher=[[American Association for the Advancement of Science]] |s2cid=32027563 |access-date=May 15, 2013 |url=http://www.physics.ucsd.edu/~tmurphy/apollo/doc/Bender.pdf |display-authors=3}}</ref>

The image on the left shows what is considered{{by whom|date=June 2024}} some of the most unambiguous evidence. This experiment repeatedly fires a laser at the Moon, at the spots where the Apollo landings were reported. The dots show when [[photon]]s are received from the Moon. The dark line shows that a large number come back at a specific time, and hence were reflected by something quite small (well under a metre in size). Photons reflected from the surface come back over a much broader range of times (the whole vertical range of the plot corresponds to only 18 metres or so in range). The concentration of photons at a specific time appears when the laser is aimed at the Apollos 11, 14 or 15 landing sites; otherwise the expected featureless distribution is observed.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://physics.ucsd.edu/~tmurphy/apollo/apollo.html |title=APOLLO (the Apache Point Observatory Lunar Laser-ranging Operation) |first=Tom |last=Murphy}}</ref> The Apollo reflectors are still in use.<ref name="lunar-geophysics">{{cite conference | url = http://ilrs.gsfc.nasa.gov/docs/williams_lw13.pdf | title = Lunar Geophysics, Geodesy, and Dynamics | first = James G. | last = Williams |author2=Dickey, Jean O. | conference = 13th International Workshop on Laser Ranging |date=October 2002 | conference-url = http://cddis.nasa.gov/lw13/}}</ref>

Strictly speaking, although retroreflectors left by Apollo astronauts are strong evidence that human-manufactured artifacts currently exist on the Moon and that human visitors left them there, they are not, on their own, ''conclusive'' evidence. Uncrewed missions are known to have placed such objects on the Moon, albeit not before 1970. Smaller retroreflectors were carried by the uncrewed landers ''[[Lunokhod 1]]'' and ''[[Lunokhod 2]]'' in 1970 and 1973, respectively.<ref name="lunar-geophysics" /> The location of ''Lunokhod 1'' was unknown for nearly 40 years but it was rediscovered in 2010 in photographs by the [[Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter]] (LRO) and its retroreflector is now in use. Both the United States and the USSR had the capability to soft-land objects on the surface of the Moon for several years before that. The USSR successfully landed its first uncrewed probe ([[Luna 9]]) on the Moon in February 1966, and the United States followed with [[Surveyor 1]] in June 1966, but no uncrewed landers carried retroreflectors before ''Lunokhod 1'' in November 1970. The retroreflectors are proof that human-made probes reached the exact locations of the Apollo 11, 14, and 15 landing sites at exactly the same time as those missions.

===Radio-telescopic observations===
In October–November 1977, the Soviet [[radio telescope]] [[RATAN-600]] observed all five transmitters of [[ALSEP]] scientific packages placed on the Moon surface by all Apollo landing missions excluding Apollo 11. Their selenographic coordinates and the [[transmitter power output]]s (20 W) were in agreement with the NASA reports.<ref name=nau78>Naugolnaia, M. N.; Spangenberg, E. E.; Soboleva, N. S.; Fomin, V. A. [http://adsabs.harvard.edu/full/1978SvAL....4..302N Determination of selenographic coordinates of objects by RATAN-600.] Pisma v Astronomicheskii Zhurnal, vol. 4, Dec. 1978, p. 562-565. (Soviet Astronomy Letters, vol. 4, Nov.-Dec. 1978, p. 302-303). {{free access}}</ref>

===Photographs===
====Ground-based telescopes====
In 2002, astronomers tested the optics of the [[Very Large Telescope]] by imaging the Apollo landing sites.<ref>{{cite news |title=World's biggest telescope to prove Americans really walked on Moon |first=Robert |last=Matthews |author-link=Robert Matthews (scientist) |url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/worldnews/northamerica/usa/1414144/Worlds-biggest-telescope-to-prove-Americans-really-walked-on-Moon.html |date=November 24, 2002 |newspaper=[[The Sunday Telegraph]] |publisher=[[Telegraph Media Group]] |location=London |access-date=May 15, 2013}}</ref> The telescope was used to image the Moon and provided a resolution of {{convert|130|meters}}, which was not good enough to resolve the {{convert|4.2|meter}} wide lunar landers or their long shadows.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.skyatnightmagazine.com/advice/skills/how-to-find-apollo-11s-landing-site-on-the-moon/|title=How to find Apollo 11's landing site on the Moon|website=Sky at Night Magazine|publisher=BBC|date=July 17, 2019|access-date=March 15, 2020|last1=Lawrence|first1=Pete}}</ref>

====New lunar missions====
[[File:Lroc apollo11 landing site 20091109 zoom.jpg|right|thumb|Apollo 11 landing site photographed by [[Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter|LRO]]]]
Post-Apollo lunar exploration missions have located and imaged artifacts of the Apollo program remaining on the Moon's surface.

Images taken by the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter mission beginning in July 2009 show the six Apollo [[Lunar Module]] descent stages, [[Apollo Lunar Surface Experiments Package]] (ALSEP) science experiments, astronaut footpaths, and the [[Lunar Roving Vehicle]]'s tire tracks. These images are the most effective proof to date to rebut the "landing hoax" theories.<ref name="LRO1">{{cite web |url=http://www.nasa.gov/mission_pages/LRO/multimedia/lroimages/apollosites.html |title=LRO Sees Apollo Landing Sites |last1=Hautaluoma |first1=Grey |last2=Freeberg |first2=Andy |editor-last=Garner |editor-first=Robert |date=July 17, 2009 |publisher=NASA |access-date=July 18, 2007 |quote=NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter, or LRO, has returned its first imagery of the Apollo Moon landing sites. The pictures show the Apollo missions' lunar module descent stages sitting on the moon's surface, as long shadows from a low sun angle make the modules' locations evident. |archive-date=November 16, 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091116012309/http://www.nasa.gov/mission_pages/LRO/multimedia/lroimages/apollosites.html |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref name="astronomy-magazine">{{cite magazine |last=Talcott |first=Richard |title=LRO takes first Moon images |magazine=[[Astronomy (magazine)|Astronomy]] |issn=0091-6358 |date=November 2009 |volume=37 |issue=11 |page=22}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://lroc.sese.asu.edu/news/?archives/76-LROCs-First-Look-at-the-Apollo-Landing-Sites.html |title=LROC's First Look at the Apollo Landing Sites |last=Robinson |first=Mark |publisher=LROC News System |date=July 17, 2009 |access-date=July 17, 2009}}</ref> Although this probe was indeed launched by NASA, the camera and the interpretation of the images are under the control of an academic group — the [[Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter|LROC Science Operations Center]] at [[Arizona State University]], along with many other academic groups.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://lroc.sese.asu.edu/EPO/Team/Bios.php |title=Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Camera - Our Team}}</ref>  At least some of these groups, such as [[German Aerospace Center]], Berlin, are not located in the US, and are not funded by the US government.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.dlr.de/irs/en/ |title=Institute of Space Systems}}</ref>

After the images shown here were taken, the LRO mission moved into a lower orbit for higher resolution camera work. All of the sites have since been re-imaged at higher resolution.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://lroc.sese.asu.edu/news/?archives/101-Apollo-11-Second-look.html |title=Apollo 11: Second look |last=Robinson |first=Mark |date=September 29, 2009 |publisher=LROC News System |access-date=May 15, 2013}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://lroc.sese.asu.edu/news/index.php?/archives/137-Exploring-the-Apollo-17-Site.html/ |title=Exploring the Apollo 17 Site |last=Robinson |first=Mark |date=October 28, 2009 |publisher=LROC news system |access-date=May 15, 2013}}</ref>
Comparison of the original 16&nbsp;mm Apollo 17 LM camera footage during ascent to the 2011 LRO photos of the landing site show an almost exact match of the rover tracks.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=oYPmitSg268 |title= How To Prove We Landed On The Moon|last=Jones |first=David |date=July 26, 2017 |publisher=EEVblog |access-date=July 26, 2017}}</ref>

Further imaging in 2012 shows the shadows cast by the flags planted by the astronauts on all Apollo landing sites. The exception is that of Apollo 11, which matches Buzz Aldrin's account of the flag being blown over by the lander's rocket exhaust on leaving the Moon.<ref name="bbcflags">{{cite news |title=Apollo Moon flags still standing, images show |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/science-environment-19050795 |work=[[BBC News]] |publisher=[[BBC]] |location=London |date=July 30, 2012 |access-date=July 30, 2012}}</ref>

====Ultraviolet photographs====
[[File:Apollo16EarthID.png|thumb|AS16-123-19657: Long-exposure photograph taken from the surface of the Moon by Apollo 16 using the [[Far Ultraviolet Camera/Spectrograph]]. It shows the Earth with the correct background of stars (some labeled)]]

[[Exposure (photography)|Long-exposure photos]] were taken with the [[Far Ultraviolet Camera/Spectrograph]] by [[Apollo 16]] on April 21, 1972, from the surface of the Moon. Some of these photos show the Earth with stars from the constellations [[Capricornus]] and [[Aquarius (constellation)|Aquarius]] in the background. The [[European Space Research Organisation]]'s [[TD-1A]] [[satellite]] later scanned the sky for stars that are bright in [[ultraviolet]] light. The TD-1A data obtained with the shortest [[passband]] is a close match for the Apollo 16 photographs.<ref>{{cite journal | last = Keel | first = William C. | title = The Earth and Stars in the Lunar Sky | journal = [[Skeptical Inquirer]] | volume = 31 | issue = 4 |date=July 2007 | pages = 47–50}}</ref>
{{clear}}

=== Apollo missions tracked by non-NASA personnel ===
This section contains reports of the lunar missions from facilities that had significant numbers of non-NASA employees. This includes facilities such as the [[Deep Space Network]], which employed (and still employs) many local citizens in [[Spain]] and Australia, and facilities such as the [[Parkes Observatory]], which were hired by NASA for specific tasks, but staffed by non-NASA personnel.

==== Observers of all missions ====

The NASA [[Manned Space Flight Network]] (MSFN) was a worldwide network of stations that tracked the [[Project Mercury|Mercury]], [[Project Gemini|Gemini]], Apollo and [[Skylab]] missions. Most MSFN stations were only needed during the launch, Earth orbit and landing phases of the lunar missions, but three "deep space" sites with larger antennas provided continuous coverage during the trans-lunar, trans-Earth and lunar mission phases. Today, these three sites form the NASA [[Deep Space Network]]: the [[Goldstone Deep Space Communications Complex]] near Goldstone, California; the [[Madrid Deep Space Communication Complex]] near [[Madrid]], Spain; and the [[Canberra Deep Space Communication Complex]], adjacent to the [[Tidbinbilla Nature Reserve]], near [[Canberra]], Australia.

Although most MSFN stations were NASA-owned, they employed many local citizens. NASA also contracted the [[Parkes Observatory]] in [[New South Wales]], Australia, to supplement the three deep space sites, most famously during the Apollo 11 moonwalk as documented by radio astronomer John Sarkissian<ref>{{cite journal |last=Sarkissian |first=John M. |title=On Eagle's Wings: The Parkes Observatory's Support of the Apollo 11 Mission |date=2001 |journal=Publications of the Astronomical Society of Australia |volume=18 |issue=3 |pages=287–310 |location=Collingwood, Victoria |publisher=[[CSIRO Publishing]] for the [[Astronomical Society of Australia]] |doi=10.1071/AS01038 |access-date=May 2, 2013 |url=http://www.parkes.atnf.csiro.au/news_events/apollo11/|bibcode = 2001PASA...18..287S |doi-access=free }} October 2000 website version, part 1 of 12: "Introduction." Original version available from [http://www.parkes.atnf.csiro.au/news_events/apollo11/pasa/on_eagles_wings.pdf CSIRO Parkes Observatory] (PDF).</ref> and portrayed (humorously and not quite accurately) in the 2000 film ''[[The Dish]]''. The Parkes Observatory is not NASA-owned; it is, and always has been, owned and operated by the [[Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organisation]] (CSIRO), a research agency of the [[Government of Australia|Australian government]]. It would have been relatively easy for NASA to avoid using the Parkes Observatory to receive the Apollo 11 lunar surface television signals by scheduling the moonwalk at an earlier time when the Goldstone station could provide complete coverage.

==== Apollo 11 ====
{{main|Apollo 11}}
* The Madrid Apollo Station, now part of the Deep Space Network, built in [[Fresnedillas de la Oliva|Fresnedillas]], near Madrid, Spain, tracked Apollo 11.<ref>{{cite web | url = http://www.honeysucklecreek.net/other_stations/fresnedillas/index.html | work = A Tribute to Honeysuckle Creek Tracking Station | title = The Fresnedillas (Madrid, Spain) MSFN station}}</ref> A large majority of the people working at this station were not employees of NASA, but of Spain's [[Instituto Nacional de Técnica Aeroespacial]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.honeysucklecreek.net/images/other_stations/madrid/Madrid_Roster_1972.pdf |title=Madrid Apollo Facility NASA/INTA Personnel Roster |date=February 29, 1972 }}</ref>

==== Apollo 12 ====
{{main|Apollo 12}}
[[Image:Surveyor3camera.jpg|right|thumb|300px|Surveyor 3 camera brought back from the Moon by Apollo 12, on display at the [[National Air and Space Museum]] ]]

Parts of [[Surveyor 3]], which landed on the Moon in April 1967, were brought back to Earth by Apollo 12 in November 1969.<ref name="Astronomy2007">{{cite journal |last=Oberg |first=James |author-link=James Oberg |date=November 2007 |title=50th anniversary of first microbes in orbit |journal=[[Astronomy (magazine)|Astronomy]] |location=Waukesha, WI |publisher=[[Kalmbach Publishing]] |volume=35 |issue=11 |page=2}}</ref> These samples were shown to have been exposed to lunar conditions.<ref>{{cite web | url = http://www.physics.berkeley.edu/research/price/Bob.Walker.Biography.pdf | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20070706201312/http://physics.berkeley.edu/research/price/Bob.Walker.Biography.pdf | archive-date = July 6, 2007 | title = Robert M. Walker | first1 = P. Buford | last1 = Price | first2 = Ernst | last2 = Zinner | date = 2004 }}</ref>

|The scientific mission was to: scan the energy spectra of inner zone protons and electrons; measure the fluxes of electrons of energy greater than 40 keV that are parallel, anti-parallel, and perpendicular to the magnetic lines of force over the auroral zone, and measure associated optical emission; and record solar protons on alert.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/nmc/spacecraft/display.action?id=1969-097A|access-date=2020-01-08|title=Azur|website=nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov}}{{NASA}}</ref>
|}

| {{Flag|UAE}} || Hope || Mars || {{success}} || [[Emirates Mars Mission|Hope]] satellite is the United Arab Emirates Space Agency's uncrewed space research project on Mars. It was launched with Japanese [[H-IIA]] rocket on 19 July and reached Mars on 9 February 2021.
|-
| {{Flag|China}} || [[Tianwen-1]] || Mars || {{success}} || Mission containing an orbiter, deployable and remote cameras, lander and ''[[Zhurong (rover)|Zhurong]]'' rover. This is China's 2nd uncrewed space research project on Mars. It was launched with [[Long March 5]] rocket on 23 July and the orbiter, lander and rover entered Mars orbit on 10 February 2021. The rover and lander landed on 14 May with rover deployment on 22 April 2021 and dropped a remote selfie camera on Mars on 1 June 2021 and while a deployable camera made a flyby around 10 February 2021 and another deployable camera was released into Mars orbit on 31 December 2021.

|rowspan=7| 2021 || {{flag|US}} || ''[[Lucy (spacecraft)|Lucy]]''||two [[Asteroid belt|main belt]] [[asteroid]]s as well as six [[Jupiter trojan]]s|| {{enroute}} || NASA probe that will complete a 12-year journey to nine different asteroids, visiting two [[Asteroid belt|main belt]] asteroids as well as six [[Jupiter trojan]]s,<ref>{{cite web|last=Hille|first=Karl|date=2019-10-21|title=NASA's Lucy Mission Clears Critical Milestone|url=http://www.nasa.gov/feature/goddard/2019/lucy-mission-clears-critical-milestone |publisher=NASA |access-date=2020-12-05}}{{PD-notice}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Kretke |first1=Katherine |title=NASA's Lucy Spacecraft Discovers 2nd Asteroid During Dinkinesh Flyby |url=https://www.nasa.gov/image-article/nasas-lucy-spacecraft-discovers-2nd-asteroid-during-dinkinesh-flyby/ |website=NASA |access-date=19 December 2023 |ref=NASA Dinkinesh}}</ref> asteroids which share [[Jupiter]]'s [[orbit]] around the [[Sun]], orbiting either ahead of or behind the planet. All target encounters will be [[Flyby (spaceflight)|fly-by]] encounters.<ref name="NYT-20170106">{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2017/01/06/science/nasa-psyche-asteroid.html|title=A Metal Ball the Size of Massachusetts That NASA Wants to Explore|last=Chang |first=Kenneth|newspaper=The New York Times|date=6 January 2017}}</ref> It was launched on October 16, 2021, on the 401 variant of [[Atlas V]] and has yet to study a trojan asteroid.

| {{Flag|Brazil}} || [[Amazônia-1]] || Earth || {{success}} || Amazônia-1 is the first Earth observation satellite developed by Brazil, helped by Argentina's INVAP, who provided the main computer, attitude controls and sensors, and the training of Brazilian engineers,[8] and launched at 04:54:00 UTC (10:24:00 IST) on 28 February 2021.

|{{flag|US}} || [[Double Asteroid Redirection Test|DART]]|| a Binary [[65803 Didymos]] asteroid system  || {{Success}} || ''[[Double Asteroid Redirection Test]]'', NASA's first mission to test planetary defense. Its uses involves test this technique by kinetically impacting the spacecraft to produce a small change in its orbital period. It was launched on November 24 with [[Falcon 9]] rocket. Accompanying the mission is [[LICIACube]] cubesat, a flyby mission that recorded the impact and its aftermaths.
|-
|{{Flag|Italy}}|| [[LICIACube]]|| a Binary [[65803 Didymos]] asteroid system  || {{Success}} || ''[[LICIACube]]'', Light Italian Cubesat for Imaging of Asteroids, is the first [[Agenzia Spaziale Italiana]]'s interplanetary mission. Ideated, designed, integrated and operated entirely in [[Italy]], it has been the witness of the first real-scale planetary defense test performed by [[Double Asteroid Redirection Test]]. [[LICIACube]] is the smallest human-made object that successfully performed a flyby of a [[Small Solar System body]]. It has been deployed two weeks before [[Double Asteroid Redirection Test|DART]]'s impact.

| {{Flag|US}} || ''[[Voyager 1]]'' and ''[[Voyager 2]]''|| None||  None|| 
In May, NASA reports that the ''Voyager 1'' spacecraft, the farthest human-made object, is sending data that does not reflect what is happening on board with the antenna apparently remaining in its prescribed orientation to Earth.<ref>{{cite news |title=Voyager is sending 'impossible data' back to Nasa from the edge of the Solar System |url=https://news.yahoo.com/voyager-sending-impossible-data-back-051015157.html |access-date=22 June 2022 |work=news.yahoo.com}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Engineers Investigating NASA's Voyager 1 Telemetry Data |url=https://www.jpl.nasa.gov/news/engineers-investigating-nasas-voyager-1-telemetry-data |website=NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) |access-date=22 June 2022}}</ref> In June, it was reported that NASA is preparing to power down the two Voyager spacecraft in the hope of using the remaining power to extend their operation to about 2030.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Folger |first1=Tim |title=Record-Breaking Voyager Spacecraft Begin to Power Down |url=https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/record-breaking-voyager-spacecraft-begin-to-power-down/ |access-date=22 June 2022 |work=Scientific American |language=en}}</ref>

|| {{flag|USA}}
|[[IM-2]]
|Moon
|{{Partial failure}}
|Lunar landing technology demonstration at [[Mare Frigoris]]. Launched on 27 February 2025 on a Falcon 9 Block 5 launch vehicle with [[Lunar Trailblazer]] and [[AstroForge#Odin (Brokkr-2)|Brokkr-2]] and landed on its side on 6 March 2025 and the mission ended sooner without conducting useful science and surface operations. Carried AstroAnt, [[Yaoki]], Micro-Nova and MAPP LV1 rovers to lunar surface.

======================================================================
WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: Timeline of space exploration
======================================================================

{{Short description|none}}
{{About|highlighting milestones in space exploration|a comprehensive list of all events|Timeline of Solar System exploration||}}
{{Cleanup list|date=February 2023}}
This is a timeline of [[space exploration]] which includes notable missions, achievements, first accomplishments and milestones in humanity's exploration of [[outer space]].

<!-- Do not removed the following sentence as it defines what should and should not be listed. -->This timeline generally does not distinguish achievements by a specific country or private company, as it considers humanity as a whole. See otherwise the [[timeline of private spaceflight]] or look for achievements [[List of government space agencies|by each space agency]].

||{{dts|14 April 1970}}
||Farthest distance from Earth traveled by humans until the [[Artemis II]] lunar flyby in 2026.
||[[File:Flag of the United States.svg|20px]] USA (NASA)
||[[Apollo 13]]
|<ref>{{cite book |editor-last=Glenday |editor-first=Craig |editor-link=Craig Glenday|title=Guinness World Records 2010|year=2010|publisher=[[Bantam Books]]|location=New York|isbn=978-0-553-59337-2|url=https://archive.org/details/guinnessworldrec00vari/page/13 |page=13}}</ref>{{NoteTag|The record was set because the Moon was nearly at [[Apsis|its furthest from Earth]] during the mission. Apollo&nbsp;13's unique free return trajectory caused it to go approximately {{convert|100|km|-1|sp=us}} further from the [[Far side of the Moon|lunar far side]] than other Apollo lunar missions, but this was a minor contribution to the record.<ref>{{cite magazine|title=The Elusive Human Maximum Altitude Record|last1=Adamo|first1=Daniel|magazine=Quest: The History of Spaceflight Quarterly|volume=16|issue=4|year=2009|issn=1065-7738|url=http://www.aiaahouston.org/Horizons/ApolloMaxH.pdf|page=37}}</ref> A reconstruction of the trajectory by astrodynamicist Daniel Adamo in 2009 records the furthest distance as {{convert|400046|km|sp=us}} at 7:34&nbsp;pm&nbsp;EST (00:34:13&nbsp;UTC). Apollo 10 holds the record for second-furthest at a distance of {{convert|399806|km|sp=us}}.{{sfn|Adamo|2009|p=41}}}}
